articles.title: 'Los Anillos de Poder' temporada 3 (★★★★☆) aprende de sus errores y arranca más vibrante y oscura que nunca
articles.text:
La serie de El Señor de los Anillos, Los Anillos de Poder, se ha convertido en estos años en el blanco de todas las miradas de los fans de la fantasía. El proyecto nació como uno de los más ambiciosos de la historia de la televisión, con la firme intención de regalar una historia épica y gigantesca en los mundos de la Tierra Media de J.R.R. Tolkien. Sin embargo, la recepción fue bastante más desigual de lo esperado.
El título demostró desde el primer momento su poderío y valor como producción. Una estética espectacular, unas visuales apabullantes... Sin embargo, muchos espectadores la atacaron duramente por ser bastante más lenta y pesada de lo que le pedían a El Señor de los Anillos. Además, por supuesto, de que los más puristas la criticaron con dureza por modificar algunos aspectos del canon.
Sea como sea, lo cierto es que Los Anillos de Poder sigue en marcha en Amazon Prime Video, que acaba de estrenar su temporada 3. Lo ha hecho con cuatro episodios de golpe, para empezar fuerte. Y es que en esta entrega se juegan el todo por el todo. Demostrar que sí son capaces de alcanzar el alto nivel exigido para preparar su gran final en futuras temporadas o terminar de hundirse y dejar las cosas a medias. Vistos esos cuatro primeros capítulos, parece que la balanza cae en el lado bueno.
Los Anillos de Poder se mejora a sí misma
Con este arranque de temporada 3, Los Anillos de Poder ha dejado clara cuál era su misión. Evitar que las críticas sobre su ritmo irregular y pesado volvieran a ahogar la serie. De hecho, no hay ninguna duda de que el equipo creativo quería abiertamente evitar eso a toda costa. Porque ene stos cuatro priemros capítulos no paran de pasar cosas.
La serie tiene acción a raudales, algo de lo que carecía en entregas anteriores salvo en capítulos muy concretos. Aquí hay duelos constantes. La decisión narrativa de dar un salto temporal de 5 años y sumirnos en plena guerra contra Sauron es quizá lo más inteligente que podían haber hecho. Ahora, el Señor Oscuro está tratando de corromper y conquistar toda la Tierra Media y, de paso, forjar su Anillo Único "para gobernarlos a todos". Por su parte, las fuerzas del bien, los pueblos que aún son libres, deben evitar a toda costa que el mal se propague.
Prueba Amazon Prime Video totalmente gratis durante 30 días y disfruta del catálogo completo de la plataforma sin límites. Solo con darte de alta tendrás acceso instantáneo a las mejores películas y series, además de envíos gratis en Amazon y otras ventajas.
Es decir, ya no estamos en los preparativos de la guerra. Estamos totalmente dentro de ella. Por supuesto, Los Anillos de Poder sabe que su historia debe extenderse aún más, por lo que se guarda todavía ciertas cartas que presumiblemente llegarán en próximas entregas. Pero sí que se aprecia, para bien, un pulso mucho más acelerado, más vibrante, más entretenido.
Eso sí, no es perfecta ni mucho menos la temporada 3 de Los Anillos de Poder. Aunque todo fluye de una manera bastante más intensa e interesante, la serie aún peca de algunos de sus errores del pasado. Pese a deshacerse de los pelosos, todavía hay tramas que se hacen más pesadas y aburridas que otras. Es, por ejemplo, el caso de todo lo que sucede en Númenor, donde al título todavía le cuesta encontrar la chispa. También hay algunas escenas donde esa comedia que quiere aliviar la tensión no funciona. Pero esos fallos se compensan de sobra con varios momentos que los fans agradecerán enormemente, como al forja del anillo de Sauron o ciertos encuentros y situaciones muy esperadas.
Sauron se hace con la serie
Como puede leerse ya entre líneas en todo lo escrito encima, hay otro elemento fundamental que hace que el arranque de Los Anillos de Poder sea destacable. Y es que Sauron definitivamente se sitúa en el centro de la trama. El gran villano, uno de los más legendarios de la literatura y el cine, llega a esta nueva entrega en su mejor momento. Es más poderoso que nunca, su fuerza es arrasadora y perversa, ya no se contiene.
Con Sauron ganando aún más peso en la serie, el actor Charlie Vickers se luce como nunca. En temporadas anteriores ya había demostrado su carisma como ese malvado tramposo, a la vez embaucador y temible. Ahora, abraza definitivamente esa segunda cara tétrica y oscura. No era nada fácil asumir un papel como este, pero el actor lleva desde la temporada 1 que da de sobra la talla.
Como consecuencia de todo ello, Los Anillos de Poder se ha vuelto también mucho más oscura y pesimista. La luz de esperanza poco a poco se desvanece de su historia, que nos lleva a la inevitable guerra con el destino de la Tierra Media en juego. especialmente sus geniales e impactantes episodios 3 y 4 son la mejor muestra de ello.
En definitiva, Los Anillos de Poder ha vuelto con fuerza en su temporada 3. Aún comete algunos errores del pasado, pero ha encontrado un ritmo mucho más entretenido y directo, con mucha acción y varios puntos de inflexión que marcan un antes y un después en la historia. Con Sauron como glorioso y maquiavélico motor, la serie abraza la oscuridad como nunca en su primera mitad de temporada. Ojalá no pierda esa garra en las próximas semanas.

articles.title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
If you’re building generative AI solutions, reusable assets can help you stop rebuilding components that already exist: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, document processors, agent scaffolding, and so on. This has a compounding cost: time not spent solving the customer’s actual problem.
This post shows you how to access a curated catalog of 23 production-ready assets from the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services. These assets can reduce your development time from months to weeks, with evidence from companies like DoorDash, Lyft, and Ricoh.
Since 2023, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center has published open source reusable assets. These production-grade building blocks give you a validated foundation to start from instead of a blank file. These assets have powered customer solutions delivering measurable results: 50x increases in testing capacity, 90 percent reductions in engineering hours, and deployment timelines compressed from months to weeks. In this post, you will learn why teams keep rebuilding generative AI components, what makes an asset truly reusable, how companies like DoorDash and Ricoh achieved measurable results by using these assets, and how to access and deploy 23 open source assets from the catalog. For a complete list of all available assets, see the asset catalog at the end of this post.
The problem: Why teams keep rebuilding
Three root causes drive redundant development across generative AI teams:
- No single source of truth – Assets scatter across repositories, wikis, and drives. Builders can’t find what exists, so they rebuild from scratch.
- No quality signal – Without verification of production readiness, security reviews, or maintenance status, builders have no way to trust existing solutions and default to writing their own code.
- No reuse culture – Sharing remains informal and ungoverned. What one team builds stays with that team, and problems get solved repeatedly.
The cost of rebuilding compounds. Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and creates maintenance burden. Even AI-generated code requires production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. These assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, avoiding that verification burden. When teams finally reach production, they’ve spent weeks on undifferentiated heavy lifting, work that should have been reusable from day one. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services resolves this challenge through reusable assets.
What a reusable asset actually is
A reusable asset isn’t a code snippet or a sample. It’s a production-grade, composable building block that implements a discrete generative AI capability. Reusable assets are validated for quality and security before publication. They include clear deployment guides for discoverability and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements. These assets are maintained across their lifecycle.
Examples from the catalog include RAG pipeline components, document ingestion modules, agent scaffolding templates, evaluation frameworks, and prompt management patterns. The assets are tested in production environments, reviewed for security compliance, and refined based on real customer feedback.
This is the difference between a one-off artifact and a building block you can trust.
Real results: Customer success stories
The value of reusable assets isn’t theoretical. Here’s what happens when teams build on proven foundations instead of starting from scratch.
Contact Center GenAI Agent: DoorDash and Lyft
According to the AWS case study, DoorDash built a fully voice-operated self-service generative AI contact center solution using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset. As reported, the solution handles over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency, achieving a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced development time by 50 percent. The team reached live testing readiness in 2 months.
Lyft used the same Contact Center GenAI Agent asset to bring agentic AI to life for riders and drivers, demonstrating the asset’s versatility across different customer engagement models.
The Contact Center GenAI Agent provides automated question answering capabilities for both text and voice channels. It employs a RAG architecture to facilitate multi-turn conversations while maintaining context. The solution integrates with Amazon Connect and uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed RAG capability, for hybrid search and metadata filtering.
Learn more:
GenAI Intelligent Document Processing: Ricoh
Ricoh serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers. These customers process hundreds of thousands of critical documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. As Ricoh scaled to serve more healthcare customers, they needed a standardized, multi-tenant document processing approach. That approach had to onboard new implementations without requiring unique development and tuning for each one.
Using the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset as a foundation, Ricoh built a standardized, multi-tenant solution for automated document classification and extraction. This transformed their document processing from a custom-engineering bottleneck into a scalable, repeatable service.
Results: As documented in the published case study, Ricoh achieved a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly. Engineering hours per deployment dropped by over 90 percent (80 hours to under 5). Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days. The system now processes 1,000 documents in minutes during traffic spikes, delivering over 1,900 potential annual person-hours in savings.
The GenAI IDP Accelerator, introduced in this 2025 blog post, is a scalable, serverless solution for automated document processing and information extraction using AWS services. This system combines optical character recognition (OCR) with generative AI to convert unstructured documents into structured data at scale. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services continuously maintains the assets as well.
Learn more:
- Blog post: AWS GenAI Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) Accelerator
- Blog post: How Ricoh built a scalable intelligent document processing solution on AWS.
- Source Code: accelerated-intelligent-document-processing-on-aws
New assets: Building the future of agentic AI
Reusable assets become more valuable as teams shift focus from infrastructure to business logic. Two recently launched assets demonstrate how reusable building blocks can accelerate the development of next-generation agentic applications.
Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST)
The Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST) is a starter project repository. With FAST, you can quickly deploy a secured React frontend connected to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. In this implementation, FAST uses a React-based frontend with the managed infrastructure of AgentCore to accelerate building full-stack agentic applications from weeks to days.
FAST deploys in under 30 minutes using infrastructure as code (IaC), with built-in integrations for AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, along with Gateway, Code Interpreter, and Observability. Authentication uses Amazon Cognito, configured with enterprise security best practices, and the template is designed for AI-assisted development with extensive documentation and steering docs.
With FAST, you can access a complete reference architecture that shows you how the pieces integrate, with a working full stack application that you can learn from and build upon. With the modular design, you can swap out major components (identity providers, frontend frameworks, hosting solutions, or agent frameworks) as your requirements evolve.
Learn more:
- FullStack AgentCore Solution Template
- Accelerate agentic application development with a full-stack starter template for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Agentic Chatbot Accelerator
The Agentic Chatbot Accelerator is a web application deployment solution that uses the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) for infrastructure as code so you can create agentic chatbots. Built on Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, this solution streamlines the development of agentic chatbot applications.
The accelerator provides rapid deployment using AWS CDK, with scalable agent runtime management through Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It is configurable and extensible for diverse chatbot use cases, with pre-configured patterns for authentication, hosting, and scaling, validated across customer deployments.
Learn more:
Walkthrough: Using an asset from the library
Let’s walk through a concrete example of selecting and using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset from the open source catalog.
Prerequisites
To follow this walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks, Amazon Connect instances, Amazon Bedrock resources, and Amazon Quick Sight dashboards.
- AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured with appropriate credentials.
- An Amazon Connect instance (or permissions to create one).
- Access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet and Anthropic Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock.
- A Jupyter notebook environment for validation testing.
The scenario
You’re building a customer support solution that needs to handle both voice and text interactions, answer questions using your company’s knowledge base, and escalate complex issues to human agents.
Finding the asset
Navigate to Contact Center GenAI Agent on GitHub. The README provides a clear overview of capabilities, architecture, and deployment steps. The following figure shows the solution architecture for the Contact Center GenAI Agent.
Evaluating the asset
The asset includes security-reviewed code with AWS CDK infrastructure as code, integration with Amazon Connect for voice and chat, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed RAG capability, for question answering. An automated testing framework and conversation analytics dashboard are built in.
Responsible-AI controls are integral to the architecture. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces production-grade safety controls, including hallucination detection, content filtering, and topic-level boundaries, making sure agents operate within defined safety parameters from day one.
The repository shows active maintenance, comprehensive documentation, and links to customer success stories (DoorDash, Lyft) that validate production readiness.
Deploying the solution
Deployment follows four steps:
- Clone the repository and install dependencies.
- Deploy two AWS CloudFormation templates: one for the Knowledge Base stack and one for the RAG solution stack.
- Integrate with Amazon Connect using the pre-built contact flows included in the repository.
- Validate the deployment using the included Jupyter notebooks.
The full process takes under an hour. The solution also includes an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard for real-time conversation analytics.
For detailed deployment instructions and prerequisites, see the deployment guide.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources created during this walkthrough. The deployment uses two AWS CloudFormation stacks, so deletion follows the reverse order:
- Delete the RAG solution stack from the AWS CloudFormation console.
- Delete the Knowledge Base stack from the AWS CloudFormation console.
- Remove the Amazon Connect contact flows created during integration.
- Delete the Amazon Quick Sight dashboard and any associated SPICE datasets.
- For detailed cleanup instructions, see the deployment guide.
The outcome
Instead of spending weeks building a contact center solution from scratch, you can deploy a security-reviewed, tested foundation in days. Your team focuses on customizing the knowledge base, refining prompts for your domain, and integrating with your existing systems. This is the high-value work that differentiates your solution.
Potential time saved: 4–6 weeks of development time
What you focus on instead: Domain-specific customization, prompt engineering, business logic integration
Access to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center open source assets
You can access 23 reusable assets as open source on GitHub and AWS Labs. Each asset includes deployment guides, sample code, and documentation to help you get started quickly.
Document processing and extraction
- GenAI Intelligent Document Processing (GenAIDP) – Scalable, serverless solution for automated document processing.
- Multi-lingual Document Processor (MDP) – Transforms complex multi-modal documents into structured text.
- Intelligent Document Processing with Generative AI – Extract information from custom documents.
- Extracting Information From Complex Documents – Hands-on workshop for document extraction.
- Semi-Structured Documents Automatic Pre-Labeling Tool – Automates pre-labeling for Amazon Comprehend.
Contact center and voice
- Contact Center GenAI Agent – Automated question answering for voice and text channels.
- Live Call Analytics with Agent Assist (LCA) – Real-time generative AI for customer and agent voice calls.
- Contact Center: Post Call Analytics (PCA) – Generative AI analysis of post-call recordings.
- Live Meeting Assistant (LMA) – Captures audio from browser-based meetings with transcription and insights.
- Recorded Voice Insight Extraction Webapp (ReVIEW) – Upload recordings and use generative AI to answer questions.
Agentic AI and chatbots
- Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST) – Deploy secured React frontend with AgentCore backend.
- Agentic Chatbot Accelerator – Web application deployment for agentic chatbots.
- Fashion Assistant Agent – Fashion assistant built with Amazon Titan on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
- Natural Language Database Agent – Query databases using natural language with LangGraph.
RAG and knowledge bases
- Deploy Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases using Terraform – Infrastructure as code for Knowledge Bases.
- Leveraging the User to Improve Agents in RAG Use Cases – Custom LangChain tool for conversational RAG.
- Reranker Fine-Tuning and Deployment – Fine-tune BAAI BGE Reranker for improved retrieval.
- Durable Semantic Caching in Amazon MemoryDB – Persistent semantic caching for GenAI applications.
Development and migration
- C to Java Code Conversion – Agentic workflow for legacy code migration.
- OpenAI Migration Framework – Systematic framework for large language model (LLM) migration.
- Fine-tuning ModernBERT for Intent Classification – Create smart LLM routing systems.
Infrastructure and operations
- Bedrock Logging Automation – Automate logging setup for Amazon Bedrock.
- Data Analyst BI – AI-powered business intelligence tool for non-experts.
To get started:
- Select one of the assets listed earlier.
- Review the README and deployment guides for assets relevant to your use case.
- Clone the repository and follow the deployment instructions.
- Customize the asset for your specific requirements.
- Reach out to the AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services team for advisory support.
Conclusion
The cost of rebuilding is real, and it compounds. When teams rebuild RAG pipelines, recreate document processing logic, or start from scratch, those hours add up in engineering time that could have been spent solving actual customer problems.
A curated, validated asset catalog changes the economics of generative AI delivery. Not by doing the work for you, but by making sure you’re not doing work that’s already been done. The 23 open source assets published since 2023 represent thousands of engineering hours, dozens of customer engagements, and countless lessons learned. They’re packaged into building blocks you can deploy today.
The assets are open source. The deployment guides are comprehensive. The customer’s success stories are real. Start with one asset that matches your current challenge. For expert assistance, reach out to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center.

articles.title: Expensive accelerators, no workload-level visibility: Introducing Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights
articles.text:
Expensive accelerators, no workload-level visibility: Introducing Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights
Accelerator bills have become one of the largest lines in the infrastructure budget. GPUs have become the most expensive resource in modern computing, and yet most organizations operate them with little visibility. A single training cluster can run for days and cost millions of dollars. Most organizations pool these accelerators across teams on shared clusters to keep them busy. But in these shared environments, platform teams cannot answer basic questions: which team is using which accelerators? Is the inference workload generating tokens efficiently? What is wasting money?
When a workload degrades (a failing accelerator, a thermally throttled node), teams find out only after a run crashes or the bill arrives. The device-level signals needed to find the cause (request traces, kernel logs, memory metrics from the accelerator itself) are not collected or connected. Without a way to isolate the problem to a single accelerator, teams fall back on cycling the entire instance, surrendering seven healthy GPUs to address a fault on one, and often waiting on scarce capacity to get the instance back.
“GPUs have become the most expensive resource in modern computing, and yet most organizations operate them with little visibility.”
Accelerator observability turns those blind spots into answers. It tells you who is using your accelerators, whether they are healthy, and what the waste is costing you, all the way down to a single device. That way, you fix one bad GPU instead of eight, and spend your accelerator budget on real work instead of idle capacity.
Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights, a new capability launched at KubeCon North America 2026, gives you a single operational view of every accelerator in your fleet. It shows platform and AI teams who are using their GPU and AWS AI Accelerators capacity across Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). In this post, we walk through what accelerated compute insights does, how it works on Amazon EKS, and how to get started.
What accelerated compute insights does
Accelerated compute insights gives you a single operational view of every accelerator in your fleet. It shows how each accelerator is being used, detects failures and bottlenecks as they happen, estimates the cost impact of each problem, and connects those findings to the actions that resolve them.
“Accelerated compute insights holds accelerator telemetry, workload boundaries, and pricing data together, a combination that monitoring tools that only see metrics cannot replicate.”
On Amazon EKS, it supports NVIDIA GPUs and NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium and AWS Inferentia. Metrics from NVIDIA GPUs and Inferentia are normalized into a common schema and presented in a single Accelerator Health view, so teams running mixed fleets manage every accelerator type in one place.
Fleet visibility with Kubernetes context
Every accelerator in your EKS cluster is enriched with Kubernetes metadata: pod, namespace, node, node group, and custom labels (team, application). You see utilization by team and workload across your entire fleet.
Accelerated Compute Insights auto-detects MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) partitioned GPUs and shows utilization and memory for each MIG instance, along with the pod using it. It also recognizes other partitioning schemes, including Kubernetes DRA (dynamic Resource allocation) and time-slicing, by reading device labels. No configuration required.
Cost waste identification
Accelerated compute insights connects real-time accelerator telemetry to workload boundary events and AWS pricing data to surface recoverable waste in three categories:
- Right-sizing opportunities: workloads running on more powerful instances than the task requires.
- Training efficiency gaps: low tensor core (MFU) utilization relative to the workload’s own historical baseline, indicating the job is not getting full value from the hardware.
- Inference below hardware capacity: endpoints serving fewer requests than the hardware supports, based on customer-emitted throughput correlated with device utilization.
For each finding, accelerated compute insights identifies the specific workload or node responsible, helping users troubleshoot and optimize. This works because accelerated compute insights holds accelerator telemetry, workload boundaries, and pricing data together, a combination that monitoring tools that only see metrics cannot replicate.
Note: CloudWatch accelerated compute insights is an operational tool, not a billing or chargeback tool. Cost figures are estimates intended to guide operational decisions. For authoritative cost and usage accounting, continue to use AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report.
Device-level remediation
When an inference workload experiences performance degradation or inefficient token generation, accelerated compute insights helps identify GPU bottlenecks, inefficient accelerator utilization, and potential resource waste. By automatically collecting and correlating inference performance metrics, request traces, logs, and accelerator telemetry, it provides end-to-end visibility into workload performance and GPU efficiency. With AI-powered insights and troubleshooting capabilities, customers can quickly identify root causes, optimize token throughput, reduce inference latency, and improve accelerator utilization without disrupting healthy workloads.
“It distinguishes between failure modes that call for different actions. By default, the agent presents a specific, evidence-backed action plan for you to approve.”
You can also route health events to the AWS DevOps Agent for deeper investigation. The agent reasons across accelerator telemetry, CloudWatch logs, recent infrastructure changes, job configuration, and any runbooks you have authored. It distinguishes between failure modes that call for different actions. For example, a node with an accelerating memory-error trend that needs replacement versus a driver issue that clears with a restart. By default, the agent presents a specific, evidence-backed action plan for you to approve. For a faster loop, you can opt in to let it carry out well-understood remediations through AWS APIs on its own.
How it works on EKS
Collection paths converge at the CloudWatch Metrics API. For NVIDIA GPUs, the CloudWatch agent and NVIDIA Exporter collect device-level metrics. The Unified Accelerator Health Layer normalizes GPU and Inferentia collection paths into a common schema and presents them in a single dashboard.
The diagram below illustrates how Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights provides end-to-end observability for AI inference workloads and accelerator efficiency on Amazon EKS. Customers can install the CloudWatch Observability add-on from the CloudWatch console or CloudWatch Omni to collect NVIDIA GPU metrics and inference workload performance metrics, logs, and traces. The telemetry data is ingested into CloudWatch’s centralized storage through the CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTLP) endpoint. Customers can monitor inference workload performance and GPU utilization directly in the CloudWatch console or leverage CloudWatch Omni and its AI-powered investigation to troubleshoot performance issues, identify accelerator inefficiencies, and optimize resource utilization.
Getting started on EKS
Install the CloudWatch Observability add-on with OTel Container Insights enabled. The add-on discovers your accelerators and collects everything the dashboard needs. No per-node setup, no agents to manage, no collection pipelines to configure. Your fleet appears in the console within minutes and stays current as nodes join and leave the cluster.
Step 1: Get your data flowing
If you run self-hosted inference on Amazon EKS, install or upgrade the Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on to v7.0.1 or above. The add-on discovers every NVIDIA GPU and AWS Inferentia device in your cluster and starts sending OpenTelemetry data, with no per-node setup and no collection pipelines to configure.
You can enable the add-on using eksctl, Helm, or Terraform. Check examples with eksctl and Helm below:
Using eksctl
eksctl create addon \
  --name amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  --cluster your-cluster-name \
  --region your-region
Using Helm
helm repo add aws-observability https://aws-observability.github.io/helm-charts
helm install amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  aws-observability/amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  --namespace amazon-cloudwatch --create-namespace
Step 2: Use your data in CloudWatch Omni
Once telemetry is flowing, open CloudWatch Omni. Omni is built for the teams that own the inference code and fix it. Instead of a wall of infrastructure metrics, you get an application-centric view: your inference workloads appear next to the services and AI agents that call them, with accelerator health, utilization, and waste tied to each workload.
When an endpoint shows low throughput or a high time to first token, Omni helps you trace the problem to the workload, node, or single accelerator responsible and shows what to change, whether that’s a configuration update or a code fix. You can go from detection to fix without switching tools.
“Instead of a wall of infrastructure metrics, you get an application-centric view: your inference workloads appear next to the services and AI agents that call them, with accelerator health, utilization, and waste tied to each workload.”
Platform and infrastructure teams who need a fleet-wide view, such as accelerator allocation across many teams, idle capacity, or a cross-account summary, can also see the same data on the accelerated compute insights page in the CloudWatch console.
Ready to see your own fleet? This documentation walks you through getting started.
Where this fits in the Amazon EKS observability stack
Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights builds on the observability foundation we have been shipping for EKS throughout 2025 and 2026: OTel Container Insights for infrastructure metrics, Application Performance Monitoring for application telemetry, and Container Network Observability for the network layer. Accelerated compute insights adds the missing layer, the accelerators themselves. Teams get GPU and Inferentia utilization, cost waste, and device-level health, all enriched with Kubernetes metadata and connected to automated remediation, in the same place they already monitor everything else
- OTel Container Insights for EKS (GA, June 2026) collects infrastructure metrics from your cluster using OpenTelemetry, with up to 150 descriptive labels per metric and PromQL support in CloudWatch Query Studio.
- Application Performance Monitoring enabled by default (February 2026) in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on gives you application-level telemetry out of the box.
- Container Network Observability (November 2025) provides service maps, flow tables, and network performance metrics for EKS traffic, powered by CloudWatch Network Flow Monitor.
- Observability patterns for AI agents on Amazon EKS (October 2026) documents observability patterns for agentic AI workloads running on EKS.
Getting started today
Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights is available today in all Regions where CloudWatch Omni is available. To get started:
- Install or upgrade to the latest CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on on your cluster.
- Open CloudWatch Omni to see your inference workloads, with accelerator health and waste for each one.
- Troubleshoot and optimize from the workload view, from time to first token down to a single device.
Check out the documentation for more.

articles.title: CyberGhost n'a pas encore dévoilé ses cartes pour le Black Friday, mais son VPN est déjà à prix cassé !
articles.text:
Le Black Friday 2026 approche à grands pas et les promotions sur les VPN commencent à attirer l'attention. Mais faut-il vraiment patienter jusqu'au 27 novembre pour s'équiper ?
CyberGhost propose déjà son abonnement longue durée à partir de 2,19 €/mois, avec une réduction affichée de 83 % par rapport à sa formule mensuelle. Une offre intéressante pour sécuriser ses connexions sans exploser son budget.
Voir l'offre CyberGhost VPN à -83% pour 2,19 €/mois
Pourquoi choisir le VPN de CyberGhost ?
- Un VPN premium à prix réduit : CyberGhost affiche jusqu'à 83 % de réduction sur sa formule longue durée par rapport à l'abonnement mensuel.
- 7 appareils protégés simultanément : sécurisez vos connexions sur ordinateur, smartphone, tablette et appareils compatibles avec un seul abonnement.
- 45 jours satisfait ou remboursé : testez les fonctionnalités du VPN et demandez un remboursement si le service ne vous convient pas, selon les conditions de l'offre.
CyberGhost VPN : une belle réduction avant même le Black Friday
Chaque année, le Black Friday est un rendez-vous incontournable pour les amateurs de bons plans high-tech. Smartphones, ordinateurs, logiciels et services numériques voient leurs prix baisser, et les VPN figurent traditionnellement parmi les produits les plus intéressants à surveiller. CyberGhost n'a pas encore annoncé, dans le cadre de cette offre, de promotion officiellement dédiée au Black Friday 2026. Pourtant, son abonnement de longue durée affiche déjà un tarif particulièrement attractif.
Pour environ 2,19 € par mois, CyberGhost propose néanmoins :
- Une réduction de 83 % par rapport au tarif de son abonnement mensuel.
- Une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 45 jours, pour tester le service dans de bonnes conditions.
- Des serveurs disponibles dans 100 pays, dont certains optimisés pour le streaming, le téléchargement et le jeu en ligne.
- Jusqu'à 7 appareils protégés simultanément, avec un seul compte.
- Un abonnement longue durée avec des mois supplémentaires offerts, selon la formule actuellement proposée.
Attention : le prix mensuel annoncé correspond à une moyenne calculée sur toute la durée promotionnelle. L'abonnement est réglé en une seule fois et se renouvelle ensuite automatiquement selon les conditions indiquées lors de la commande.
Un VPN complet pour protéger sa vie numérique au quotidien
Au-delà de son prix, CyberGhost présente de sérieux arguments pour les internautes soucieux de leur confidentialité. Un VPN permet de chiffrer le trafic entre votre appareil et son serveur, notamment pour sécuriser vos échanges lorsque vous utilisez un réseau Wi-Fi public, dans un hôtel, un aéroport ou un café.
CyberGhost s'appuie notamment sur le protocole WireGuard, reconnu pour son bon équilibre entre sécurité et performances. Le service intègre également un Kill Switch automatique, qui bloque le trafic Internet si la connexion VPN est interrompue. Autre fonctionnalité appréciable : ses serveurs spécialisés. CyberGhost facilite le choix d'une connexion adaptée à différents usages, qu'il s'agisse de regarder des contenus en streaming en déplacement, de télécharger des fichiers ou de jouer en ligne.
Le service applique par ailleurs une politique de non-conservation des journaux d'activité, régulièrement soumise à des audits indépendants.
Enfin, les sept connexions simultanées permettent d'utiliser le VPN sur plusieurs appareils du foyer : PC Windows, Mac, smartphones Android, iPhone, tablettes et certains téléviseurs connectés.
Faut-il attendre le Black Friday pour s'abonner à CyberGhost ?
C'est évidemment la grande question à quelques semaines du rendez-vous commercial de novembre. CyberGhost propose déjà un abonnement de longue durée à un tarif bien inférieur à celui de sa formule mensuelle. Il est donc difficile de savoir si une éventuelle offre du Black Friday permettra de réaliser des économies supplémentaires. Pour les utilisateurs qui souhaitent s'équiper dès maintenant, l'offre actuelle présente néanmoins plusieurs avantages : un tarif mensuel réduit, une couverture pouvant aller jusqu'à 7 appareils et une garantie de remboursement particulièrement généreuse.
Les 45 jours de garantie constituent un argument intéressant : ils permettent de tester réellement le service avant de décider de le conserver, tout en respectant les conditions de remboursement. Il convient toutefois de rappeler qu'il ne s'agit pas d'un essai gratuit : le montant de l'abonnement est acquitté lors de la souscription.
✅ Les points forts
- Un prix particulièrement attractif
- 7 appareils protégés simultanément
- Un vaste réseau international
- Une sécurité complète

articles.title: 30 heures de panne d’électricité : il branche sa maison sur son Renault Scénic et ne perd que 8 % de batterie
articles.text:
Quand on parle de la batterie d’une voiture électrique comme réserve d’énergie, on pense surtout au vehicle-to-grid (V2G), qui renvoie du courant vers le réseau pendant les pics de consommation, ou au vehicle-to-home (V2H), qui alimente directement une maison. Pour la plupart des propriétaires de véhicules électriques, ces deux usages restent relativement abstraits car ils sont peu développés.
En revanche, le vehicle-to-load (V2L), lui, est déjà répandu. Ce mode transforme le port de recharge en prise électrique, et il peut vraiment dépanner en cas de coupure de courant. Nick Gibbs, journaliste d’Automotive News Europe, l’a vérifié à ses dépens pendant ses vacances et raconte son expérience dans un article publié ce mardi 10 novembre. Privé d’électricité pendant 30 heures, il a branché sa maison de location sur son Renault Scénic électrique.
Le V2L du Renault Scénic à la rescousse
Fin octobre, une tempête a frappé le Lake District où la famille louait une maison, mettant à mal les installations électriques et coupant le courant. Les coupures sont rares au Royaume-Uni, et Nick Gibbs reconnaît que la panne l’a d’abord inquiété. Puis il s’est souvenu d’un petit sac livré avec la voiture. Dedans, il y avait un adaptateur (vendu 400 € en accessoire) qui se branche sur le port de recharge et la transforme en prise domestique. Une fois une rallonge branchée, la maison a retrouvé 3,7 kW de puissance électrique.
Seuls les appareils à portée de la rallonge étaient alimentés. Alors que le manuel de Renault déconseille de brancher plusieurs rallonges bout à bout, le journaliste britannique n’a pas voulu tenter le diable pour étendre son réseau de fortune. La famille a donc tout regroupé dans la cuisine : deux réfrigérateurs, plusieurs lampes sur pied, une station de recharge pour les téléphones et même le grille-pain au petit-déjeuner.
Pourquoi le four est resté éteint ?
En relisant le manuel, Nick Gibbs a découvert que le système est limité à 16 ampères. Sur le réseau britannique en 230 volts, ça correspond aux 3,7 kW maximum délivrés par le Scénic. Or, au Royaume-Uni, les fours électriques sont en général raccordés directement à l’installation de la maison, avec un interrupteur dédié, parce qu’ils tirent trop de puissance pour une prise classique. Le dîner s’est donc fait en mode camping, sur la plaque au gaz.
Certains modèles chinois vont plus loin. Le pick-up hybride rechargeable BYD Shark peut fournir jusqu’à 6,6 kW en V2L, de quoi faire tourner un four, une douche électrique et même une pompe à chaleur. Mais il faudrait alors des câbles bien plus adaptés pour supporter une telle charge sans danger.
Pour Nick Gibbs, les 3,7 kW du Scénic sont donc proches de la limite utile avec une rallonge standard. En Europe, les constructeurs vendent d’ailleurs surtout le V2L comme un accessoire de camping, tandis que les fabricants d’utilitaires le présentent comme un remplaçant du groupe électrogène sur des chantiers isolés.
Une panne qui n’a presque rien coûté à la batterie
En 30 heures, la famille a utilisé environ 8 % des 87 kWh du Scénic, soit à peu près 7 kWh. Le seul accroc est venu de la voiture elle-même lorsque le Scénic a coupé automatiquement le courant quand la demande est devenue trop faible. Nick Gibbs explique que son réfrigérateur ne consommait presque plus rien une fois arrivé à température, ce qui a laissé croire à la voiture que plus aucun appareil n’était branché.
Ce qu’il faut prévoir avant la prochaine coupure
Avant de brancher quoi que ce soit, lisez aussi la partie du manuel qui donne la puissance maximale. D’après le journaliste, le seul achat utile est une rallonge d’extérieur renforcée, plus sûre et plus pratique qu’un câble domestique. Pour l’hiver à venir, il compte faire attention à maintenir régulièrement son Scénic chargé à 100 % en cas de coups durs.

articles.title: Nigerian agri-tech startup Bridge Merchant connects smallholder farmers to institutional buyers - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian agri-tech startup Bridge Merchant is combining a network of rural agents, storage infrastructure and its own technology platform to link smallholder farmers more efficiently with processors, manufacturers and other institutional buyers.
Founded in 2020 by CEO Chinwendu Nweke, Bridge Merchant began as an agricultural trading and aggregation business before evolving into a tech-enabled supply chain company. It is now led by a four-person founding team, with six core employees and a network of more than 1,300 rural agents, around 65 per cent of whom are women.
“Bridge Merchant was established after I saw first-hand how much value farmers were losing, not necessarily because they could not produce, but because the infrastructure between production and the market was fragmented,” Nweke told Disrupt Africa.
The startup’s platform, Aladinn Agro, is used alongside its field network to onboard and verify farmers, map farms, aggregate produce, manage quality and traceability, and coordinate logistics. Bridge Merchant works mainly with staple commodities such as maize, soybeans, paddy rice, sorghum, millet and beans, as well as selected export and agricultural by-product value chains.
“We realised that Nigeria does not necessarily have a production problem alone; it also has a significant market-access and agricultural infrastructure problem,” said Nweke. “A farmer can produce successfully and still lose income because there is inadequate storage, fragmented demand, poor logistics, quality inconsistencies or no reliable buyer available at the right time.”
At the other end of the chain, processors and large buyers struggle to source consistent volumes of traceable, quality-controlled commodities from thousands of fragmented smallholders. Bridge Merchant aims to solve both problems at once.
Nweke said the startup faces competition from other agricultural marketplaces, aggregators, commodity traders and supply chain technology companies. It differentiates itself by integrating the digital and physical layers of the supply chain rather than solving only one part of the problem.
“The real challenge is building a system that works reliably in rural communities where connectivity, storage, logistics and trust remain major constraints,” Nweke said.
Bridge Merchant has engaged more than 10,000 farmers and aggregated more than 20,000 tonnes of agricultural commodities to date. It has access to around 3,000 tonnes of partner warehousing capacity and has deployed three solar-powered storage units in northern Nigeria.
“The strongest indication of uptake for us is repeat demand. Farmers and agents continue to work with us because we provide access to structured markets, while institutional buyers return because they need reliable aggregation, quality control and fulfilment at scale,” said Nweke.
The startup makes most of its money from commodity aggregation and trade, earning a margin between procurement and final sale on transactions where it acts as principal. On larger transactions it facilitates without taking ownership of the commodity, it earns commissions of between two and five per cent.
The startup has grown mainly through operating revenue, founder capital, grants and non-dilutive funding, and has received support from organisations including Acumen, Heifer International, Standard Chartered Foundation, Access Bank and Sahara Group Foundation. It is now progressing towards institutional debt financing to boost its working capital for commodity aggregation.
“Agricultural commodity transactions are capital intensive. A business can have farmers ready to supply and buyers ready to purchase but still be unable to execute the transaction because it does not have enough capital to bridge procurement and buyer payment,” Nweke said.
Bridge Merchant has built a presence across 16 Nigerian states over time, and is currently focusing its expansion on major production corridors in Kaduna, Niger, Benue and Nasarawa states. Nweke said the immediate priority is to deepen operations in Nigeria, but the model could eventually extend to other West African markets facing similar challenges.
“Our ambition is to build agricultural supply-chain infrastructure that can work across borders while remaining deeply connected to local farming communities,” Nweke said.

articles.title: CERT-In flags critical security flaws, urges Chrome users in India to update browsers
articles.text:
CERT-In flags critical security flaws, urges Chrome users in India to update browsers
One of the reported vulnerabilities is already being actively exploited in real attacks, the cyber security agency has warned.
India's cyber security agency has advised Google Chrome users to update their browsers immediately, warning of multiple critical security vulnerabilities, which could let attackers take control of their device.
One of the reported vulnerabilities is already being actively exploited in real attacks, the agency said.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) published the advisory, Vulnerability Note CIVN-2026-0544, on November 10, 2026 and rated it "critical".
The note covers Chrome versions older than 157.0.8103.50, as well as Chrome Extended Stable versions older than 156.0.8078.96. It lists several separate weaknesses across the browser. They include a use-after-free fault in its XML handling, type confusion in the V8 JavaScript engine, and out-of-bounds memory writes in the GPU component. The agency also names incorrect authorisation in the FileSystem component, a buffer overflow in Compositing, and uninitialised resource bugs in WebGL and the GPU.
According to CERT-In, an attacker would only need to persuade a victim to open a specially crafted webpage. A successful attack could allow arbitrary code to run on the machine, get around the browser's security restrictions, or trigger a denial-of-service condition. The agency describes the risk of code execution and system compromise as high.
The advisory singles out one flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, as being actively exploited in the wild. For that reason, CERT-In says users should apply the latest patches without delay. Its recommended fix is to install the updates released by Google.
Updating takes a few moments. Users have to open Chrome, click the three-dot menu at the top right, go to Help, and choose 'About Google Chrome'.
The browser will check for and download any available update, after which it needs to be relaunched to complete the installation. Until then, users are advised to avoid suspicious links and unfamiliar websites, particularly if they are running an older version.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes audio issues caused by September security updates
articles.text:
Microsoft says the November 2026 cumulative updates resolve USB audio issues plaguing Windows users who have installed security updates released since September.
The company explained, when it acknowledged this known issue days after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday, that USB Audio Class 1.0 devices failed to start or produce audio on some systems after installing recent updates.
Some affected users reported seeing no audio output, unresponsive volume controls and sound settings, and "This device cannot start (Code 10)." errors in Device Manager, while others said the impacted USB audio speakers fail only when using multichannel audio features, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes.
These audio issues affect both server (Windows Server 2012 and later) and client (Windows 10 and Windows 11) systems.
Microsoft released out-of-band updates on September 14 to fix the symptoms experienced on devices using 8-channel or 3D audio modes and has now addressed the remaining issues in security updates released as part of this month's Patch Tuesday.
"The symptoms are resolved in the Windows security update released on November 10, 2026 (KB5132061) and later updates," Microsoft said in a Windows release health dashboard update.
"We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one."
While Microsoft has yet to provide an official workaround for those who can't immediately install the November 2026 security updates, some users have restored audio on affected Windows PCs by switching to 2-channel mode.
Previous audio issues affecting Windows systems
Two years ago, Microsoft also confirmed an issue that caused game audio to unexpectedly increase to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems and blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on systems with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers due to blue screen of death (BSOD) issues.
In January 2025, Microsoft addressed a similar issue triggered by the KB5050094 optional preview cumulative update, which caused audio playback issues and Code 10 errors on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers.
More recently, in September 2025, it lifted a safeguard hold preventing Windows 11 24H2 upgrades on systems with Dirac audio improvement software because compatibility issues caused Bluetooth speakers and headsets to malfunction.
With the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft also resolved Outlook sign-in and mail delivery issues on Exchange Server systems triggered by the October 2026 Windows Server security updates.

articles.title: Javier Calvo: “A la gente le llama la atención que una película como La bola negra se haya podido hacer con menos de 15 millones de euros, pero se ha podido hacer porque tiene dos directores”
articles.text:
“La han podido hacer dos personas”, contesta Javier Calvo cuando alguien le pregunta por qué se ha podido rodar “La bola negra” con un presupuesto inferior a los 15 millones de euros. El director atribuye la posibilidad de rodarla con ese presupuesto a trabajar en pareja con Javier Ambrossi. Podían cubrir las necesidades. Ambrossi se encarga de esto y Calvo de aquello. Y así van avanzando.
Un director no podría ocuparse solo de todo ese trabajo porque tiene muchas otras cosas que hacer. Ocurre, por ejemplo, con la selección de figurantes.
A los extras los han ido seleccionando uno a uno. Ellos querían que fueran diferentes en las tres líneas de la historia. Han visto vídeos y han hecho castings. Han seleccionado a miles de personas. Mientras Ambrossi estaba haciendo esto, Calvo estaba preparando el día siguiente con la dirección de fotografía.
Dos directores para una película en tres épocas
La acción transcurre en tres momentos distintos (1932, 1937 y 2017), según la ficha oficial del Festival de Cannes. Está basada en parte de la obra inacabada de Federico García Lorca y en “La piedra oscura” de Alberto Conejero. Se ha rodado en 12 semanas en España y Grecia.
También es fácil verlo en las escenas colectivas. Una secuencia con Penélope Cruz ha tenido 500 figurantes. En Granada se han utilizado hasta 250 disfrazados de la época para recrear la ciudad de 1932.
Además de Penélope Cruz y Glenn Close, el reparto está formado por Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes y Lola Dueñas. Las productoras detrás son Suma Content Films, El Deseo, Movistar Plus+ y Le Pacte (info de la productora).
En cuanto al presupuesto, hay que detenerse en algunas cuestiones. Los 9,9 millones de euros que aparecen en la resolución de ayudas del Instituto de la Cinematografía y de las Artes Audiovisuales corresponden a la parte española de la coproducción. Es decir, no es el total del coste de producción y de promoción y distribución.
La taquilla y la venta de derechos
El 27 de octubre de 2026 tenía 34,3 millones de euros de taquilla. Además, había vendido más de cinco millones de entradas en España y se situaba en el cuarto puesto de recaudación de las películas españolas en salas nacionales.
El primer día de taquilla fue de 1,32 millones. También creció en el segundo fin de semana sobre el primero. El 17 de octubre, en su cuarto fin de semana en cartel, tenía un acumulado de 28,6 millones.
El salto internacional empezó con Netflix, que compró los derechos para Norteamérica después de su paso por Cannes (los Javis han ganado el premio de dirección ex aequo). Se ha calculado que la venta ha sido de unos cinco millones de dólares.
También ha sido galardonada por el público en Toronto y Sídney. Mantener los pies en la tierra y ser metódicos es lo que ha defendido Calvo después de recibir el Premio del Público en San Sebastián. Por su parte, Ambrossi ha dicho: “Estamos los dos juntos en esta aventura y eso siempre lleva a casa”.

articles.title: Broken: LearnArk’s mission to make tech truly accessible
articles.text:
When Adedolapo Oguntayo-Williams arrived at a conference hosted by one of Nigeria’s premier banks in 2024, she was pushing her daughter in a stroller. There was no ramp. If a multi-billion-naira financial institution could overlook something as fundamental as a wheelchair pathway, what chance did persons with disabilities have inside Africa’s digital economy? She stopped waiting for corporate panels to figure it out. From childhood dreams of the cockpit and washing dishes in Cyprus on a state scholarship, to negotiating vendor contracts for Ruff ‘n’ Tumble and running global cybersecurity compliance remotely from Abule Egba, Lagos, Adedolapo’s career has never followed a straight line. Now, she is using that enterprise playbook to bootstrap LearnArk Inclusion Academy—a tuition-free tech training engine designed to move deaf, blind, and physically impaired talent from the margins into high-value tech roles. “Inclusion had to go beyond conversations and good intentions,” she tells TechCabal. “It had to translate into access, opportunities, and the ability for people to build independent lives.” In this edition of My Life in Tech, JOHN ADOYI charts Adedolapo Oguntayo-Williams’s journey from industrial engineering to building digital ramps for Africa’s most overlooked talent.
In 2024, when Adedolapo Oguntayo-Williams, an inclusion educator and technology advocate, arrived at a conference hosted by one of Lagos’s leading commercial banks, she was pushing her daughter in a stroller. There was no accessible pathway for them.
An industrial engineer by training, she had spent years in business analysis and product management, learning to scrutinise operational problems and understand whom they affect. The experience stayed with her. “If a leading financial institution could overlook something as fundamental as an accessible pathway, what would the situation be like in many other public spaces?” she remembers thinking.
The incident prompted her to examine physical and digital accessibility wherever she went. More often than not, she observed that persons with disabilities were largely overlooked. She began asking what she could do to change that.
“I knew I could not solve Nigeria’s wider accessibility challenges on my own, but I could contribute in an area I understood: education and technology,” she says.
Her answer was the LearnArk Inclusion Academy, a free technology training programme for persons with disabilities offered through her edtech platform, LearnArk. “For me, inclusion had to go beyond conversations and good intentions. It had to translate into access, opportunities, and the ability for people to build independent lives.”
It is the latest chapter in a career that began with a very different ambition.
From a childhood dream to Cyprus
Oguntayo-Williams once aspired to become a pilot, drawn to aviation and the prospect of seeing the world from a distinct vantage point. At the time, women were rarely seen in the cockpit, which made the career path even more compelling. “I wanted to be the different one. I wanted to go into a field where there were not a lot of women,” she says.
By her fifth year in secondary school, she and her mother had begun researching aviation colleges in Nigeria. They found one in Zaria, Kaduna State, in north-west Nigeria, but the tuition was well beyond what her family could afford. She pivoted towards petroleum engineering and applied to the University of Lagos, but was offered an alternative course instead.
“You know how the Nigerian university thing is, where you apply to study something and they offer you something else. Obviously, I wasn’t having it,” she says.
An alternative route emerged through her pastor’s wife, whose son had secured admission to a university in Cyprus. She shared the institution’s prospectus with Oguntayo-Williams’s mother; industrial engineering was the closest discipline to petroleum engineering on offer.
“As God would have it, I gained admission to Eastern Mediterranean University to study industrial engineering,” she says. In 2012, at the age of 16, she left Nigeria for Cyprus.
“My university experience was honestly amazing,” she says.
In 2013, she was awarded the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) State Scholarship, which included a monthly stipend. That same year, she enrolled in business administration as a second major, eventually graduating top of her class in her department.
University also afforded her the latitude to explore broader entrepreneurial pursuits. During her second year, Oguntayo-Williams founded Deroy Consults, organising entrepreneurship seminars to encourage undergraduates to look beyond traditional degrees and build viable enterprises.
“Looking back, I am particularly proud that I did not limit my university experience to writing examinations and graduating,” she says. “I genuinely took advantage of the opportunities around me.”
Studying abroad also transformed her outlook on education and equity. Engaging with peers from diverse backgrounds in an unfamiliar academic environment demonstrated how access to quality education can expand what individuals believe they can accomplish.
“Most importantly, it gave me the confidence to see myself as someone who could contribute beyond my immediate environment,” she says.
She began reflecting on young people in Nigeria who possessed the intellect and drive to excel, but lacked comparable access to global opportunities. Although she was not yet certain how to act on that realisation, the thought remained with her.
“I left university with a broader understanding of what was possible, and a strong conviction that education should not merely prepare you for employment; it should equip you to create opportunities, solve systemic problems, and make an impact.”
Finding her footing in the workplace
After graduating in 2016, Oguntayo-Williams moved to the United States, working as a paralegal secretary in Brooklyn, New York. By 2017, however, she had returned to Nigeria.
A friend establishing a management consulting practice hired her as its director of marketing on a salary of ₦50,000 a month (around $140 at the prevailing 2017 exchange rate). She remained there for nine months.
“I didn’t want to stay at home, and I didn’t want to be a broke babe. Imagine being exposed to a lot of money in Cyprus and America, then coming back with no money,” she says.
In 2018, she left and joined Ruff ‘n’ Tumble, a Nigerian children’s fashion and apparel brand, first as an executive assistant and later as a buyer. The company had vendors in Turkey, and its founder, Adenike Ogunlesi, was looking for someone who could speak Turkish.
Oguntayo-Williams says she had learned the language while studying in Cyprus, where she lived on the Turkish side of the island.
“While I was in school, I took jobs in cafes as a dishwasher and waitress. Interacting with local people helped me pick up the language quickly,” she says.
At Ruff ‘n’ Tumble, she worked directly with Ogunlesi, whose approach shaped how she approached business. She recalls how the founder reacted whenever she came to her office without a pen and notebook.
“Sometimes I would go to her office without a pen and a book, and she would shout at me. She would say, ‘Your brain is not to jot down notes; your brain is to think.’ That scared me. I made sure I always had a pen and a book with me,” she says.
Ogunlesi also taught her to read beyond the subjects she naturally enjoyed and introduced her to negotiation. Those lessons have remained useful throughout her career.
“The skills I learned while working with Mrs Ogunlesi have been instrumental in everything I do,” she says. “Whether I am hiring, doing business or working in my current role at ShortPoint.”
Moving into technology
In 2019, Oguntayo-Williams left Ruff ‘n’ Tumble to join AXA Mansard as a business transformation analyst. A contact at the insurance and asset management group informed her of its transformation programme, which targeted first-class graduates, and urged her to apply.
“He told me, ‘Girl, you are a first-class graduate. I think you are perfect for this job.’ I said, ‘Put me on.’ I sent my CV, attended the interview, and got the job,” she says.
At AXA, she worked on core internal restructuring, replacing legacy manual workflows with automated digital systems. She describes the remit as an intersection of business analysis, product management, and process optimisation.
The company invested heavily in professional development, and she complemented internal training by pursuing external technical certifications independently.
“Beyond the training they provided, I took more courses, earned certifications, and kept improving myself,” she says.
AXA provided her initial formal grounding in enterprise technology and delivered her first industry credential, clarifying the operational landscape across the digital economy.
In August 2020, Oguntayo-Williams left AXA and joined ShortPoint, a global software company that develops tools for building and customising corporate intranet websites, as an associate product manager. Her experience in business transformation, alongside the additional courses and certifications she had pursued, helped her secure the role, and she worked remotely from her mother’s home in Abule Egba, Lagos.
“I would never have thought that I could be in Lagos and be working for someone in another continent,” she says.
Within a year, she was promoted to product manager, directing software development cycles from conception to release. By 2023, she transitioned into cybersecurity and compliance, taking charge of the company’s governance and information security operations.
The pivot carried significant regulatory responsibilities, but her grounding in product design and systems architecture gave her the requisite technical foundation.
“Cybersecurity and compliance deepened my focus on what allows organisations to innovate responsibly: protecting information, managing risk, and building trust,” she explains.
In January 2026, she broadened her remit further by assuming responsibilities as human resources manager.
“My experience has really been amazing. I’ve learned a lot, and I’ve been able to excel working with colleagues from diverse countries and nationalities. My interpersonal and leadership capabilities have matured considerably,” she says.
Building LearnArk
The conceptual framework for LearnArk originated during Oguntayo-Williams’s undergraduate years in Cyprus. Experiencing how an international academic environment unlocked professional mobility made her consider the millions of young Africans unable to study abroad who nonetheless warranted high-calibre instruction.
Her initial model was an online portal where accredited universities could deliver subsidised or tuition-free courses to African students. She initiated discussions with Rutgers University, while Eastern Mediterranean University agreed to supply curriculum content. She hired a software engineer and deployed her personal savings to construct the architecture.
“Eventually, I had to pause the project because I could not sustain it financially,” she admits.
In 2023, while on maternity leave, she re-evaluated the concept. Years of informally mentoring aspiring technology professionals had revealed that the primary obstacle was not access to academic theory, but navigating the transition into formal employment.
“People were eager to learn, but finding structured learning opportunities, practical guidance, mentorship, and a clear pathway to employment was difficult,” she says.
That deficit defined LearnArk’s strategic pivot. Shifting away from an academic marketplace, she restructured the venture around practical, industry-aligned technical instruction.
“I wanted to address the gap between wanting to enter technology and knowing how to take practical steps towards a career,” she says. “People can find lots of information online, but they still struggle to understand which pathway fits them, what skills are required, and how to apply what they learn in a commercial environment.”
LearnArk now runs structured cohorts in product management, data analytics, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies, augmented by interview coaching and recruitment placement support.
“LearnArk has trained more than 1,000 learners, which is an important milestone, but I want us to deepen how we track outcomes: whether learners secure roles, apply their skills in the workplace, or advance within their respective disciplines,” she says.
Building an inclusive pathway into technology
Central to this mandate is the LearnArk Inclusion Academy, through which Oguntayo-Williams delivers tuition-free virtual technology instruction to persons with disabilities.
“We designed the academy to make technology education genuinely accessible to individuals with physical disabilities, visual impairments, and hearing impairments,” she says.
Candidates register via the portal, specifying their preferred tracks and accessibility requirements. The operational team and mentors provide specialised support throughout the cohort, while the organisation works to scale up its closed-captioning capabilities and sign-language interpretation.
“I have been bootstrapping the academy from inception. There are real costs attached to providing learner support, upgrading accessibility tools, and expanding our intake,” she says. “We are open to strategic partnerships, institutional grants, and technical resources that will help us scale our reach without compromising our commitment to zero tuition fees.”
Her underlying objective remains straightforward.
“For me, the real measure of success is not simply the number of people we enrol, but whether the academy enables individuals who have historically faced structural barriers to acquire skills, secure viable opportunities, and participate meaningfully in the technology ecosystem,” she says.
Balancing work, family and purpose
For Oguntayo-Williams, one of the hardest lessons of building a career and a business while raising a family was learning that she could not do everything at once.
After experiencing burnout, she realised she could not keep relying on motivation or assume she had to do everything herself to prove her commitment. The experience changed how she approaches work. She now plans her week ahead, prioritises fewer tasks, delegates where possible and sets clearer boundaries.
“I no longer see being constantly busy as proof of impact,” she says. “I want to build things that create real value and can continue to grow without requiring me to sacrifice every other part of my life to keep them going.”
Over the next year, she wants to strengthen LearnArk’s learning pathways, build more industry partnerships and create better opportunities for learners to turn their training into employment and career progression. She also hopes to expand the Inclusion Academy, so more people with disabilities can access technology education, mentorship and opportunities in the digital economy.
Ultimately, Oguntayo-Williams wants to be remembered for more than the positions she held or organisations she built.
“I want to be remembered for the doors I helped open, the systems and policies I helped improve, and the people whose lives became different because I chose to make a contribution,” she says.

articles.title: Un vecino de Salamanca se puso a lanzar bolas de papel mojado desde un sexto piso. Ahora se enfrenta a una multa publicada en el BOE
articles.text:
Todavía recuerdo las clases donde más de uno y más de dos mojaban una bolita de papel, la introducían en el tubo vacío de un boli y, a modo de cerbatana, la proyectaban sobre el cuello o la mochila de algún cándido estudiante que ni sabía por dónde le había llegado el ataque. Ahora imagina esto a escala más “industrial”.
Hace un par de meses, una patrulla de la Policía Local de Salamanca vio a alguien lanzar bolas de papel mojado desde la terraza de un sexto piso. Las bolas caían cerca de la terraza de un bar y salpicaban. Ahí quedó la cosa, ¿no? No: semanas más tarde, el Ayuntamiento publicó en el BOE una propuesta de sanción al vecino, cazado con 751 euros. No es ninguna broma y tiene un precedente jurídico.
Qué pasó. El lanzamiento partió de una vivienda en la calle Bordadores. Las bolas llegaron a las inmediaciones de la terraza de un establecimiento de hostelería. Este estaba en la calle Condes de Crespo Rascón. La notificación no precisa cuántas fueron, no habla de heridos ni daños y no cita a vecinos o peatones afectados. Pero la broma fue cazada por la Policía Local, quienes advirtieron la escena e identificaron al presunto autor. Hasta hay un precedente de 200 euros por una situación análoga.
Y si hubiera caído algo más duro. El Código Civil prevé otro tipo de multa para quien arroja objetos más contundentes. Su artículo 1910 dice que quien habita una casa responde de los daños causados por las cosas que se arrojen o caigan de ella. No hablamos de banderas ni de tejas, que casi siempre son fruto de accidentes. Hablamos de un “agua va” malintencionado o sortear de milago como por desgracia me consta, un pañal bomba. El Supremo lo aplica a propietarios, inquilinos e incluso negocios. Aquí nadie reclama por daños, pero deja meridianamente claro por qué tirar objetos desde un piso nunca es un juego.
Por qué una multa. El Ayuntamiento aplica el artículo 11 de su Ordenanza Municipal de Limpieza Urbana y Gestión de Residuos. Prohíbe arrojar a la vía pública “todo tipo de residuos u objetos de pequeña entidad”. Una bola de papel encaja porque la ley de residuos define como residuo cualquier objeto que su poseedor desecha o tiene intención de desechar. Mojado o no, da igual. Y ojo porque la ordenanza califica la conducta de grave.
Por qué 751. Aquí está el dato curioso: la Ley de Bases del Régimen Local permite a los ayuntamientos sancionar el incumplimiento de sus ordenanzas, pero establece un techo económico. Las multas leves llegan hasta 750 euros. Las graves, hasta 1.500. Las muy graves, hasta 3.000. Por eso las graves arrancan en 751. Un euro más que la leve más cara, porque no se aprecia reincidencia ni agravantes, pero sí malas intenciones.
Qué decide la gravedad. La ley estatal siempre fija los criterios generales, gradúa las infracciones según la intensidad de cuánto se perjudica a la salubridad o qué daños se infringen al ornato público. Pero cada ordenanza concreta qué conducta cae en cada escalón. En Salamanca, tirar algo de pequeña entidad ya es grave. Getafe, por ejemplo, prevé hasta 1.500 euros por tirar pipas, chicles o colillas, al techo de lo grave.
Cuándo sería muy grave. La ley reserva el multazo de hasta 3.000 euros a perturbaciones relevantes de la convivencia. Por ejemplo, las que afectan de forma grave, inmediata y directa a la tranquilidad o a los derechos de otras personas. Pintarrajear un escaparate o reventarlo ya es delito. En cualquier situación, los ayuntamientos solo pueden sancionar así cuando no existe una norma sectorial específica que ya regule la materia.
Las fechas. Los hechos son del 3 de septiembre y el informe se emitió el 28 de septiembre. Entretanto, la comisión de Medio Ambiente lo ha estado analizando. Como la notificación no pudo entregarse en el domicilio indicado, el Ayuntamiento recurrió al BOE. También es de Salamanca el vecino que montó una piscina en un patio de luces sin pedir permiso y también se hubo de recurrir al BOE. Es lo que prevé la Ley de Procedimiento Administrativo cuando no se localiza al interesado. Entre los hechos y el análisis en comisión han pasado casi dos meses: ahora el vecino tiene 10 días para presentar alegaciones. Pasado el plazo llegará la resolución.
¿Multa firme? No, no que se publicó es una propuesta dentro de un expediente sancionador. El vecino puede alegar, aportar pruebas o negar los hechos. La misma ley contempla reducciones: si el infractor reconoce su responsabilidad o paga de forma voluntaria antes de la resolución, la sanción baja. Cada reducción es de al menos el 20 %, y se pueden sumar. En este caso, 751 euros quedarían en unos 601 con una de ellas y en unos 451 con las dos. Poca cuantía, papel mojado.
