articles.title: Managing performing assets when VC fund lifecycles expire
articles.text:
Conversations about venture exits usually start with the portfolio company. Is the business ready? Is there a buyer? Yet as a fund ages, another question becomes equally critical: how long can the vehicle holding the company afford to wait?
The Stears–Ventures Platform Africa Venture Capital Exit & Liquidity Report tracks 181 verified VC-backed exits across Africa between 2011 and 2026. However, for a fund manager, the primary challenge rarely lies in underperforming investments. Instead, it stems from performing companies that retain meaningful upside but no longer align with the fund’s remaining life. This misalignment transforms an exit-timing issue into a residual portfolio paradox.
Market responses are beginning to emerge. For instance, GIZ’s ICAMA Initiative, alongside MEDA in Q3 2026, explores a Pan-African Secondary Fund for performing, de-risked late-stage assets. The core structural mismatch is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: an investor may reach the end of a fund’s lifecycle before a company’s value can be realised on appropriate terms. This raises a fundamental question: what happens when the fund runs out of time before that value crystallises?
The three clocks
It is helpful to evaluate an investment across three concurrent timelines: The Company Clock represents the time required for a business to achieve the scale, profitability, or market position necessary to support a liquidity event. The Market Clock reflects the time required for a credible buyer, a suitable transaction structure, and an acceptable price to converge. The Fund Clock dictates how much time the investment vehicle has, contractually and economically, to maintain and realise the holding.
These timelines frequently diverge. In African venture capital, value creation and business development often require extended horizons. Continued company performance alone cannot resolve liquidity constraints if the investor reaches the fund’s final years without established exit pathways. An asset may remain fundamentally attractive even as its underlying vehicle becomes ill-suited to support its required holding period.
When the fund becomes the constraint
Consider a $100 million fund in its eighth year with $75 million invested. Of that, $15 million has been written off. A further $35 million has been realised, bringing total realised capital to $80 million, while the remaining $25 million of invested capital is valued at $120 million.
These remaining assets are not merely a long tail to be cleared out as the fund reaches maturity. They are material to its overall outcome and may require an additional two to three years to deliver full value. At this stage, contractual life and economic reality diverge: while legal documentation may permit continued holding, management fee step-downs often collide with ongoing reporting, audit, and governance costs.
A forced sale is rarely the optimal solution. Divesting prematurely forfeits potential upside, while selling under temporal pressure frequently compromises transaction terms. This encapsulates the Residual Portfolio Paradox: high-value assets become ill-fitted to their holding vehicles when optimal execution horizons exceed the fund’s contractual lifecycle.
While fund extensions and secondary transactions offer remedies, their efficacy drops significantly when introduced reactively near the end of a fund’s term.
As fund managers scale, launching subsequent vehicles can provide platform-level support for maturing funds, allowing ownership decisions to be deferred. However, repeating this practice across vintages leaves older funds accumulating unliquidated assets. Over time, this overhang becomes a major fundraising liability, as LPs evaluate actual capital returned and wind-down progress alongside gross performance metrics.
Create optionality before the clock runs out
The objective is not to force every company to exit before year ten, but to proactively map out ownership trajectories while maintaining strategic flexibility. General Partners (GPs) should systematically evaluate realistic asset timelines, remaining fund life, and vehicle suitability. Identifying timeline divergence early ensures adequate operational runway to execute strategic solutions.
Establishing this optionality window enables a manager to retain assets, execute exits as market conditions dictate, or transition holdings into specialised continuation structures. Initiatives such as the proposed Pan-African Secondary Fund provide crucial liquidity mechanisms while preserving upside for incoming investors.
Fund expiry should never be the moment when a GP discovers that high-performing assets require extended holding periods. Long before reaching maturity, managers should have clear frameworks determining which assets to hold, transition, or realise.
Ultimately, the most challenging residual asset is rarely the one without market demand. It is the recognised, high-value asset whose fund ran out of time before its value could be fully realised.
Hafeez Bakare leads Fund Operations at Ventures Platform. A chartered accountant with deep private equity and real estate fund management expertise, he supports portfolio company valuations (DCF, multiples, comparables), oversees cross-border audits, liquidity forecasting and multi-jurisdictional compliance, and delivers strategic insight through rigorous financial reporting, scenario analysis and KPI-driven evaluation.

articles.title: Más de 30 años: un programador muestra el programa más antiguo que todavía funciona en Windows 11
articles.text:
Si alguna vez te has preguntado hasta dónde llega la compatibilidad de Windows, un desarrollador que firma como Enlyth ha intentado responderlo buscando la aplicación con interfaz gráfica más antigua que todavía arranca en Windows 11 sin emulación ni modificaciones. El autor lo cuenta en su blog, donde apunta a que la búsqueda acabó a principios de los noventa, aunque con un poco de trampa puede llegar a retrasarse más atrás.
Sin sitio para los 16 bits. Windows 11 no puede ejecutar programas de 16 bits. Y es que, según la documentación de compatibilidad de Microsoft, las versiones x64 y ARM de Windows no admiten código x86 de 16 bits de ningún tipo, así que cualquier candidato tiene que ser una aplicación de 32 bits. Eso lleva a los inicios de Windows NT, cuya primera versión, Windows NT 3.1, salió el 27 de julio de 1993 como sistema de 32 bits.
Un solitario de 1993. Pero hay un atajo que adelanta un poco el reloj. Como explica en la misma entrada, en un foro anónimo alguien le habló de Win32s, unas bibliotecas que permitían ejecutar aplicaciones de 32 bits sobre Windows 3.1, o sea que hacían de puente entre las dos épocas. Las primeras versiones de Win32s traían el FreeCell, y la copia que encontró, del 22 de febrero de 1993, funciona en Windows 11 sin tocar nada.
Un reproductor de CD de 1992. El desarrollador siguió buscando en versiones preliminares de Windows NT 3.1 hasta dar con el reproductor de CD de la compilación 347, enlazado el 16 de noviembre de 1992, que también arranca en Windows 11. Eso sí, como su ordenador no tiene lector de CD, al abrirlo aparece un aviso de que no hay ninguna unidad de CD-ROM, así que para comprobar que reproduce música tiró de una pequeña biblioteca que emula la unidad con audio falso, según detalla el propio autor.
Hay un truco para ir más atrás en el tiempo. Para ir más atrás hay que saltarse las reglas del experimento. Con otvdm, una adaptación de Wine para programas de 16 bits que permite ejecutarlos en Windows de 64 bits, Enlyth consiguió jugar en Windows 11 al Reversi de Windows 1.01, fechado el 15 de noviembre de 1985. Es la versión para ordenador de un juego de tablero de la década de 1880 que se atribuye a Lewis Waterman, aunque el autor admite que recurrir a otvdm es como hacer trampas.
Por lo tanto, sin ayudas ni pequeñas trampas el programa más antiguo que ha logrado hacer funcionar en Windows 11 tiene unos 34 años, pero si recurre a la adaptación de Wine que ha utilizado para añadir una capa de compatibilidad la cifra va hasta los 41 años.
Foto | enlyth.com

articles.title: Bitdefender a retiré Internet Security : voici ce qui change vraiment
articles.text:
Bitdefender Internet Security en 2026 : remplacé par Total Security, que choisir ?
Entre les faux emails de livraison, les liens bancaires frauduleux, les réseaux Wi-Fi publics et les fichiers téléchargés trop vite, la sécurité d’un PC ne se joue plus seulement sur la présence d’un antivirus. Bitdefender Internet Security répondait précisément à ce besoin sous Windows, mais l’offre n’est désormais plus commercialisée. Elle a été remplacée par Bitdefender Total Security Individual, qui reprend les principales protections d’Internet Security et les étend à 5 appareils sous Windows, macOS, iOS et Android. Le VPN standard reste limité à 200 Mo par jour et par appareil, ce qui en fait surtout une protection ponctuelle.
Avis : Bitdefender Internet Security reste une référence connue, mais l’offre appartient désormais au passé commercial de l’éditeur. Total Security Individual est son successeur logique : plus large, multiplateforme et toujours solide sous Windows, avec un VPN standard volontairement limité.
Points forts
• Jusqu’à 5 appareils sous Windows, macOS, iOS et Android
• Reprend les protections Windows d’Internet Security et ajoute la protection contre le cryptominage
• Password Manager, anti-tracker, protection micro et webcam, pare-feu et protection web
Points faibles
• Internet Security n’est plus disponible à l’achat
• VPN standard limité à 200 Mo par jour et par appareil
• VPN illimité réservé à Premium Security Individual
À retenir : Bitdefender Total Security Individual est actuellement affiché à 49,99 € la première année pour 5 appareils, contre un prix public de 94,99 €. Premium Security Individual est proposé à 69,98 € la première année pour 5 appareils, contre 109,99 € au prix public, avec VPN illimité.
Une suite pensée pour les risques réels du quotidien
On ne croise pas forcément un malware spectaculaire tous les matins. En revanche, les petites menaces crédibles, elles, sont partout. Une fausse facture glissée dans un email. Un lien de suivi colis qui mène vers une imitation presque correcte d’un site connu. Un logiciel gratuit récupéré sur une page douteuse. Une extension de navigateur qui demande plus d’autorisations que nécessaire. Ce sont ces situations ordinaires qui mettent le plus souvent un ordinateur en danger.
Bitdefender Total Security Individual reprend cette logique de protection par couches. Sous Windows, la suite inclut les fonctions d’Internet Security, puis ajoute notamment la protection contre le cryptominage et des outils d’optimisation. Elle surveille les téléchargements, les pages web, les comportements suspects et les connexions réseau, tout en couvrant désormais plusieurs plateformes avec un seul abonnement.
Crédit : Equipe Services | Bitdefender Total Security protège le PC par couches successives : filtrage web, antivirus, analyse comportementale, pare-feu et VPN interviennent chacun à un moment différent du parcours de menace.
Dans un scénario classique, la protection web peut bloquer une URL dangereuse avant même le téléchargement. Si un fichier arrive tout de même sur la machine, l’antivirus l’analyse. Si le programme tente ensuite de modifier des fichiers, de contacter un serveur inconnu ou d’agir comme un ransomware, la détection comportementale prend le relais. Ce n’est pas infaillible, aucun éditeur sérieux ne devrait le prétendre, mais cette accumulation de barrières complique nettement la tâche des attaquants.
Pour un ordinateur Windows utilisé au quotidien, c’est déjà beaucoup. Travail, achats en ligne, documents administratifs, messagerie personnelle, stockage de photos, accès à des comptes sensibles : le PC reste souvent le centre nerveux de la vie numérique. Il mérite donc plus qu’un simple scan occasionnel.
Protection web et anti-phishing : le vrai nerf de la guerre
La protection contre le phishing reste l’une des fonctions les plus utiles de Bitdefender Total Security. Pas la plus spectaculaire, certes. Mais dans la vraie vie, elle sert souvent plus qu’un module capable de détecter un malware exotique.
Les campagnes de phishing ont beaucoup progressé. Les fautes grossières existent encore, mais elles ne sont plus systématiques. Certains messages reprennent correctement le logo d’une banque, d’un transporteur ou d’un service administratif. Le ton est crédible, l’urgence bien dosée, le lien semble presque naturel. Et parfois, il suffit d’un moment d’inattention. On est pressé, on attend vraiment un colis, on clique.
Bitdefender intervient à ce niveau avec son filtrage web et sa protection anti-phishing. L’idée est de bloquer les pages frauduleuses avant la saisie des identifiants. C’est essentiel, car un antivirus seul ne suffit pas toujours dans ce cas. Le danger ne vient pas forcément d’un fichier infecté, mais d’une page qui pousse l’utilisateur à donner lui-même son mot de passe.
Légende : Un scénario courant, du faux mail au blocage avant la saisie des identifiants.| Equipe services
Crédit : Equipe Services.
Le VPN, lui, ne règle pas ce problème. Il chiffre la connexion, masque l’adresse IP visible par les sites consultés, protège davantage sur un Wi-Fi public. Mais s’il faut détecter une fausse page bancaire, c’est la protection web qui travaille. Cette distinction est importante, parce que beaucoup d’utilisateurs mélangent encore confidentialité, chiffrement et protection contre les arnaques. Ce sont trois sujets liés, mais pas identiques.
Un pare-feu utile, surtout pour les PC nomades
Le pare-feu intégré à Bitdefender Total Security sous Windows ajoute une autre couche de contrôle. Sur un ordinateur fixe branché au même réseau domestique toute l’année, son rôle paraît parfois abstrait. Sur un PC portable qui passe d’un réseau à l’autre, il devient plus intéressant.
Le réseau de la maison, celui d’un hôtel, d’un café, d’une gare ou d’un espace de coworking n’offrent pas le même niveau de confiance. Le pare-feu aide à surveiller les connexions entrantes et sortantes, à limiter certaines expositions et à repérer les comportements inhabituels. Une application qui tente de communiquer avec un serveur distant n’est pas automatiquement malveillante. Mais elle mérite parfois d’être observée.
C’est particulièrement vrai avec les logiciels installés rapidement. Un convertisseur de fichiers trouvé sur un site secondaire, un outil de compression, un vieux pilote, un utilitaire système recommandé sur un forum… Ces programmes ne sont pas tous dangereux, loin de là. Mais certains embarquent des composants publicitaires, des services inutiles ou des mécanismes de collecte plus intrusifs que prévu.
Le pare-feu ne remplace pas le bon sens. Il ne transforme pas un téléchargement douteux en logiciel propre. Mais il participe à cette logique de surveillance permanente, silencieuse, qui fait la différence entre une protection basique et une suite de sécurité plus complète.
Ransomwares : une protection devenue indispensable
Les ransomwares ont changé la manière de penser la sécurité personnelle. Avant, beaucoup d’utilisateurs craignaient surtout “un virus” qui ralentit l’ordinateur. Aujourd’hui, le scénario le plus redouté est souvent plus brutal : fichiers verrouillés, photos inaccessibles, documents de travail chiffrés, sauvegardes touchées, demande de rançon.
Bitdefender Total Security intègre une défense contre ce type de menace. Sous Windows, la suite combine Advanced Threat Defense et la remédiation des ransomwares afin de repérer les comportements suspects et de limiter les dégâts lorsque des fichiers commencent à être chiffrés de façon anormale.
Prenons un exemple simple. Un utilisateur télécharge une archive censée contenir une facture. Il l’ouvre, puis lance un fichier qui semble inoffensif. En arrière-plan, le programme commence à parcourir les dossiers Documents, Images et Bureau. Une suite de sécurité doit alors repérer non seulement le fichier, mais aussi son comportement. C’est là que l’analyse comportementale prend de la valeur.
La protection ransomware n’exclut pas les sauvegardes. Au contraire. Elle les complète. Un bon réflexe reste de conserver une copie externe ou cloud de ses fichiers importants, avec un historique de versions lorsque c’est possible. La sécurité logicielle réduit le risque. La sauvegarde limite les conséquences.
Vie privée : webcam, micro et anti-tracker
Les fonctions de confidentialité de Bitdefender Total Security méritent aussi un peu d’attention. La suite conserve notamment l’anti-tracker, la protection du micro et de la webcam, ainsi que Password Manager pour sécuriser les identifiants.
La surveillance de la webcam et du micro, par exemple, n’est plus un gadget. Les appels vidéo se sont installés partout : travail, cours en ligne, consultations, réunions familiales, messageries, plateformes collaboratives. Les navigateurs et applications demandent régulièrement des autorisations. La plupart sont légitimes. Certaines peuvent être mal configurées, trop curieuses ou simplement oubliées.
Bitdefender permet de mieux contrôler ces accès. Ce n’est pas une protection spectaculaire, mais elle évite qu’une application utilise la caméra ou le micro sans que l’utilisateur s’en rende compte. Dans un monde où le PC reste souvent ouvert toute la journée, ce genre de garde-fou a du sens.
L’anti-tracker vise un autre problème : la collecte de données pendant la navigation. Il ne remplace pas un navigateur bien configuré, ni des réglages de confidentialité sérieux, mais il limite une partie des traceurs publicitaires. Pour l’utilisateur, cela peut aussi améliorer le confort de navigation sur certains sites trop chargés en scripts.
Le VPN intégré : pratique, mais limité
C’est ici que l’analyse doit être plus fine. Bitdefender Total Security inclut un VPN standard limité à 200 Mo par jour et par appareil. Ce quota convient surtout à une protection ponctuelle. Pour un trafic illimité, Bitdefender Premium Security Individual ajoute un VPN sans limite de trafic, avec plus de 3 000 serveurs répartis dans plus de 100 pays, ainsi que des bloqueurs de publicités et de trackers à l’échelle du système.
Son rôle principal est de chiffrer la connexion entre l’appareil et le serveur VPN. Cela devient utile sur un Wi-Fi public : hôtel, café, aéroport, bibliothèque, gare. Sur ces réseaux, l’utilisateur ne sait pas toujours qui administre l’accès, comment il est configuré, ni qui d’autre y est connecté. Le VPN ajoute alors une couche de confidentialité bienvenue.
Pour consulter ses emails dans un aéroport, vérifier un compte bancaire depuis un hôtel ou envoyer quelques documents depuis un espace partagé, le VPN intégré peut suffire. Il réduit l’exposition de la connexion locale et masque l’adresse IP visible par les sites consultés. C’est déjà utile.
En revanche, il ne faut pas lui demander ce qu’il n’est pas conçu pour faire. Un usage VPN régulier suppose souvent un trafic illimité, le choix du pays de connexion, une bonne stabilité sur la durée, des serveurs nombreux, une politique de confidentialité claire, parfois un kill switch et des réglages avancés. Le VPN intégré à une suite de sécurité n’offre pas toujours cette souplesse.
C’est une distinction importante pour les lecteurs. “VPN inclus” ne signifie pas automatiquement “VPN premium”. Pour un usage occasionnel, la fonction a du sens. Pour protéger toute sa navigation au quotidien, regarder du streaming, travailler à distance plusieurs heures ou choisir précisément sa localisation virtuelle, il vaut mieux se tourner vers une solution VPN plus complète.
Ce qu’un VPN ne protège pas
Le VPN souffre parfois d’une image un peu magique. On l’active, et tout serait réglé. Ce n’est pas le cas.
Un VPN ne bloque pas automatiquement les fichiers infectés. Il ne reconnaît pas toujours une fausse page de connexion. Il ne corrige pas un mot de passe faible. Il n’empêche pas un utilisateur de transmettre volontairement ses identifiants à un faux service client. Il ne protège pas non plus contre toutes les formes de pistage, notamment lorsqu’un utilisateur reste connecté à ses comptes Google, Meta, Microsoft ou Amazon pendant toute sa navigation.
Son rôle est plus précis : chiffrer le trafic entre l’appareil et le serveur VPN, réduire l’exposition sur les réseaux non fiables, masquer l’adresse IP auprès des sites visités et limiter certaines formes d’observation réseau. C’est déjà beaucoup. Mais ce n’est qu’une brique.
C’est pour cela que l’association entre VPN, antivirus, anti-phishing et pare-feu reste pertinente. Chaque outil couvre une partie du risque. Le VPN protège le transport des données. L’antivirus surveille les fichiers et les comportements. La protection web bloque les sites dangereux. Le pare-feu contrôle les échanges réseau. L’utilisateur, lui, garde un rôle central : vérifier les liens, éviter les téléchargements douteux, activer la double authentification, maintenir ses logiciels à jour.
Performances : une suite discrète, mais pas invisible
Bitdefender garde une bonne réputation sur la question des performances. Les essais indépendants récents le placent généralement parmi les suites capables d’offrir une protection solide sans alourdir excessivement l’ordinateur. Il faut toutefois rester raisonnable : un logiciel qui analyse les fichiers, surveille le web et contrôle les connexions consomme forcément des ressources.
Sur un PC récent équipé d’un SSD et d’une quantité correcte de mémoire vive, l’impact devrait rester discret dans les usages courants. Navigation, emails, bureautique, vidéo, installation d’applications classiques : Bitdefender travaille en arrière-plan sans monopoliser la machine. L’utilisateur le remarque surtout lorsqu’une analyse complète est lancée ou quand de nombreux fichiers sont copiés, extraits ou installés.
Sur un ordinateur plus ancien, la situation peut être différente. Un vieux PC portable avec peu de mémoire vive, un disque dur mécanique et plusieurs programmes qui se lancent au démarrage pourra ressentir plus nettement la présence d’une suite complète. Dans ce cas, quelques réflexes aident : programmer les analyses à des moments calmes, éviter de multiplier les logiciels de sécurité actifs, désinstaller les anciens antivirus et nettoyer les programmes inutiles.
Le point important, ici, est l’équilibre. Une suite de sécurité doit protéger sans transformer chaque action en attente. Bitdefender s’en sort bien sur ce terrain, à condition de ne pas l’installer sur une machine déjà à bout de souffle en espérant un miracle.
Installation et prise en main
L’installation de Bitdefender Total Security Individual reste assez simple. L’utilisateur passe par Bitdefender Central, active son abonnement, puis installe la protection sur les appareils couverts. L’abonnement permet désormais de protéger jusqu’à 5 appareils sous Windows, macOS, iOS et Android.
Une première analyse complète est recommandée après l’installation. Elle permet de vérifier les fichiers déjà présents sur le PC, surtout si celui-ci n’avait pas d’antivirus à jour ou s’il a accumulé des années de téléchargements. C’est parfois un peu long, mais utile. Ensuite, la protection se fait surtout en arrière-plan.
L’interface reste accessible. Les fonctions principales sont visibles sans obliger l’utilisateur à comprendre chaque terme technique. Les profils automatiques permettent aussi d’adapter le comportement du logiciel selon l’usage : travail, navigation, jeu, vidéo. Ce n’est pas indispensable, mais cela évite quelques interruptions inutiles.
Pour un utilisateur avancé, certains réglages mériteront d’être explorés : règles du pare-feu, exceptions, paramètres de protection web, autorisations webcam et micro, notifications, scans planifiés. Pour un utilisateur classique, les réglages par défaut suffisent dans la plupart des cas.
À qui s’adresse vraiment le remplaçant de Bitdefender Internet Security ?
Bitdefender Total Security Individual convient aux utilisateurs qui veulent conserver le niveau de protection d’Internet Security tout en couvrant plusieurs appareils. La formule protège jusqu’à 5 appareils sous Windows, macOS, iOS et Android, ce qui la rend plus adaptée aux foyers équipés de plusieurs ordinateurs, smartphones ou tablettes.
La formule a aussi du sens pour ceux qui veulent mieux encadrer la navigation sans multiplier les outils séparés. Antivirus, pare-feu sous Windows, anti-phishing, protection ransomware, anti-tracker, protection micro et webcam, Password Manager et VPN standard sont réunis autour du même abonnement.
En revanche, il faut être clair sur le besoin VPN. Si le lecteur cherche uniquement une protection occasionnelle sur Wi-Fi public, le VPN intégré peut dépanner. Si son objectif principal est la confidentialité avancée, le télétravail sous VPN permanent, le choix régulier de pays de connexion ou une utilisation intensive, une offre VPN plus robuste sera plus adaptée.
Verdict : Total Security reprend le flambeau, avec un VPN toujours d’appoint
Bitdefender Internet Security n’est plus proposé à la vente. Son remplaçant, Bitdefender Total Security Individual, reprend les protections essentielles sous Windows et élargit la couverture à 5 appareils sur plusieurs plateformes. L’offre ajoute aussi Password Manager, la protection contre le cryptominage, la détection des violations de données et des outils d’optimisation.
Son principal point de vigilance concerne le VPN. La fonction est utile, mais elle doit être comprise comme une protection d’appoint. Elle sécurise une connexion ponctuelle, notamment sur un réseau public, mais ne remplace pas forcément un VPN complet pour les usages intensifs.
C’est finalement le bon prisme de lecture : si vous cherchiez Bitdefender Internet Security, c’est désormais Total Security Individual qu’il faut regarder. La formule protège jusqu’à 5 appareils et reprend les fonctions Windows de l’ancienne offre, mais son VPN standard reste limité à 200 Mo par jour et par appareil. Pour un VPN illimité, Premium Security Individual est la formule la plus adaptée.
FAQ - Bitdefender Internet Security en 2026
Bitdefender Internet Security est-il encore disponible à l’achat ?
Non. Bitdefender indique avoir remplacé Internet Security par ses nouvelles solutions de protection. Pour retrouver ses principales fonctions tout en protégeant plusieurs plateformes, il faut désormais se tourner vers Bitdefender Total Security Individual.
Le VPN inclus remplace-t-il un vrai VPN premium ?
Pas vraiment. Le VPN standard de Total Security est limité à 200 Mo par jour et par appareil. Pour un usage intensif ou permanent, Bitdefender Premium Security Individual ajoute un VPN illimité et donne accès à plus de 3 000 serveurs répartis dans plus de 100 pays.
Bitdefender protège-t-il contre les faux sites bancaires ?
Oui. Total Security conserve la prévention des menaces en ligne et les protections contre les arnaques et le phishing. Le VPN, lui, chiffre la connexion mais ne remplace pas ces mécanismes de détection des pages frauduleuses.
Bitdefender ralentit-il l’ordinateur ?
Sur un PC récent, l’impact reste généralement discret. Les ralentissements peuvent surtout apparaître pendant une analyse complète, une installation lourde ou sur une machine ancienne. Il vaut mieux éviter d’utiliser deux antivirus en même temps, car cela peut créer des conflits et ralentir fortement le système.
Faut-il lancer une analyse complète après l’installation ?
Oui, c’est recommandé. Une première analyse permet de contrôler les fichiers déjà présents sur l’ordinateur. C’est particulièrement utile si le PC n’était pas correctement protégé auparavant ou s’il contient beaucoup d’anciens téléchargements.

articles.title: Ring unveils AI security drone that patrols your home and a robot that guards businesses
articles.text:
Highly anticipated: Most home security cameras are stuck watching whatever sits in front of them, so there's always a hallway or back room left out of frame. Ring now wants its cameras to go and check on those spots themselves. The Amazon-owned company has unveiled an AI-powered indoor drone for homes and a rolling patrol robot for businesses.
The Ring Drone Cam costs $249.99 and is set to arrive in the US on January 27. It's essentially a second run at the Always Home Cam. Ring showed that one off back in 2020 at the same price, but it never actually shipped.
Owners can set the new drone to fly scheduled routes or send it out on demand. It can also take off on its own when a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered. Once it gets there, it streams 2K video with a 148-degree field of view and can spin around for a full look at the room.
The Verge, which got some hands-on time with it, notes that the drone weighs just 165 grams and carries no sensors beyond what it needs to land. So most of the work falls to AI Pilot, the system Ring built to steer both new devices. It turns a space into a floor plan, labels the rooms, and suggests patrol points like side doors and windows.
Businesses, meanwhile, get a wheeled robot called the Ring Rover Cam. It costs $999.99 and is already up for preorder ahead of its December 16 release. The Verge points out that it borrows much of its design from Amazon's Astro home robot – Astro's cupholder has even made way for a stubby tower with a siren and flashing light.
Amazon already tried pitching Astro to businesses in 2023, though it shut that version down just seven months later.
Of course, a camera that wanders around on its own raises some obvious privacy questions, especially after Ring's AI-powered Search Party feature for lost dogs drew backlash earlier this year. Ring says the drone's camera stays covered and switched off while docked. The Rover, for its part, has a sleep mode that retracts its camera and cuts the microphone.
Even the January date comes with an asterisk. Fine print in Ring's announcement admits the drone still hasn't been authorized by the FCC. The agency has been a lot stricter about drones since it blocked new foreign-made models last December. Scheduled patrols on both devices also need a Ring Protect subscription.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 built a shooter in 1 prompt — and it only took 8 hours and $550
articles.text:
Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 built a shooter in 1 prompt — and it only took 8 hours and $550
An Anthropic engineer gave Claude Fable 5.2 one prompt to build a first-person shooter and let it run for eight hours without human feedback. By the end, the model had processed 445 million input tokens, generated 2.7 million output tokens, and produced a playable browser game at an estimated API cost of $550.
The result was Saltline, a shooter set in a rain-soaked shipping port where players battle drones and robotic dogs while disabling communications relays. Anthropic engineer Felix Rieseberg shared the game when Fable 5.2 launched on Monday, describing it as an experiment in how much the model could accomplish from one instruction.
The engineer says Fable generated the game’s visuals procedurally rather than relying on imported assets. A public mirror packages the game into a roughly 1.4MB HTML file containing bundled Three.js code.
According to a note on the game’s title screen, Rieseberg spent about two hours improving the weapon models, sounds, and gameplay, while preserving a link to the original one-shot version.
The real price tag
YouTuber Matthew Berman took the experiment further, asking Fable to recreate a level from Gears of War: E-Day in Unreal Engine 5 using just three lines of instructions. The result was a playable shooter where players could take cover, fight enemies alongside AI teammates, and reload their weapons using the game’s signature active reload mechanic.
Berman reports that the project consumed approximately 8.5 billion tokens over several days, with an estimated API-equivalent cost approaching $15,000.
His browser-based Excel clone, complete with ribbon tabs, formulas, and pivot tables, required nearly 50 hours and an estimated $11,700.
Berman had early access to the model, so the figure does not necessarily reflect what he paid, but it is a good indication of the computational resources involved in running agents for extended periods.
Not Fable alone
Not every game credited to Fable was built with Fable alone. Creative developer Kevin Ngo writes, “Claude Fable 5.2 made this game demo, playable in the browser. It’s a boat ride through 8 dreamlike worlds,” about his project What the Water Keeps.
Ngo used Tripo to generate 3D assets and Suno v6 for the game’s soundtrack, while Fable composed the trailer music using royalty-free instrument samples.
Matt Shumer, co-founder of HyperWrite, spent considerably more time experimenting with the model. He used Fable to build a browser-based voxel destruction engine with physics-based damage before moving on to a much larger project of an unfinished simulation of Earth with real locations, weather, and transportation systems.
“It nailed the voxel engine I’ve been trying to get out of almost every model for a year,”
“It nailed the voxel engine I’ve been trying to get out of almost every model for a year,” Shumer writes on his blog, adding that Fable built it from scratch and that it ran on his MacBook.
His Hogwarts-meets-Fortnite battle royale reportedly took roughly two weeks to develop. Shumer initially experimented with multiple agents but found that a single agent produced better results with little intervention.
“It works best as one agent that owns a whole project,” he says, although he acknowledges that the approach could be frustratingly slow.
Shumer says Fable still needs direction, particularly when it makes projects more complicated than necessary. “You still have to steer it. Framing the problem and keeping it on track with your goals is on you.”
“You still have to steer it. Framing the problem and keeping it on track with your goals is on you.”
Shumer hosts his demos on Spawn, a platform he also lists among his investments. He doesn’t mention that connection in his review, and it’s unclear whether Spawn provided anything beyond hosting the finished projects.
The token math
Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, but those prices don’t tell the whole story when an agent runs for hours.
Rieseberg says much of Saltline‘s 445 million input tokens came from cached context, which Anthropic charges less to process. Without caching, those input tokens alone would have cost approximately $3,560, compared with his estimated $550 for the entire run.
There’s also the developer’s time to consider. Someone still has to decide what to build, review the code, and fix whatever doesn’t work. Shumer, for example, had to rethink his approach when running multiple agents produced disappointing results, while Ngo used separate tools to create assets for his game.
From demo to product
The demos leave plenty of questions about what happens after the first working build. Another developer still needs to understand the code, modify features without breaking existing functionality, and track down performance problems. Berman’s spreadsheet faces its own challenges, since working formulas in a demo don’t guarantee accurate results across larger datasets or more complicated calculations.
The demos also raise the question of what they’re based on. The most striking builds recreate games that already exist, with Berman cloning a level of Gears of War: E-Day, a current entry in Microsoft’s shooter franchise, and Shumer borrowing from both the Wizarding World and Fortnite for his battle royale.
“It’s a great model, a LOT of things got better but not every single thing,”
Peter Gostev, who works on AI evaluation at Arena, has tested dozens of prompts and come away impressed, though he isn’t ready to abandon Opus. “It’s a great model, a LOT of things got better but not every single thing,” he writes on X, noting that one experiment cost $2,618.
Saltline and Berman’s projects show that developers can now hand off substantial implementation work and return hours later to something playable or functional. The cost of that work is becoming easier to measure, but the quality of what comes back still needs human judgment.
Learning Path

articles.title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process.
AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype.
The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff.
AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces, AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page.
The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff.
Architecture
The diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the AI-PDLC framework.
It starts with the signals most teams lose track of, that is, the Slack threads, Jira tickets, docs, and call transcripts that hold the why behind a decision and what customers actually said. Enterprise connectors pull that context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many more enterprise sources.
AWS Quick can build a personal knowledge graph from your connected apps and folders, linking the people, projects, and decisions across your tools.
Those signals feed the brain: the set of agents on AWS Quick, led by an Orchestrator that runs Discovery, Prioritize, Working Backwards, Spec Generator, and Designer. Everything they produce lands in one common language: a prototype_spec.md holding the acceptance criteria, personas, screens, data model. Every decision traces back to a source.
AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). ACP is an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock-in. Customers can use their preferred coding agent like Kiro or Claude Code to build against the specification generated by AI-PDLC.
Underneath it all runs a human approval gate at every stage. You validate the pain points, approve priorities, sign off the spec, gate the build, and accept the review. Production data then flows back into Discovery, closing the loop. The agents do the work while you make the calls, and nobody has to leave their tool to do it.
Solution overview
The AI-PDLC lifecycle spans eight phases: Discover, Decide, Design, Prototype, Engineer, Ship, Operate, and Learn. This post focuses on the first four, where the product team works. The last four are handled by coding agents such as Kiro, which build from the specifications the upstream phases produce. The upstream phases are implemented as six agents in AWS Quick.
Users interact only with an Orchestrator, which reads each specialist’s question framework at runtime, asks targeted questions for the current phase, and dispatches artifact generation to the right specialist. A single conversation drives the whole journey, and the pipeline advances only after human approval at each step in the workflow.
Phase 1: Discover
The Discovery agent guides structured pain point analysis across interactive Q&A, URL ingestion, and direct pulls from connected enterprise sources like Slack, Jira, support tickets, Salesforce, and research repositories. It scores every pain point for severity and frequency, producing a Pain Point Board that gives the team one evidence-grounded view of what customers struggle with.
Phase 2: Decide
The Prioritize agent scores each use case against weighted criteria using two transparent 0–10 frameworks: one purpose-built for agentic use cases (large language model (LLM) capability match, tool availability, user acceptance) and one for traditional applications (feasibility, business impact, effort). The team can open the Scoring Matrix and trace exactly why one use case outranks another.
Once the top use case is selected, the Working Backwards agent generates a full PR/FAQ using the Amazon Working Backwards method with customer FAQs and internal FAQs covering unit economics, failure modes, regulatory risk, and competitive landscape. If a concept can’t survive this scrutiny, the team learns that on paper before committing engineering resources.
Phase 3: Design
The Spec Generator agent turns the validated use case and PR/FAQ into a build-ready specification, with separate templates for agentic versus application use cases plus a Design Handoff Brief for UX teams. Each spec contains acceptance criteria, user flow, constraints, and metadata that traces every requirement back to its source pain point, prioritization score, and the PR/FAQ that validated it. Those acceptance criteria serve a dual purpose: they’re the build contract the coding agent follows, and the review rubric the review agent audits against. What used to take multiple sprints of drafting and review becomes a focused session, detailed enough for engineering to build from design spec immediately, with few or no clarifying meetings required.
Phase 4: Prototype
The Designer agent generates journey maps, wireframes, and clickable HTML prototypes directly inside AWS Quick. It works from the Design Handoff Brief, personas from Discovery, user flow from the PR/FAQ, screens to design, brand context, and the emotional target drawn from the customer quote, so teams can validate concepts with stakeholders before committing to Figma or other design tooling. After the spec is approved, it’s dispatched to the engineering team for development.
The entire loop is iterative, with humans reviewing and approving at every gate. Nothing ships without explicit signoff. What traditionally takes multiple weeks of prototyping and iteration could become days or even just hours of guided agent collaboration depending on the complexity of the problems.
Every decision is logged at two levels. Each specialist records its own decisions, scores, and rationale inside the artifact it produces, and the Orchestrator independently checks that those entries exist while keeping a shared log across the whole pipeline. If one layer slips, the other still holds a complete record, so no gate approval goes untracked.
AI-PDLC can be executed across two pacing modes. Deep Discovery asks 8–12 questions per phase, chasing ambiguities and edge cases. It fits a new problem space where the team wants thorough exploration. Fast Track trims each phase to 3–5 essential questions and suggests defaults from context it already holds, letting you confirm or override each one. It fits time-boxed sessions where the team knows the space and needs to move quickly.
Agent implementation details: Step by step
We will walk through the details of the agent creation and implementation process.
Prerequisites
- An AWS Quick workspace with the Desktop client installed.
- Access to create custom agents in AWS Quick with Enterprise connectors configured for Slack, Jira, SharePoint, or other tools your team uses.
Step 1: Clone the AI-PDLC repository
The full agent suite, reference architecture, prompt templates, and setup instructions are available in the AI-PDLC GitHub repository.
The repository contains:
- Agent instruction files for all six agents.
- Question framework samples for each specialist agent.
- Configuration files and setup guide.
Step 2: Create the specialist agents
In AWS Quick, create the specialist agents using the instructions from the repository:
Step 2.1: Download the JSON file from the GitHub repository for agent building.
Step 2.2: Go to Quick Desktop → Customize → Agents → Create, then choose Create from File.
Step 2.3: The chat window opens up.
Step 2.4: The following six agents with instructions are created:
The Orchestrator is the central architectural component. It dynamically reads each specialist’s instructions at runtime:
Step 3: Configure Quick Spaces (artifact repository)
Create a shared Quick Space for storing pipeline artifacts:
- Open Quick Spaces and select Create New Space.
- Name: AI-PDLC Artifacts.
- Grant access to relevant team members.
Step 4: Run the pipeline
- Open AWS Quick Desktop.
- Select AI-PDLC Orchestrator from the agent picker.
- Enter: “Run the full pipeline” (or “Fast Track” for an abbreviated session).
- Answer the Orchestrator’s structured questions as it guides you through each phase.
- Review artifacts as they are produced at each gate.
You can select the pace, Deep Discovery or Fast Track, based on your needs.
Watch it in action
For a live demonstration of AI-PDLC in action, from customer insight through all four phases to a working prototype, watch our YouTube video walkthrough:
- YouTube Part 1: End-to-end product lifecycle with AWS Quick and AI coding agents (51:49)
- YouTube Part 2: Creating AI-PDLC agents
The video covers:
- Setting up the agent suite.
- Running the full Orchestrator pipeline through a real-world use case.
- Real-time artifact generation in action.
- The ACP handoff to coding agents.
- Tips for choosing between Deep Discovery and Fast Track modes.
AI-PDLC scenarios
We will walk through some common scenarios where the AI-PDLC framework can be applied:
Scenario 1: New product development, starting from scratch
When a team identifies a new market opportunity or unmet customer needs, they face the classic cold-start problem: scattered signals, competing ideas, and no structured way to move from insight to action. AI-PDLC guides the team through the full upstream journey, surfacing pain points from real customer data and scoring competing ideas against transparent criteria. It also validates the concept through a rigorous PR/FAQ and produces a build-ready spec so the first line of code is written against a validated plan, not a hunch.
Scenario 2: Feature addition to an existing product, roadmap-driven or customer-driven
Product teams continuously receive signals that inform what to build next: customer feedback in support channels, feature requests from sales, usage data showing dropoff points, or strategic priorities from leadership. AI-PDLC accelerates this by pulling those signals from connected tools (Slack, Jira, Salesforce, AWS Quick Sight). The framework structures them into a prioritized backlog with evidence-backed scoring and produces a spec that preserves the “why” behind each feature, so engineering receives context-rich work items instead of one-line Jira tickets stripped of intent.
Scenario 3: Bug fixes and incident-driven improvements
When a production issue surfaces through customer complaints, monitoring alerts, or support escalations, the response often skips structured analysis and jumps straight to a code fix. AI-PDLC brings discipline to this reactive workflow by capturing the root cause as a documented pain point, assessing whether the fix warrants a broader design change or a targeted patch. It produces a scoped spec with testable acceptance criteria so the fix addresses the underlying problem rather than just the symptom, and the decision trail is preserved for future reference.
Each scenario follows the same pipeline (Discover → Decide → Design → Prototype) but enters at different depths. New products run the full journey, feature additions may skip deep discovery, and bug fixes may compress to a single focused cycle. The methodology adapts while the audit trail and governance remain consistent regardless.
Clean up
The resources this walkthrough creates incur no cost at rest, so you can safely keep the entire AI-PDLC suite in place if you plan to run the pipeline again.
To remove what you no longer need, delete the six agents under Customize → Agents in Quick Desktop, delete the AI-PDLC Artifacts Space (or just the test artifacts within it) and revoke any team access you granted, and disconnect any Enterprise connectors or coding agent links you added solely for this exercise. You can also remove the cloned GitHub repository from your local machine.
Conclusion
The bottleneck in product development has shifted. Coding agents have made implementation fast. However, the upstream work still constrains teams: discovering customer problems, deciding what to build, validating the concept, and producing clear specifications. Teams that compress this upstream cycle can gain a compounding advantage: they build the right product, faster, with fewer costly pivots.
AI-PDLC addresses this directly. It provides a structured, AI-native framework, implemented as a suite of agents in AWS Quick that guides product teams through Discover, Decide, Design, and Prototype with built-in governance at every gate. AI-PDLC attributes every decision. Every artifact traces back to customer evidence. And when the spec reaches engineering, it carries the full context of why it exists, who validated it, and what “done” looks like.
The product team’s role isn’t to write code. It’s to make the right decisions about what to build and why, quickly and traceably. AI-PDLC makes that possible.
Get started today
- Clone the repository.
- Follow the setup guide in the repository to create five specialist agents and one Orchestrator.
- Select “AI-PDLC Orchestrator” from the agent picker and say: “Run the full pipeline”.

articles.title: Asus, Zoom Release Security Patches
articles.text:
Asus and Zoom are among the tech companies that have released fresh security updates for their products this week.
Computer maker Asus published an advisory describing four high- and medium-severity vulnerabilities in certain router firmware releases.
Successful exploitation of the flaws could allow attackers to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges or overwrite memory and cause a crash.
Zoom has patched two vulnerabilities in Workplace for Windows, including a critical-severity unauthenticated privilege escalation bug tracked as CVE-2026-108186 (CVSS score of 9.6).
The second issue (CVE-2026-108187, CVSS score of 8.1) could also allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to elevate their privileges.
Zoom Workplace for Windows versions 7.1.8 and later contain patches for both bugs. Zoom makes no mention of any of these flaws being exploited in the wild.
Additionally, Cisco updated several advisories: it added fresh information on Node2Shell’s impact and on an authorization bypass’s impact on ISE and ISE-PIC, and added new details on the availability of fixes for seven critical- and high-severity CVEs in Meraki products.
On Tuesday, both Cisco and SonicWall announced they have removed root certificates affected by compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates.
The fresh security updates arrived among hundreds of patches from Apple, Fortinet, Citrix, Ivanti, Intel, AMD, Microsoft, Adobe, SAP, and multiple ICS vendors.

articles.title: Google libera Gemini 4 Carbon ao público com recurso para equipes de agentes de IA • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Google libera Gemini 4 Carbon ao público com recurso para equipes de agentes de IA
Modelo chega a assinantes do Google AI Ultra e desenvolvedores, com foco em tarefas complexas de programação.
Após algumas semanas restrito a especialistas em cibersegurança, o Gemini 4 Carbon finalmente começou a chegar para para usuários comuns e empresas nesta terça-feira (10/11). O modelo é considerado a inteligência artificial mais avançada do Google.
O modelo pode ser acessado por desenvolvedores por meio da API no Google AI Studio, no Android Studio e no Gemini for Business, por US$ 2 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 10 por milhão de tokens de saída (aproximadamente R$ 10 e R$ 53). O preço, no entanto, vale apenas até o fim do mês: deve dobrar após o período, chegando ao patamar de custo do Claude Opus 5.5, por exemplo.
Segundo o The Verge, a estratégia de preços deve aumentar a competitividade da empresa diante das concorrentes. Mesmo após o encerramento da promoção, previsto para o fim de novembro, o custo por token do Carbon permanecerá inferior ao dos modelos GPT-6 Astra e Fable 5.2.
Para o público geral, o acesso está sendo liberado no app do Gemini, no Modo IA da Busca e no Google Antigravity apenas para assinantes do Google AI Ultra, que custa a partir de R$ 779,90 por mês.
O Gemini 4 Carbon chega como a IA mais avançada entre as opções do Google, acima do Gemini 4 Argon, apresentado em outubro, destinado a tarefas que exigem ainda mais capacidade de raciocínio e processamento, como auditorias de sistemas, identificação de problemas em códigos e investigações científicas que demandam várias etapas de análise.
Segundo o Google, o modelo usa mais tokens que o Argon para executar essas atividades, mas consegue manter ciclos prolongados de verificação. Isso permite que a IA analise diferentes possibilidades, revise resultados intermediários e explore alternativas.
Uma das principais novidades que acompanham a liberação do Gemini 4 Carbon é o comando /swarm, disponibilizado inicialmente no Google Antigravity. Ele permite que uma mesma tarefa seja distribuída entre diferentes agentes de IA, que trabalharão coordenadamente.
No processo, o Carbon pode assumir atividades que exigem raciocínio mais complexo, como planejamento de arquitetura de um sistema, enquanto as tarefas menores podem ser delegadas a modelos mais rápidos. A proposta é permitir que projetos com várias etapas sejam executados sem que o usuário precise organizar manualmente cada atividade .
Em demonstrações apresentadas pelo Google DeepMind, a tecnologia foi utilizada para desenvolver uma biblioteca de interfaces gráficas na linguagem Rust durante a madrugada. Em outro exemplo, os agentes criaram um jogo tridimensional com Three.js que simula o campus da empresa.
Além das ferramentas de programação, o modelo alcançou 100% de sensibilidade na detecção de ameaças no Project Fortify, sistema interno do Google para identificação e mitigação de vulnerabilidades. Em outras simulações, bloqueou 99% das tentativas de intrusão.
O avanço também ocorre nos mecanismos de proteção para evitar que a IA caia em injeções de prompt. Em testes internos, o Gemini 4 Carbon não foi enganado em nenhuma das tentativas de ataque. A companhia também avaliou o comportamento do modelo em situações nas quais agentes poderiam inventar resultados, alcançando uma taxa de sucesso de 92% nos testes de honestidade.

articles.title: Worried about home intruders? Anker’s new Eufy TrackLight Cam S1 security camera automatically lights them up and follows them as they move
articles.text:
Eufy’s new smart home camera can light up intruders and automatically follow them like a Hollywood searchlight
Proactive deterrence for your home
- Eufy’s new smart home camera features a spotlight and siren
- The spotlight automatically follows intruders as they move
- It recognizes friends and family and takes a different approach for them
Many of the best home security cameras are equipped with spotlights that switch on at the merest hint of movement, and you might even have one yourself. But finding a device that combines recorded footage with a light that autonomously moves and follows intruders is a different proposition entirely — and one that takes a more proactive approach to protecting your home and encouraging potential trespassers to go fish.
That setup is exactly what you get with Anker’s new $299.99 Eufy TrackLight Cam S1. Anker claims that it is “the world’s first outdoor security track light camera with an auto-tracking light designed to actively deter intruders.” That active deterrence comes in the form of a light beam that follows unidentified personnel on your property, hopefully spooking them into turning around and leaving.
The camera can sense targets within 12 meters and illuminates them with 20 lux of light. The beam itself can be widened or narrowed between 10 and 30 degrees, adaptively broadening as the person gets closer and responding as they move within 355 degrees of horizontal rotation.
To really scare off any unwanted presences, a siren can be activated alongside the spotlight. Additionally, to further deter, the light can be changed to red and blue flashing modes.
Everything is recorded in 4K-resolution night vision, with 10x digital zoom picking out objects further away. There’s also a separate floodlight that works alongside the tracking beam to provide extra detail in the dark.
Recognizing friends and family
If you’re concerned about getting blinded by your own home security camera when you come home late from a night out, the good news is that the Eufy TrackLight Cam S1 can recognize friends and family members and instead activate a soft light instead of the harsh spotlight and siren. So long as the person’s phone has been added to the product’s companion app, the camera will identify them using Bluetooth and provide a much friendlier greeting.
Anker also says that the Eufy TrackLight Cam S1 comes with a 15,000mAh battery and built-in solar panels, so it should have plenty of juice come rain or shine. Its IP65 rating also means it’s resistant to dust and water ingress.

If you’re concerned about burglars, home invaders, or anyone else who shouldn’t be on your property, the TrackLight Cam S1 brings a bit of extra clout with its moving spotlight and siren combo. Even if you’re not able to monitor its footage 24/7, its autonomous light beam gives the impression that you are — and that might be all that’s needed to keep your home protected.

articles.title: Modder routes PC water cooling loop to radiator outside to beat the winter heat — winter cold keeps CPU and GPU temperatures below 50C under load
articles.text:
Modder routes PC water cooling loop to radiator outside to beat the winter heat — winter cold keeps CPU and GPU temperatures below 50C under load
This modder thought opening a window was too much work, so he did something cool about it
u/Motor_Attention1865 on Reddit didn't like how his PC added extra heat to his room in the winter, so he went the extra mile to dump the heat outside in a fashion similar to mini-split air conditioners. The external cooling system is controlled by an Arduino Mega that the PC communicates with when it needs extra cooling. The system opens a three-way valve to route coolant outside and prevents condensation by keeping the coolant temperature above the dew point.
Our intrepid modder's room has heated floors, and the PC was dumping too much heat under the table where his PC sits, even in 25 °F (-4 °C) weather. He grew tired of manually opening a window to regulate the temperature in his space, so he put in much more effort to create a split cooling system that puts another radiator outside in the below-freezing temperatures, cooling down the PC significantly.
Motor_Attention1865's build itself is impressive enough, with a delidded Core Ultra 7 270K Plus cooled by a Thermal Grizzly 1851 Mycro Pro direct-die water block with Thermal Grizzly Conductonaut Extreme liquid compound. Not only is his RTX 4070 Ti Super also watercooled with a Bykski water block, but the 2x24GB DDR5-8400 G.Skill RAM is also watercooled using Bykski heat spreaders with an IceManCooler two-channel water block. The cooling system within the PC has two radiators: a 120mm in the back and a 360mm in the front, all fed by an EK Kinetic D5 pump-reservoir.
The external cooling system, however, is even more impressive. The 240mm outdoor radiator with two Noctua iPPC-3000 fans isn’t outrageous, but the automated system that makes it useful is what’s interesting. Next to the PC is a box with a Bykski D5 pump and reservoir that pushes water outside, but it doesn’t use the external radiator until the PC needs the extra cooling.
Upon startup, the PC runs a Python script that communicates with an Arduino Mega connected to three temperature probes checking the coolant temperature and three more temperature and humidity sensors that monitor the PC case and the ambient air. The sensors give the Arduino Mega information on where to switch the motorized three-way valve depending on the temperature and humidity.
The problem with extreme cold in any PC is condensation. If coolant gets below the dew point of the environment, condensation forms, potentially shorting out PC components. To prevent this disaster, the Arduino determines the dew point based on the humidity and temperature of the room and in the PC. Motor_Attention1865 set the Arduino to close off the outside radiator at +10 °C above the dew point, or +5 °C during benchmarking, allowing for low temperatures without risking droplets forming in the PC.
Because of the freezing or below-freezing temperatures at which this external loop is meant to operate, Motor_Attention1865 also added pure ethylene glycol to the Aquacomputer Double Protect Ultra Clear coolant in the loop, lowering its freezing point from -18 °C to -28 °C.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Thanks to the supplemental cooling system and delidding, the system achieves temperatures below 50 °C under heavy use. According to Motor_Attention1865, the RTX 4070 Ti sits at 37 °C and the CPU hovers around 45-50 °C while gaming. Temperatures were higher in benchmarks, however — in Cinebench R23, the CPU sat at 52 °C, while in 3DMark Steel Nomad, the GPU was at 48 °C.
Above all, however, Motor_Attention1865 no longer needs to bother himself with opening a window if their room gets too hot with the PC under load. It's the small things.

articles.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
articles.text:
The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
Plus: COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.
To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud.
Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be.
—Antonio Regalado
This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.
The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible”
Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. (NYT $)

Quote of the day
“What a dereliction of duty. He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.”
—Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy.
One more thing
How refrigeration ruined fresh food
Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus.
According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.
Read the full story on her research.
