articles.title: GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls
articles.text:
GitHub has made GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available. The open-source project runs coding agents inside GitHub Actions for repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration (CI) failure analysis. Agents start with read-only permissions, and any changes they propose are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens.
That separation has limits. The project's FAQ says the protections do not automatically extend to direct write permissions or to custom jobs a workflow author adds, so the safety of a workflow depends on how it is configured. Authors can also add a GitHub Environment protection rule to require a reviewer before a write job runs.
Developers describe the work in natural-language Markdown, with YAML frontmatter for configuration. The project compiles that definition into a standard Actions workflow, which reuses existing runner groups and policy constraints, and teams can use Copilot or bring another coding agent. According to the general availability announcement, agents run in a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied. The project entered public preview in June 2026.
Since the preview, GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller (ARC), its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker (DinD). DinD runs a Docker daemon inside the runner pod so the agent can start its sandbox containers. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the DinD sidecar as a privileged container by default, a privileged component sitting alongside an agent designed around least privilege.
Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits (AIC) at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC ($10) per run. The project's enterprise controls reference adds defaults of 5,000 AIC a day, 400 AIC per threat-detection run and a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, all of which organisations can override. The gh aw forecast command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending, including threat detection.
In the announcement, Ben Alton, senior manager in Accenture's Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team, said: "One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone." The announcement does not explain how that figure was measured.
Engineers testing the project have taken a more cautious line. In a walkthrough of an issue-triage workflow, Sascha Mirow-Stanitzok, team lead for middleware at freenet, judged the default budget far too generous for triage and capped his runs at 100 AIC, 15 turns and 10 minutes. He also wrote that telling the agent to ignore instructions in issue text does not protect a workflow by itself, and said he would not use the same pattern for workflows that change code or open pull requests.
GitLab takes a different route with its Duo Agent Platform flows, which run on runners under a composite identity that pairs a service account performing the actions with the human user who started the request. Its triggers, such as a mention or an assignment, must come from a human user, so one flow cannot start another. That rule stops agents from chaining work across flows without a person starting it.
GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the right choice for reproducible builds and tests, with agent workflows suited to tasks that need interpretation or generation. The project is available on GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise on github.com, and the default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence.

articles.title: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
articles.text:
Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.
Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Toyota is reviving the Scion badge as an experimental mobility incubator—starting with an Indiana-built, 25-mph kei truck engineered for American fleets.
Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan, telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.
Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016, would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.
When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.
It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.
The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.
Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.
Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.
Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.
To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.
Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.
The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.
Images by Toyota

articles.title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one.
This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning.
In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework.
UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks
UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF.
Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again.
The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop.
Canonical trace and adapters
Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace, which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace, so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them.
A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace.
Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale.
Evaluation engine
The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. Tool calling measures whether the agent selected the right tools, called them in a sensible order, and passed valid arguments. Response quality measures whether the final answer is relevant, complete, accurate, and grounded in the provided context rather than hallucinated.
Responsible AI measures safety, bias, toxicity, and resistance to prompt injection. Performance measures operational cost in latency, token use, and throughput. Multi-turn measures how well the agent sustains a conversation, including context retention, coherence, and goal completion across turns. Multi-agent measures coordination in systems of cooperating agents, such as task delegation and the division of work. Reasoning measures the internal logic of the agent’s chain of thought, including consistency and freedom from fallacies.
Each dimension is computed by one or more of 36 built-in metrics, and every metric returns a normalized score in the interval [0, 1], where 1 is best, so dimensions and the overall result share one scale. Metrics come in two families. Deterministic metrics compute a score directly from the trace and the ground truth and reproduce exactly on repeated runs. Large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics score qualities that resist a closed-form definition, such as response relevance or safety, by prompting a judge model on Amazon Bedrock. You can also add your own custom metrics or draw on the RAGAS and DeepEval integrations.
Because judge metrics feed an agent’s own output back into a prompt, that content is treated as untrusted input: an agent that can influence its judge can influence its own scores. The rubric is sent separately from the content, and the content is escaped so it cannot break out of its delimiter and be read as instructions. Each judge response is parsed strictly and must cite a verbatim span of the content it scored. A score whose evidence is not found is rejected rather than recorded. Judge scores are evaluation signal, not a safety decision, and should not gate a security control. For runtime enforcement on the agent itself, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails in its own invocation path. The full model is in SECURITY.md.
Experiment management and comparison
UAEF records each evaluation as an experiment, so results from different agent versions can be compared later. Calling evaluate() or batch_evaluate() with persist=True creates a new experiment, identified by an optional name and objective, and writes it to two stores with complementary roles. Amazon DynamoDB holds one row per experiment with the metadata used for listing and comparison: evaluation count, the average score per metric, and an overall average. Amazon S3 holds a JSON file with the full evaluation results, including per-metric scores and the judge’s reasoning. Teams that handle sensitive data can turn on PII redaction for the stored copy.
The Python library also models a finer-grained structure. An experiment contains runs, and each run records the agent design under test: framework, model, tools, system prompt, and parameters. A run can also record a configuration snapshot and a Git commit. You can mark one run as the baseline for its experiment. This ties each score to the change that produced it, whether a new prompt, a different model, or an added tool.
Comparison works on the stored per-metric averages. For each metric that two runs have in common, the comparison engine calculates the absolute and percentage change. It then classifies the metric as a regression, an improvement, or unchanged, using a configurable threshold with a default of 5 percent. Several runs can be compared against a single baseline in one call. The regression detector also assigns a severity to each regression: minor (5–10 percent), moderate (10–20 percent), or severe (over 20 percent). It groups regressions by dimension, which shows, for example, whether a prompt change affected tool calling but not response quality.
In the web UI, the Compare tab lists stored experiments and filters them by framework or dataset. You select two or more experiments. The first is used as the baseline, and the UI shows per-metric scores with regressions and improvements highlighted. The UI calls the same library comparison engine, so results match what the Python API returns.
Report and insight generation
After an evaluation is stored, UAEF reports on it at three levels, each answering a different question. How did this run perform? Why did it score that way? How does it compare with earlier versions?
Results view. When an evaluation finishes, the web UI shows a summary of the experiment: the overall score, the number of test cases evaluated, the framework, and queries that failed to run. Per-metric averages appear with a dimension radar chart and a metric bar chart. A table lists every test case with its query, the agent’s response, the expected answer, and the score. Expanding a row shows the full response with its dimension and metric scores. For a multi-turn conversation, it shows each turn with its own scores and the tools the agent called.
Detailed report. From the results view or the experiment list, you can generate a statistical report on demand. UAEF loads the stored results from Amazon S3 and opens the report in a new browser tab. The report breaks results down by dimension and by metric. It shows confidence intervals and outliers for each metric, score distributions, correlations between metrics, a responsible AI summary, and test cases that reported failures. It closes with recommendations that point to the lowest-scoring dimensions and the metrics that vary most across test cases. The report is computed from the scores alone, without an LLM, so the same results produce the same report.
LLM-generated insights. In the Python library, you can pass a report to a model on Amazon Bedrock for analysis. For a single run, the analysis covers strengths, critical weaknesses, hypotheses about root causes, and prioritized recommendations. For a comparison of several runs, it covers the overall trend, likely causes of regressions and improvements, the risk each regression carries, and next steps. These insights suggest what to change in the prompt, model, or tools before the next evaluation.
Two ways to use it
You can run UAEF two ways over the same engine. With the Python library, you can evaluate agents in code from notebooks, scripts, and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. You can use the deployable AWS service to evaluate agents through a low-code web interface. You upload your dataset, select a framework and metrics, run the evaluation, and review the scores. Both paths run the identical evaluation engine and write to the same stores, so a result does not depend on which path produced it. You can start in the interface and move to code without changing how your results are scored or compared.
Evaluating agents with UAEF: A playbook
Knowing what UAEF can measure is different from knowing what you should measure. A travel-booking agent and a policy Q&A agent fail in different ways, and scoring both on every dimension wastes time and Amazon Bedrock invocations. Use this playbook to pick the metrics that match your agent, then add more as new questions come up.
Getting started
UAEF is open source under the Apache 2.0 license in the awslabs/uaef GitHub repository. It includes the Python library, framework adapters, built-in metrics, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) infrastructure for the deployable service, the web interface, and runnable notebooks for each supported framework. The Installation Guide covers requirements, installing from a built package, and the development setup.
The service deployment guide covers deploying UAEF as a service with the web interface, the config reference, and teardown.
See it in action
A complete evaluation in the UAEF web interface, from ground-truth upload to per-dimension scores.
Choosing the metrics
Start from your scenario, not the metric list. Find the column that matches your agent and begin with the metrics checked in it. The Needs ground truth column shows which metrics compare against a reference answer or expected tool calls.
| Dimension | Metric | Needs ground truth | Scenarios |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  |  |  | RAG / knowledge Q&A | General Q&A | Tool-using agent | Multi-turn conversation | Reasoning | Safety and compliance | Multi-agent | Production monitoring | 
| Response Quality | answer_relevance |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | accuracy |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | completeness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | hallucination_score |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | ragas_faithfulness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | ragas_context_precision |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | ragas_context_recall |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Tool Calling | tool_selection_accuracy |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | tool_sequence_correctness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | parameter_quality |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | mcp_compliance |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Multi-Turn | context_retention |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | coherence |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | conversation_completeness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | user_satisfaction |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | turn_efficiency |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Reasoning | chain_of_thought_coherence |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | logical_consistency |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | reasoning_step_correctness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | fallacy_detection |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Responsible AI | safety_score |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| Multi-Agent | workflow_completion |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| Performance | latency_score |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

|  | throughput |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
The table shows recommended starting metrics for each scenario. For the complete list of supported metrics, see the metrics catalog.
Pass the metrics you picked as the metrics argument to evaluate() or batch_evaluate(). For a worked example, see the Example notebooks section that follows. Deterministic metrics, such as tool calling and performance, are computed directly from the trace, whereas others call an LLM judge. UAEF automatically skips metrics that need a reference answer when no ground truth is present, so partially labeled datasets and unlabeled production traffic are still worth evaluating.
Choosing the pipeline
Metrics decide what you measure. Six independent choices decide how the evaluation runs. Use the question in each row to settle it.
| Choice | Ask yourself | Then use | In code | 
| Passive or active | Do I already have traces, or do I need to generate them under controlled conditions? | Passive: evaluate a trace you already have. Active: call an invoke_* helper so UAEF runs the agent. | evaluate(trace=recorded, adapter=“langgraph”) or raw = invoke_http_agent_for_framework( ENDPOINT, query, “strands”) | 
| One trace or a dataset | Am I debugging one case or measuring a release? | Use evaluate() for one trace or conversation. Use batch_evaluate() for a dataset. | evaluate(trace=trace) or batch_evaluate(traces=traces, max_workers=4) | 
| Single-turn or multi-turna | Does any test case depend on an earlier turn? | Multi-turn: add session_id and turn_id to the dataset and pass every turn to the adapter, which assembles each conversation. | sessions = adapter.transform_to_canonical( turn_payloads) batch_evaluate(traces=sessions) | 
| Single-agent or multi-agent | Does more than one agent handle a single request? | Nothing to configure. The adapter returns an AgentTrace or MultiAgentTrace, and UAEF selects the matching evaluator. | adapter = get_adapter(FRAMEWORK) trace = adapter.transform_to_canonical(raw) | 
| Offline or online | Am I testing before release or monitoring production? | Offline: a prepared dataset in development and CI. Online: live conversations, scored turn by turn. | batch_evaluate(…) or OnlineEvaluator().evaluate_response( trace=trace) | 
| Ephemeral or persistedb | Will I compare this run with a later one? | Persisted: set persist=True with an experiment name. Otherwise, use the returned result. | batch_evaluate(traces=traces, persist=True, experiment_name=“Support agent v2”) | 
a Multi-turn – For details, refer to the multi-turn evaluation workflow guide.
b Only persisted runs can be compared.
Preparing your dataset
Provide one row per test case in a CSV or XLSX file. Only Question is required.
| Column | Required | Purpose | 
| Question | Yes | Input sent to the agent | 
| Answer | No | Expected response | 
| context | No | Reference documents for retrieval-style evaluation | 
| expected_tool_calls | No | Expected tool calls as a JSON array | 
| session_id | Multi-turn only | Groups rows into one conversation | 
| turn_id | Multi-turn only | Orders turns within a conversation, starting at 1 | 
Question and Answer are matched case-insensitively and accept common aliases such as Query and Expected_Output, so existing test files usually work without renaming.
Multi-turn datasets. Rows that share a session_id are sent in order to a single agent session, so later turns can depend on earlier ones. Your agent endpoint must maintain its own conversation state, because UAEF sends each turn with its session ID rather than replaying history. Use lowercase session_id and turn_id. Otherwise, the file is evaluated as single-turn.
Protect sensitive data. Before sharing or persisting a dataset drawn from real traffic, use uaef.security.PIIDetector to detect and redact personally identifiable information such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers.
Example notebooks
If you want to see more examples, check our notebooks/ folder. The notebooks cover scenarios such as batch evaluation, multi-turn conversations, multi-agent, and experiment management across frameworks including LangGraph, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
| Notebook | What it covers | 
| 00_langgraph.ipynb | LangGraph: single, batch, multi-turn, and multi-agent evaluation | 
| 02_langchain.ipynb | LangChain agents | 
| 04_json.ipynb | Custom frameworks, through the generic JSON adapter | 
| 05_strands.ipynb | Strands Agents, including multi-agent | 
| 06_agentcore.ipynb | Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, including multi-agent | 
| 07_langfuse.ipynb | Traces already collected in Langfuse | 
| 01_langgraph_ragas_deepeval.ipynb | RAGAS and DeepEval integrations | 
| 08_experiment_management.ipynb | Experiments, baselines, and regression detection | 
| 10_reporting_pipeline.ipynb | Reports and dashboards from stored results | 
| 11_pii_detection.ipynb | PII detection and redaction in traces | 
Clean up
Running the library creates nothing on its own, but persisting a run writes experiment metadata to Amazon DynamoDB and full results to Amazon S3. Delete both when you no longer need the saved experiments. The default names are uaef-experiments and uaef-results, overridable through the UAEF_DYNAMODB_TABLE and UAEF_S3_BUCKET environment variables. The bucket has to be emptied before it can be deleted.
If you deployed the service, the service deployment guide has the teardown sequence for both deployment modes. Read its retained-resources note before you assume teardown is complete: the DynamoDB tables, S3 buckets, and Amazon Cognito user pool are created with a retain policy, so deleting the stack leaves them, and their contents, in place. That is deliberate, so a teardown does not destroy saved experiments, but it means the storage keeps costing you until you remove it yourself.
Conclusion
UAEF separates agent evaluation from the framework that produced the agent. Adapters convert traces from LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Langfuse into a common format, and a generic JSON adapter handles other frameworks. The same 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions then apply regardless of how a team built the agent. UAEF evaluates individual traces or runs batch evaluations over historical traces, then stores results per experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Teams can then compare runs across agent versions, detect regressions, and use the generated reports and insights to decide what to change in the next iteration. The web UI and the Python library share the same evaluation engine, so teams can start low-code and move to code without changing how scoring or storage works.
To get started, see the open source repository.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 11, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 11, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here’s the roundup for Wednesday, November 11, 2026.
From Kunal Shah’s plans for WhatsApp’s next phase to a pilot-turned-entrepreneur blending Ayurveda with modern science, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Featured stories
This pilot-turned-entrepreneur blends Ayurveda with modern science to build a wellness brand for women
After spending a decade flying for IndiGo, Natasha Chaudhary is spreading her wings in a different direction.
On October 1, she took off on an entrepreneurial journey with the launch of Everyday You, a women’s health and wellness brand, after a year of research, formulation and building the business.
Natasha’s idea is simple yet profound for women navigating the health concerns that come with middle age. Her take is pragmatic. “You don’t have to suffer through it all,” she says.
Latest news
Kunal Shah outlines WhatsApp’s next phase with AI, payments, richer conversations
WhatsApp is preparing to move beyond messaging, making conversations more expressive, bringing everyday transactions into the app and using artificial intelligence (AI) to handle practical tasks. CEO Kunal Shah set out these priorities in a post on X, more than four months after succeeding Will Cathcart as WhatsApp’s global head.
“We want anything you do on WhatsApp to be as simple as sending a message,” Shah wrote.
Other news
BITS Pilani Hyderabad develops system to convert food waste into animal feed
Researchers at BITS Pilani Hyderabad have developed a low-cost black soldier fly system that converts food waste into protein-rich animal feed. Developed by Prof. Sankar Ganesh Palani and research graduate Dr Atun Roy Choudhury, the system uses larvae to process vegetable, fruit and cooked food waste in approximately two weeks. Built using readily available materials, it costs Rs 2,500 and requires limited space.
Initial trials recorded a yield of around 2 kg of larvae daily over 20 days. The larvae contain approximately 20% protein and 25% fat, making them potential feed ingredients for poultry, pig farming and aquaculture. The residual material, known as frass, can also be used as a soil amendment. The system is designed for hotels, hospitals, educational institutions and residential communities.
IIT Madras Pravartak, BodhBridge launch free online skill training
IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation has partnered with BodhBridge Education to offer free live online training programmes for school students, teachers and educators from November 2026 to January 2027. Students in Classes 7 to 12 can enrol in courses covering AI fundamentals, electric vehicles, future mobility, entrepreneurship, design thinking and innovation.
Teachers and educators can access training in career counselling, leadership development, classroom management and student engagement. The programmes combine expert-led sessions, case studies and practical activities to develop problem-solving, communication and innovation skills. Training is free, with optional certification from IIT Madras Pravartak. More than 45,000 teachers have previously benefited from its free training programmes.
EkaCare selected by NHA to develop AI-powered voice scribe for public healthcare
Bengaluru-based health AI company EkaCare has been selected by the National Health Authority (NHA) as a technology partner for its Ambient AI-enabled Voice Scribe under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. The solution converts doctor-patient consultations into structured digital health records, supporting over 15 Indian languages and mixed-language conversations.
Built on EkaCare’s open-weight Parrotlet-A 2.5 Pro speech model and open-source Lipi agentic framework, it generates clinical notes covering patient history, medications, diagnosis and treatment plans in FHIR format. Doctors must review and approve notes before they are linked to patients’ ABHA accounts. The system will operate on NHA infrastructure powered by AWS and is designed for secure deployment within NHA-controlled environments. Hospitals can integrate it with existing management systems through embedded software or APIs.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: Solo hoy puedes llevarte (en el Single Day de MediaMarkt) esta PS Portal por apenas 180 euros
articles.text:
Aunque el 11.11 de AliExpress es una de las campañas más esperadas hoy, MediaMarkt ha decidido contraatacar y está celebrando su propio Single Day hasta mañana a las 9 de la mañana. Uno de los chollos más atractivos que hemos encontrado (sobre todo para los usuarios que juegan en PS5) es la PlayStation Portal, que ahora puedes llevártela por 180,96 euros, alcanzando así su precio mínimo histórico.
Streaming a 1080p, ergonomía de mando DualSense y pantalla de 8 pulgadas
A diferencia de las consolas portátiles independientes con procesador propio, la PS Portal actúa como una extensión inalámbrica de tu PS5 a través de la red WiFi de casa. Esto te permite liberar la tensión principal de tu hogar manteniendo la misma experiencia háptica y de inmersión que ofrece la consola de sobremesa.
La PlayStation Portal incorpora un panel táctil LCD de 8 pulgadas con resolución Full HD (1.080p) a 60 fps, ofreciendo una nitidez excelente para apreciar los detalles gráficos de los juegos de PS5 en la palma de tu mano.
Además, integra controles DualSense, por lo que mantiene la retroalimentación háptica y los gatillos adaptativos originales del mando de Sony, conservando la vibración inmersiva y la resistencia variable en cada acción.
Se conecta de forma remota mediante Remote Play. Así que solo basta encender el dispositivo y conectarlo a la red WiFi local para encender la PS5 en reposo de forma remota y empezar a jugar al instante sin latencia apreciable.
La PS Portal cuenta con salida de audio jack de 3,5 mm y PlayStation Link, por lo que permite conectar auriculares de cable estándar o vincular auriculares con la tecnología de audio sin pérdidas de propiedad de Sony.
Aunque originalmente, solo se podía usar PS Portal de forma remota con tu PS5, desde hace un tiempo, esto cambió, ya que se puede usar para jugar en la nube sin tener una PS5. Para ello solo necesitarás una conexión estable a Internet y una suscripción activa a PlayStation Plus Premium. Eso sí, para la primera conexión si necesitarás tener la consola de Sony.

articles.title: SA’s fintechs want to become more than payment providers
articles.text:
South Africa’s fintechs have spent years making it easier to move money. Now they want to help people and businesses access it when they need it most.
Yoco’s $100 million credit facility from Victory Park Capital, a United States investment firm, is the latest sign of that shift. The South African payments and fintech company is expanding its cash advances business, betting that transaction data can help it finance small businesses that traditional banks struggle to assess.
The opportunity is substantial. But financing requires more than customer numbers and transaction volumes. It demands capital, risk management and the ability to finance responsibly to customers whose financial circumstances can change quickly.
The next phase of South Africa’s fintech boom will depend on whether companies can turn transaction data and customer relationships into sustainable financing businesses. South Africa’s fintech giants, Yoco, Optasia, and Paymenow, are pursuing this opportunity from different angles, responding to a common problem: consumers and small businesses need more than payment services to manage their finances.
South Africa fintechs move beyond payments
For Yoco, financing extends its relationship with independent businesses through card machines, point-of-sale software and online payments.
The company has advanced more than R6.5 billion ($395 million) to over 40,000 merchants since 2018, working with specialist credit providers. Its new facility is expected to give it greater control over the pricing and risk of its cash advances operation.
Yoco uses sales data to assess merchants and present funding offers through its app. Advances range from R2,000 ($122) to R1.5 million, with repayments deducted from daily takings rather than fixed monthly instalments.
The model reflects a broader shift in how fintechs assess borrowers. Traditional financial institutions often rely on credit histories, payslips and collateral. Payment platforms, however, can observe how businesses trade, how sales fluctuate and whether revenue can support financing.
That information could help identify viable businesses lacking the formal documentation conventional banks require.
The opportunity is significant. The 2025 Finfind and African Bank SA MSME Access to Finance Report estimates South Africa’s small-business financing gap at R350 billion ($21.3 billion). Small and medium-sized enterprises receive just 13% of national bank lending, compared with 51% for large corporations.
For fintechs, the gap offers an opportunity to build new revenue streams around customers they already serve.
A bigger market, a bigger responsibility for fintechs
Yoco is not alone. Optasia, which built its business around airtime advances distributed through telecommunications operators, is shifting towards broader microfinance services for consumers and small businesses.
The company generated $270 million in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, up 45% year-on-year. Microfinance contributed $194 million, or approximately 72% of group revenue, as Optasia pursued its ambition to derive more than 80% of revenue from these services.
Its expansion illustrates how alternative data and artificial intelligence are becoming central to digital finance. By analysing behavioural patterns and transaction signals, fintechs can assess customers with limited formal credit histories.
But identifying a potential borrower does not automatically mean financing is affordable or appropriate.
Optasia says its technology assesses not only whether customers qualify but also how much they can borrow and realistically afford to repay.
That distinction matters in a market where financial exclusion and vulnerability often coexist. FinMark Trust found that 75% of South Africans who borrowed in 2024 used credit to cover essentials such as food. Nedbank’s 2024 Financial Health Monitor found that 10% of workers had turned to payday lenders to manage financial stress, while 12% had borrowed from informal lenders.
The figures highlight demand for short-term financial support, but also the risk that financing could deepen the pressures it is meant to ease.
The cost of accessing money
Paymenow, an employee financial wellness and earned-wage access fintech, approaches the problem differently, allowing employees to access wages they have already earned before payday.
By 2026, the company reported serving more than 750,000 employees across South Africa, Namibia, Zambia and Pakistan. Its merger with PayCurve in May broadened its offering beyond wage access to include debt rehabilitation, savings and financial education.
The expansion reflects a wider understanding of financial inclusion. Giving customers access to money is one thing; helping them manage it is another.
For workers facing unexpected expenses, accessing earned wages may offer an alternative to expensive short-term borrowing. But its long-term value depends on whether it improves financial management rather than simply shifting pressure to an earlier point in the month.
The same applies to merchant cash advances. Flexible repayments can help businesses manage fluctuating sales, but deductions from daily takings may also leave less money for stock, wages and operating costs when revenue falls.
Can the fintechs’ economics hold?
Fintechs already have customer relationships, transaction data and digital distribution networks. Financing can deepen those relationships while creating revenue beyond payments.
But the economics are more complicated than identifying demand. Capital has a cost, defaults erode returns, and data cannot eliminate uncertainty when household budgets and small-business revenues remain under pressure.
Yoco says it has not recorded an unprofitable cohort of cash advances since beginning operations in 2018, including during the Covid-19 pandemic. However, it has not disclosed cohort-level performance figures, default rates or write-offs alongside its latest facility announcement.
Those details will become important as the business scales. The same scrutiny applies to Optasia’s microfinance expansion and Paymenow’s broader workplace financial services.
South Africa’s fintechs have made financial services more accessible. Their next test is whether they can turn that access into sustainable businesses. For a merchant waiting to restock or a worker counting down to payday, success is not another transaction. It is having enough money to keep going.

articles.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
articles.text:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.
Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.
JioHotstar’s benchmark setup for evaluating code retrieval approaches for AI coding agents. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)
The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.
CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.
The report also highlighted the importance of tool design. Agents frequently preferred familiar developer operations such as searching text, reading files, and locating symbols over higher-level abstractions that required additional verification.
Tool call breakdown by category across coding agent knowledge base approaches. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)
Siddharth Vaithinathan raised a broader architectural question in a LinkedIn post discussing the study:
Whether coding agents should understand not only the code but also the company that produced it. He argued that repository indexing alone cannot capture why architectural decisions were made, which constraints shaped them, or what earlier incidents taught the engineering team.
Vaithinathan suggested extending agent knowledge beyond code and documentation to include architecture, constraints, decisions, rationale, incidents, and outcomes. Such context could help agents evaluate existing design choices before proposing changes, particularly in systems where historical operational experience influences architectural decisions.
Tarun Bhargava raises a relevant question for benchmark interpretation, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.
Cost/accuracy numbers with multiple runs of the same setup.
JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

articles.title: Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb say almost nobody is using AI agents
articles.text:
In a nutshell: The promise that personal AI agents would revolutionize the way we use ride-hailing apps, order food, and book accommodation is looking a bit shaky right now. Leaders of these industries say almost nobody is using the likes of Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots to interact with their services. Uber, for example, said only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during the week of Halloween, its busiest week in October.
Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb have all said that AI agents are responsible for only hundreds of transactions on their platforms, a tiny fraction compared to the millions completed by real people daily.
Uber chief financial office Balaji Krishnamurthy said the company took around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats during the week of Halloween. In addition to just four rides being placed by AI agents, only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by these AIs.
"It is very, very early and very limited traction that we are seeing so far," said CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. "Listen, we hope that there will be more traction."
DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said it was a similar story at the food delivery company. He told analysts that AI agents have generated just several hundred orders in total since they became available. Muse launched on September 8, while Dots launched on September 29. DoorDash receives billions of orders globally each year.
More AI companies are offering personal agents, including Anthropic, Google, Instinct, and SpaceXAI. Muse was even top of the US App Store last month. But some say they are solutions in search of a problem.
In the case of Uber, Khosrowshahi pointed out that it takes most people around 50 seconds to book a ride and 90 seconds to reorder their favorite food. It's hard to imagine many people so pushed for time that they decide using an AI agent would be a more optimal method.
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky, meanwhile, said that of its nearly half a million daily bookings, only a negligible number are made through AI agents such as Muse and Instinct. Chesky pointed out most people like to research and plan their trips themselves, checking out which areas to stay in, what sights to see, and what the homes look like, rather than letting an AI make the choices.
Not many users want to put their faith in an AI, either. There have been plenty of stories about AI agents performing tasks they weren't supposed to – or going about it in a less-than-ethical way. One recent example was that of an Australian user who asked an agent to book a gym class. Wanting to get the user in quickly, it found a weakness in the booking platform's API, removed the person at the top of the class waitlist, and replaced them with the user.

articles.title: 3,500 laser-armed AI submarine drones patrol Norwegian salmon farms, killing sea lice and protecting 112 million fish — parasites get zapped by high-tech alternative to harsh chemical baths
articles.text:
3,500 laser-armed AI submarine robots patrol Norwegian salmon farms, killing sea lice and protecting 112 million fish — parasites get zapped by high-tech alternative to harsh chemical baths
Stingray systems are deployed in salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish.
Submarine AI laser robots have been a surefire success for Norwegian salmon farmers, according to the most recent annual report from the aptly named Stingray Marine Solutions. The Oslo, Norway-based firm now has over 3,500 units deployed around salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish. Stingray deployments are up by about 1,000 over the last year. This operation has grown to become one of the largest commercial AI deployments in Scandinavia.
These high-tech AI-enhanced submarines protect 20-25% of farmed salmon in the country, according to the latest figures. Using this high-tech AI laser solution to ‘optically delouse’ the salmon means fish don’t have to be passed through harsh chemical baths to prevent infestations of these tiny parasitic crustaceans. The result is improved salmon growth and welfare, and consistently cleaner fish exhibit reduced mortality.
The video above shows a behind-the-scenes peek at the 250-employee-strong Stingray operation. There’s some colorful laser action with two Stingrays seen zapping away in a salmon pen included in the clip. They use AI to recognize and target the sea lice.
Sea lice are a big problem for fish farmers, with the control of these parasites being a central challenge for the industry. Traditionally, measures such as chemical treatments were used to help control the buildup of sea lice. However, while chemicals can treat a large number of fish simultaneously, they can be bad for the environment, can stress fish, lice can develop resistance, and the introduction of any kind of poison or toxin into food production isn’t usually good for humans either.
In contrast, the Stingray AI laser system identifies and targets only sea lice, works continuously 24/7 as the fish go around normally in their pens, and avoids any chemical introduction or resistance issues. The reduction in sea lice around the farming area is better for other wild fish populations nearby, too.
Solutions like Stingray do have a few drawbacks. Primarily, fish farming businesses might look sheepishly at the up-front costs of deployment. Moreover, it might be best used as a preventative measure, keeping localized lice populations low. The Stingray’s range is limited now by its deployment in the salmon pens, so lice can gather in darker, murkier corners and outside their patrol area.

articles.title: Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
articles.text:
Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more.
Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
Tabletop provides customizable, collaborative spaces for all your personal planning needs.
“Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.”
Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist, and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.

articles.title: 5,4 Milliarden Tonnen CO2 weniger pro Jahr? Was am großen KI-Versprechen noch dran ist
articles.text:
Sam Altman versprach die „Rettung des Klimas“ durch KI: Was ist davon heute übrig?
Während sich Vertreter aus aller Welt im türkischen Antalya zur Klimakonferenz der Vereinten Nationen treffen, dürfte ein Thema die Gespräche dominieren: Künstliche Intelligenz. Das Gastgeberland hat die Teilnehmenden bereits aufgefordert, sich zu verpflichten, KI so zu konzipieren und zu betreiben, dass sie den Klimaschutz stützt. Wie viel Effekt diese Selbstverpflichtung hat, sei dahingestellt. Bislang tut die Industrie weltweit jedenfalls bei weitem nicht genug – im Gegenteil. Statt die Technologie so zu nutzen, dass sie tatsächlich die Treibhausgasemissionen senkt, sorgt Big Tech für neue Emissionen.
Doch zunächst zum optimistischen Teil. Noch 2024 erklärte Sam Altman, CEO von OpenAI, dass KI „erstaunliche Erfolge“ für die Menschheit erzielen werde, darunter die „Rettung des Klimas“. Im Jahr zuvor schrieben die Leiterin der Nachhaltigkeitsabteilung bei Google und ein Co-Autor in einem Gastbeitrag im Magazin Fortune, dass KI die globalen CO₂-Emissionen bis 2030 um 5 bis 10 Prozent absenken könnte.
Die strittige Frage: Hilft KI nun gegen den Klimawandel oder nicht?
Mittlerweile hat eine Reihe von Wissenschaftler:innen diese Behauptungen aus dem Bereich KI und Klimaschutz untersucht. Dabei gibt es durchaus positive Stimmen. Eine im vergangenen Jahr veröffentlichte, bereits von Fachkolleg:innen begutachtete Studie unter der Leitung von Forscher:innen des Grantham Research Institute der London School of Economics und des Unternehmens Systemiq gibt sich optimistisch. KI kann nach den Grantham-Prognosen bis 2035 dazu beitragen, die weltweiten Emissionen um umgerechnet 3,2 bis 5,4 Milliarden Tonnen Kohlendioxid pro Jahr zu senken. Was im oberen Bereich in etwa den jährlichen gesamten energiebezogenen Emissionen der USA entspricht, selbst nach Abzug des eigenen Energieverbrauchs von KI. Diese potenziellen Einsparungen konzentrieren sich demnach auf drei Sektoren: Stromerzeugung, Fleisch- und Milchwirtschaft sowie Fahrzeugemissionen.
Doch Prognosen wie diese sind nur so gut wie unsere Bereitschaft, sie anhand der heutigen Realität zu überprüfen. Gibt es also Belege dafür, dass die größten Unternehmen in diesen drei Sektoren beginnen, KI entsprechend den Prognosen der Studie zu integrieren. Und wenn ja: Entsprechen die Ergebnisse den Erwartungen? Oder ist die Zahl für 2035 noch immer größtenteils ein Wunschziel?

articles.title: Indústria automotiva brasileira perde espaço para veículos importados
articles.text:
A produção e as vendas de veículos no Brasil recuaram em outubro na comparação com setembro. Dados divulgados nesta quarta-feira (11) pela Associação Nacional dos Fabricantes de Veículos Automotores (Anfavea) mostram que a fabricação de automóveis e comerciais leves, caminhões e ônibus caiu 5,1% no período. Já os emplacamentos no mercado interno tiveram retração de 5,6%.
Apesar do resultado negativo na comparação mensal, os indicadores permaneceram no campo positivo em relação a outubro de 2025. A produção cresceu 2,7%, enquanto as vendas avançaram 1,8%.
A indústria brasileira produziu 254,5 mil veículos em outubro. No mercado interno, foram registrados 265,5 mil emplacamentos. No acumulado de janeiro a outubro, a produção chegou a 2,420 milhões de unidades, alta de 8% em relação ao mesmo intervalo do ano passado. As vendas somaram 2,522 milhões de veículos, crescimento de 16,1%.
Exportações caem e importações avançam
- O comércio exterior apresentou cenário menos favorável para as montadoras instaladas no Brasil. Em outubro, as exportações somaram 29,1 mil veículos, queda de 28,3% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025. Na comparação com setembro, o recuo foi de 26,9%;
- Entre janeiro e outubro, os embarques para outros países totalizaram 363,1 mil unidades, redução de 23,5% na comparação anual;
- Segundo a Anfavea, o desempenho está relacionado à perda de participação dos fabricantes brasileiros em mercados vizinhos, especialmente diante da concorrência de produtos provenientes da Ásia e do México. A Argentina, historicamente o principal destino das exportações nacionais, também enfrenta retração nas vendas internas;
- Na direção oposta, as importações continuam crescendo. O Brasil recebeu 56,7 mil veículos estrangeiros em outubro, alta de 22,3% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025. Na comparação mensal, o volume ficou praticamente estável, com recuo de 0,8%;
- No acumulado do ano, as importações chegaram a 520,7 mil unidades, crescimento de 29,5%.
Leia mais:
- BYD fecha acordo com a TIM para conectar 200 mil carros no Brasil
- Justiça proíbe programa da Uber que faz motorista pagar para conseguir passageiros
- Free flow: motoristas recebem aviso pelo WhatsApp para quitar débitos
Um dos destaques desse movimento é a presença dos fabricantes chineses no mercado brasileiro. Segundo a associação, os modelos provenientes da China já somam 288 mil emplacamentos, o dobro dos 143 mil veículos argentinos. A mudança representa inversão em relação à liderança histórica da Argentina entre as origens dos automóveis importados pelo Brasil.
A combinação entre o avanço das importações e a retração das exportações levou a balança comercial de autoveículos a registrar déficit de 157,6 mil unidades nos dez primeiros meses de 2026. No mesmo período do ano passado, o setor havia apresentado superávit.
O presidente da Anfavea, Igor Calvet, afirmou que o cenário representa mudança importante na dinâmica do comércio exterior brasileiro. Ele também destacou que, mesmo com o imposto de importação de 35%, o Brasil está entre os países produtores que menos impõem limites à entrada de veículos estrangeiros.
Veículos eletrificados crescem no Brasil
Enquanto o comércio exterior enfrenta dificuldades, os veículos eletrificados ampliam sua participação no mercado brasileiro. Entre janeiro e outubro de 2026, foram comercializadas 495,7 mil unidades de automóveis e comerciais leves eletrificados, crescimento de 125,7% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025.
Com isso, esses modelos passaram a representar 20,5% dos emplacamentos de veículos leves novos no país. No ano passado, a participação era de 10,7%.
Os veículos totalmente elétricos, por sua vez, já correspondem a 7,4% das vendas de automóveis e comerciais leves no acumulado de 2026.
Outro fator apontado pela Anfavea para estimular o mercado interno é o Programa Carro Sustentável, lançado em julho de 2025. Desde o início da iniciativa, foram emplacadas 671 mil unidades de modelos contemplados. Apenas nos dez primeiros meses deste ano, foram 412,8 mil veículos, alta de 22,3% na comparação anual.
O segmento de veículos pesados, por outro lado, continua enfrentando dificuldades. As vendas de caminhões recuaram 4,1% no acumulado até outubro, enquanto a produção caiu 4,7% em relação aos dez primeiros meses de 2025. Segundo a Anfavea, o programa Move Brasil contribuiu para estimular a demanda e evitar retração ainda maior.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Starlink Mini 2 es oficial: batería intercambiable, Wi‑Fi 6 y conexión satelital en segundos
articles.text:
Starlink ha renovado su equipo más portátil con una nueva antena diseñada para ofrecer acceso a internet satelital prácticamente desde cualquier lugar. La nueva Starlink Mini 2 incluye una batería intercambiable que ofrece hasta 4,5 horas de autonomía con una sola carga. En caso de que el usuario necesite extender el tiempo de conexión, podrá sustituirla por otra batería de repuesto de forma sencilla.
Junto con la nueva batería, otra de las novedades del Mini 2 es que ofrece soporte para Wi-Fi 6. De acuerdo con Starlink, la cobertura inalámbrica alcanza unos 167 metros cuadrados, superando a los 111 metros que ofrecía su predecesor. La antena también es más delgada y resistente que la generación anterior, manteniendo la certificación IP67 que la protege de condiciones adversas como lluvia, polvo o arena.
Al igual que ocurría con el Starlink Mini, el usuario solo necesita colocar el dispositivo en un lugar con una vista despejada del cielo. La antena se comunicará con los satélites de Starlink y compartirá la conexión con los dispositivos que desees a través del Wi-Fi. Según la compañía, la Mini 2 puede ponerse en línea en apenas 60 segundos y opera tanto con batería como conectada a la corriente eléctrica a través de un cargador USB-C de 60 vatios.
"Con materiales más resistentes, una carcasa rediseñada y una certificación IP67, el Mini 2 está diseñado para mantenerte conectado durante la lluvia en el sendero, el viento en el agua y la arena en la playa", mencionó SpaceX en una publicación de su cuenta de X.
Starlink Mini 2: con batería intercambiable pero más caro
Lamentablemente, el Starlink Mini 2 no cuenta con puerto Ethernet, por lo que no podrás aprovechar al 100% toda la conexión que llega desde el satélite. De acuerdo con la web, la antena tendrá un coste de 999 dólares en Estados Unidos e incluye roaming ilimitado. A esto tendrás que sumarle el coste del plan mensual, que parte en los 45 euros al mes para usuarios en movimiento.
En comparación con el primer Starlink Mini, el Mini 2 cuesta tres veces más. Originalmente, la compañía lanzó la antena en 399 euros en 2024, pero después aplicó un recorte de 100 euros para hacerla más atractiva. Starlink también ha lanzado promociones en el país que ofrecen conexión a internet por 10 euros durante los primeros 3 meses, esta última sin necesidad de pagar por el hardware o la antena.
No está de más mencionar que Starlink Mini está pensado para el público que está en constante movimiento, o que vive en lugares donde la fibra o la cobertura móvil no llegan. Personas como los viajeros frecuentes, profesionales que trabajan en campo o aficionados al aire libre pueden sacar provecho de la conectividad satelital de SpaceX. La ventaja de contar con una batería intercambiable en la Mini 2 permitirá que te puedas alejar de un tomacorriente sin temor a quedarte sin internet.
Por ahora, Starlink Mini 2 se encuentra en fase de reserva por invitación. La antena se comenzará a vender a los usuarios de Estados Unidos, aunque posteriormente se ampliará a otros países en donde el servicio ya se encuentra operando.

articles.title: Dukosi Samples Contactless Battery Communication System - EE Times
articles.text:
BUDAPEST, Hungary – At the Pretzl Connect 2026 press event, Edinburgh-based Dukosi announced it has begun commercial sampling of its DK-NFLNK, a contactless intra-battery communication solution designed to eliminate wiring harnesses and improve battery safety.
By transmitting voltage and temperature data wirelessly across a single bus antenna via near-field RF rather than copper cabling, the system removes failure points from the battery architecture, contributes to real-time thermal monitoring using data collected from Dukosi’s DKCMS chips, and supports data tracking helpful for the battery passport.
The Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council mandates that “From 18 February 2027 each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh, and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service shall have an electronic record (‘battery passport’).”
Vulnerability of physical cabling
“Connector failure rates in a conventional wiring harness are around 10 parts per million,” said Joseph Notaro, president of Dukosi in Budapest. “In the automotive and industrial arenas where you’re looking at parts-per-billion-level reliability, that failure rate is simply too high and an unacceptable risk of failure.”
Wired networks also risk galvanic coupling between high-voltage circuits and low-voltage controls, plus added labor and weight. “With contactless technology, we decouple the high-voltage circuits and get rid of the physical connectors, which makes the system safer, higher quality, and more reliable over its entire operating life,” Notaro said.
Synchronous sensing at cell level
At the heart of Dukosi’s architecture is C-SynQ, a protocol that uses near-field radio signals along a single bus antenna wire. The signals operate at the cell level and stay within the enclosure, providing noise immunity without the need for line of sight.
“Smarter battery management starts with better data, and better data starts at the individual cell,” Notaro said. “When you’re deciding available power or charge limits, you want every cell being measured at the same time under the same conditions. That’s the technical equivalent of taking a high-speed photo of every cell at the same time.”
Notaro continued, “The weakest cell dictates the state of charge and the overall performance of the pack. If you don’t measure the cells in synchronization, then measurement errors creep in, and you’re forced to add in design margins, which in turn limit performance.”
Early warning for thermal safety
Li-ion battery safety is all about preventing thermal runaway. A short circuit in one cell can trigger an exothermic reaction that then spreads to adjacent cells. Older pack designs had only two or three temperature sensors across the whole module, so they didn’t monitor individual cells.
“In the traditional layouts with very sparse temperature sensing, the heat from a failing cell can take 10 to 15 minutes to get to an external sensor,” Notaro said. “With sensing capability on every cell, temperature excursions are detected almost immediately, well before the heat has a chance to propagate to the adjacent cells.”
Cell-level monitoring lets the software run outlier-detection algorithms by comparing the thermal profiles of the various cells and flagging minor deviations before they become a problem.
“Some manufacturers try to cut costs by getting rid of the sensors and just assuming the cells are all the same,” Notaro said. “Every chemical manufacturing process has variation. You can’t have a battery pack that’s that uniform and then ignore the cell-level monitoring without increasing your operating risk.”
During the briefing, EE Times asked whether battery manufacturers in China take a different approach to monitoring and safety compared to companies in other regions, specifically questioning if their strategies are primarily cost-driven.
Notaro responded that China actually has two distinct tiers of customers: One that prioritizes safety and total system value, and another strictly focused on short-term component costs. He emphasized that this split is not unique to China, as carmakers globally divide between safety-conscious and cost-driven mindsets.
He added that the massive volume of EVs in China provides domestic manufacturers with extensive operational data, accelerating their ability to refine battery quality over time.
Usable energy and lifetime traceability
Measurement precision directly affects usable energy capacity. The Dukosi Cell Monitoring System (DKCMS), built around the DK8102 Cell Monitor chip and DK8202 System Hub, directly addresses the system measurement errors that traditionally degrade usable battery capacity. “By providing consistent cell-level data, operators can reduce safety buffers and increase usable energy by 6% to 12%,” Notaro said. “You are not altering cell chemistry or adding weight; you are simply extracting energy previously locked away by measurement margins.”
For utility-scale energy storage, that efficiency gain has a direct financial impact. In a 200-MW installation, you can generate $8 million in additional revenue from the extra capacity or reduce capex by $2 million by needing fewer cells.
Dukosi’s monitoring technology could also support the collection of operational data relevant to the EU Battery Passport. From Feb. 18, 2027, batteries covered by the EU Batteries Regulation will require an electronic record containing information about their identification, composition, performance, and health. DKCMS chips incorporate onboard non-volatile memory and a unique silicon identifier attached to each cell.
“Every cell has its own digital passport on chip, which records the maximum temperature it’s ever seen, its voltage history, and total charge cycles,” Notaro said. “When the battery has finished its life in the car, the recyclers and integrators simply read the chip to determine the health of the cell, which allows them to sort it efficiently for either grid use or recycling.”
Bridges to adoption for legacy architectures
While chip-on-cell represents a move to smart cell architectures, Dukosi said DK-NFLNK is an upgrade path for manufacturers still using traditional module design. The system connects the node chip to the analog front ends via a serial interface, enabling wireless capability without changing the module hardware structure.
“DK-NFLNK and our full cell monitoring system are built on the same C-SynQ communication platform, giving battery manufacturers a real migration path,” Notaro concluded. “The engineers can upgrade their architecture today and move to full chip-on-cell monitoring in future product cycles.”
Dukosi’s monitoring technologies are now in commercial testing across several sectors. Nordic Marine Power has received DNV maritime approval for its PowerStack system using Dukosi monitoring, and Yichuan Intelligent Technology has incorporated the system into marine vessels in China.
As battery production scales globally, the industry is moving beyond pack manufacturing to long-term reliability and data.

articles.title: Tesla fait homologuer le FSD dans un pays aux conditions parmi les plus hostiles d'Europe
articles.text:
Depuis que les Pays-Bas lui ont accordé une homologation provisoire en avril 2026, Tesla avance pays par pays en Europe avec son FSD, car le vote de l’Union européenne n’a toujours pas eu lieu. C’est désormais au tour de la Finlande de rejoindre l’Estonie, la Croatie ou encore la Belgique. Son autorité des transports, Traficom, a reconnu ce mardi 10 novembre l’homologation néerlandaise et a annoncé sa décision ce mercredi 11 novembre. Dans la foulée, Tesla Europe a confirmé sur X que le déploiement commencerait « bientôt ».
Le pays avait prévenu. En juin, Traficom se disait prêt à aller plus vite que Bruxelles, dont le vote était alors attendu en octobre. Dans son avis publié à l’époque, l’autorité listait les points à vérifier sur les routes finlandaises : le temps qu’il faut au conducteur pour reprendre la main, les dépassements quand la visibilité est mauvaise, et le décalage de vitesse (speed offset), un réglage qui permet au système de rouler jusqu’à 50 % au-dessus de la limite détectée. C’est ce point qui inquiétait la Suède et la Norvège, voisines de la Finlande. Pour mémoire, environ 6 500 voitures immatriculées en Finlande étaient alors équipées pour utiliser le système, soit 0,24 % des 2,7 millions de voitures particulières du pays.
Pour obtenir ce feu vert, Tesla a dû retoucher son logiciel. Selon Traficom, le conducteur ne peut plus demander au système de rouler en permanence au-dessus de la limite. Les réglages qui autorisent un dépassement reviennent aussi à zéro à chaque redémarrage de la voiture. Les informations sur la vitesse choisie par le système sont enfin plus complètes. Elle a aussi abandonné en Europe le nom Full Self-Driving (« conduite entièrement autonome »), que le ministère allemand des Transports jugeait trompeur. Le système s’appelle désormais Tesla Assisted Driving (Tesla Conduite Assistée en France et en Belgique) sur le continent.
La neige peut encore aveugler les caméras
La Finlande offre un terrain exigeant. Traficom a évalué le système sur des routes limitées entre 60 et 100 km/h, où les virages et les bosses masquent souvent la visibilité. Pour autant, l’autorité ne cache pas les limites d’un système qui se repère uniquement avec ses caméras.
Dans son communiqué, Jukka Juhola, expert principal chez Traficom, explique que l’hiver a été pris en compte dans l’évaluation. Il prévient cependant que le système peut être limité « lorsque les caméras sont recouvertes de neige, de neige fondue ou d’autres saletés », et lorsque les conditions de circulation deviennent plus complexes que d’habitude.
Le vote européen attendu cet hiver
Le vote européen qui décidera de l’homologation finale et globale du FSD doit avoir lieu au cours de l’hiver, lors de la prochaine réunion du Comité technique des véhicules à moteur (TCMV) prévue le 1er décembre. Pour mémoire, le texte doit réunir une majorité qualifiée, soit au moins 15 des 27 États membres représentant 65 % de la population de l’Union. S’il est favorable, il faudra environ trois semaines pour que l’autorisation s’applique dans toute l’Union, France comprise. Afin de faciliter l’adoption de son logiciel, Tesla a accepté d’autres modifications réclamées par les États membres, comme la Lettonie.
