articles.title: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Secure Software and Firmware in Connected Devices
articles.text:
Product security firm Finite State announced on Tuesday that it raised $27 million in a Series C funding round to grow its international presence and make its connected device security platform more autonomous.
Private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund led the round, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners.
The company tied the investment to two pressures on manufacturers. One is a wave of critical flaws uncovered by AI-powered research in October, dubbed the ‘Vulnpocalypse’, and the other is a growing set of product security mandates.
Finite State’s platform inspects the code that actually ships in a device, covering both software and firmware. It works from compiled firmware and binaries, so source code is not required.
Its users are makers of vehicles, medical devices, industrial equipment, consumer electronics and utility infrastructure. The platform identifies both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and helps manufacturers fix the ones that can be exploited.
On the compliance side, the platform continuously produces SBOMs, VEX documents and signed compliance packages to help device makers meet regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA). The company also cites FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, the UNECE R155 and R156 vehicle regulations, and the IEC 62443 industrial standard among the rules manufacturers face.
AI agents carry out analysis, triage and testing on the platform and draft regulatory reports. Customers can also connect their own agents through an API and an MCP server.
“The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it,” said Matt Wyckhouse, founder and CEO of Finite State. “Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers.”

articles.text:
Home >

                                                                Variable-Length Prompts on Chimera GPNPU                                                    
Low Power-High Performance
                        WHITEPAPERS
		
How a flexible binary can serve every length up to the capacity you set.
								November 11th, 2026 - 
								By: Quadric.io
								
							
If you are sizing a language model for an edge product, the prompts it will see span a wide range. A spoken command is a dozen tokens, a pasted document is several thousand, and the same device serves both. Somewhere in the software stack, a decision is made about the gap between the longest prompt you provisioned for and the prompt that actually arrives. That decision sets how many binaries you build and qualify. It also sets how much of every inference is spent computing padding.
Most compiled inference stacks do not make that decision at all. A graph compiled for 1024 tokens processes 1024 positions every time it runs. If you send it 50 tokens, it computes the other 974 as padding. To serve short prompts efficiently as well as long ones, you have to build a separate binary for each length range and qualify all of them. Quadric Chimera GPNPU does not work this way. It gives you one guarantee and one optimization.

articles.title: 3 protections déjà incluses dans votre VPN, et que presque personne n’active
articles.text:
Vous utilisez peut-être un VPN pour masquer votre adresse IP ou protéger votre connexion. Pourtant, si vous avez souscrit à CyberGhost, il est probable que vous disposiez d’outils supplémentaires très utiles afin de sécuriser davantage votre navigation et vos données personnelles. Voici comment les activer.
Installer l’application de votre VPN sur un smartphone ou un ordinateur et cliquer sur le bouton de connexion suffit pour chiffrer votre trafic Internet par le biais d’un serveur privé virtuel.
Certaines offres limitées s’arrêtent là, mais ce n’est pas le cas de CyberGhost : en plus d’une connexion VPN, ce service donne accès à plusieurs outils et fonctionnalités utiles, mais pas toujours connus des utilisateurs. Quelques minutes suffisent pour les configurer.
CyberGhost VPN en fait plus que vous ne le pensez
CyberGhost VPN permet de protéger jusqu’à sept appareils simultanément. Ses applications sont disponibles sur Windows, macOS, Linux, Android et iOS, ainsi que sur certains téléviseurs et boîtiers multimédias.
En plus de ses milliers de serveurs répartis dans 100 pays, CyberGhost propose des fonctions moins visibles, mais très utiles. Leur emplacement varie selon l’appareil, et certaines doivent être activées depuis l’espace client.
Soyez alerté en cas de fuite de données personnelles
Les fuites de données sont fréquentes, et toutes ne sont pas systématiquement signalées. Votre adresse e-mail peut donc apparaître dans une base de données compromise sans que vous le sachiez.
Pour rester à l’affût de ce genre de situation, vous pouvez activer l’outil ID Guard de CyberGhost. Ce dernier peut surveiller jusqu’à deux adresses e-mail. Pour l’utiliser, connectez-vous à votre compte sur le site de CyberGhost, puis ouvrez la rubrique « ID Guard ». Vous serez alors guidé dans l’ajout de vos adresses e-mail.
Une fois cette étape terminée, le service effectuera des recherches dans les fuites connues et vous alertera s’il détecte quelque chose concernant vos données.
En complément, CyberGhost propose Password Checker. Cet outil permet de vérifier si un mot de passe figure dans une base de données compromise. Le principe est donc le même qu’ID Guard : vous alerter dès qu’un risque concret de piratage de compte est identifié, afin de vous permettre d’agir rapidement en modifiant vos accès.
Limitez le partage de vos données et le pistage publicitaire
Inclus gratuitement dans l’abonnement, Privacy Guard permet aux utilisateurs de Windows de contrôler plus finement les informations que leur ordinateur partage avec Microsoft. Il agit notamment sur les réglages du Microsoft Store, d’Edge, de Defender, des mises à jour de Windows et de la synchronisation.
Pour l’utiliser, ouvrez l’application CyberGhost sous Windows, sélectionnez « Privacy Guard » dans la barre latérale, puis cliquez sur « Commencer ». Vous pouvez ensuite choisir le niveau de confidentialité de votre choix, et même personnaliser certains paramètres.
Il faut noter que Privacy Guard ne bloque pas lui-même les publicités présentes sur les sites. Cette mission revient à Content Blocker, un autre outil inclus qui bloque les domaines connus pour diffuser des publicités, des traqueurs ou certains contenus malveillants. Sous Windows, il s’active dans la rubrique « Privacy Settings » de l’application, grâce à l’interrupteur « Block content ». Il est également proposé sur Android, mais sa disponibilité varie selon les plateformes.
Automatisez la protection des Wi-Fi publics
Les réseaux Wi-Fi publics des gares ou des hôtels sont utiles, mais ils sont peu sécurisés. Pour autant, tout le monde n’a pas le réflexe d’activer son VPN au moment de s’y connecter. C’est là que les Smart Rules de CyberGhost entrent en jeu : elles évitent cet oubli en lançant automatiquement une connexion sécurisée.
Pour activer cette fonction sous Windows, rendez-vous dans les paramètres de CyberGhost, puis dans la rubrique « Smart Rules ». Dans la partie consacrée à la protection Wi-Fi, plusieurs comportements peuvent être définis selon le type de réseau détecté. Vous pouvez notamment demander à l’application de toujours lancer le VPN lorsqu’elle reconnaît un réseau non sécurisé ou inconnu. Vous pouvez aussi sélectionner à l’avance le serveur ou le pays dans lequel vous désirez situer virtuellement votre connexion.
CyberGhost peut se connecter automatiquement dès le démarrage de l’ordinateur, à l’ouverture d’une application précise ou lors d’une connexion sur un nouveau réseau Wi-Fi. Les intitulés peuvent différer sur macOS et Android, mais le principe est le même sur chaque plateforme.
CyberGhost à 2,19 € par mois pendant 26 mois
Si vous n’êtes pas encore abonné à CyberGhost, sachez qu’en ce moment, la formule incluant 24 mois d’abonnement et deux mois supplémentaires offerts coûte 2,19 € par mois. Les 26 mois sont facturés en une seule fois, soit 56,94 € hors taxes. CyberGhost occupe actuellement la première place du comparatif des meilleurs VPN de Clubic, avec une note de 9,8 sur 10.
Cependant, si vous préférez vous faire votre propre idée sur la qualité du service et de ses différentes fonctionnalités, l’abonnement comprend une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 45 jours. Une raison de plus de tester CyberGhost dès à présent.

articles.title: À la recherche de la preuve parfaite : Google a lâché 80 agents IA sur le code de Signal pour prouver qu’il était sûr
articles.text:
Le système a été baptisé AlphaProof Code.
Pendant quatre semaines, des équipes comptant jusqu’à 80 agents d’IA ont travaillé sans interruption sur les machines de cinq chercheurs de Google DeepMind, avec une mission précise, démontrer mathématiquement que le code qui chiffre les conversations Signal tient ses promesses de sécurité.
Google a dévoilé le résultat le 10 novembre 2026. Le travail porte sur libsignal, la bibliothèque qui met en œuvre le protocole de chiffrement de bout en bout de Signal, dont des variantes équipent aussi WhatsApp, Messenger et Google Messages.
Prouver plutôt que tester
D’ordinaire, on évalue la sécurité d’un logiciel en le testant, en l’auditant ou en y cherchant des failles, ce qui permet d’affirmer qu’aucun problème n’a été trouvé, sans garantir qu’il n’en existe aucun.
Mais il existe une autre approche, la vérification formelle.
Reposant sur des méthodes mathématiques, elle consiste à démontrer, comme on le ferait pour un théorème, que le code ne peut pas enfreindre certaines propriétés. Problème, la méthode est réputée extrêmement coûteuse. La vérification de seL4, un noyau de système d’exploitation dont des chercheurs australiens ont démontré formellement le bon fonctionnement en 2009, a par exemple demandé l’équivalent de vingt ans de travail pour une seule personne.
Et c’est à cela que s’est attaqué Google DeepMind avec AlphaProof Code.
Dans ce système, explique Google, « des experts humains travaillent avec l’IA pour décider de ce qu’il faut prouver, et un groupe d’agents IA s’en charge ».
Les chercheurs ont donc d’abord défini les propriétés à vérifier, en s’appuyant sur les travaux académiques consacrés à Signal. Les agents, fonctionnant eux avec le modèle Gemini 4 Carbon, ont ensuite rédigé environ 6,5 millions de lignes de démonstration dans le langage Lean, dont le vérificateur contrôle automatiquement chaque étape.
Aucun des chercheurs n’a écrit lui-même une ligne de preuve. « Nous avons décidé du périmètre et de l’ordre du travail, choisi les modèles de référence, guidé et approuvé les énoncés », résument-ils dans leur article technique.
Ce que Google a démontré
L’objectif principal était de prouver que le programme compilé de libsignal applique bel et bien le « ratchet », le mécanisme du protocole Signal qui renouvelle en permanence les clés de chiffrement au fil de la conversation, et qu’il en offre réellement les protections.
Ainsi, selon l’article technique, les preuves établissent qu’un attaquant parvenant à voler les clés stockées sur un téléphone ne pourrait pas pour autant lire les messages échangés auparavant, puisque chaque message est chiffré avec une clé dérivée de la précédente, puis effacée. Elles montrent aussi que la conversation redevient sûre dès que les deux interlocuteurs ont échangé de nouveaux messages, ceux-ci générant des clés neuves que l’attaquant ne connaît pas, et que personne ne peut se faire passer pour l’un des deux.
Pour vérifier que la méthode fonctionne, les chercheurs ont réintroduit deux anciens bugs de libsignal, corrigés depuis, et le système a démontré que ces versions n’offraient plus les garanties attendues.
Signal a réagi par la voix de son directeur technique Ehren Kret, qui a salué « une avancée majeure ».
Les équipes de Google ont tout de même tenu à mentionner les limites de ce travail de recherche. La preuve couvre uniquement les conversations à deux, et elle suppose que les briques cryptographiques de base fonctionnent parfaitement, sans les vérifier elles-mêmes. Elle porte aussi sur une version de test tournant sous Linux, et non sur les applications mobiles.
« Maintenant que les preuves deviennent bon marché, la question difficile devient de savoir quoi prouver » concluent les auteurs, qui en font la principale leçon de leur expérience.

articles.title: Why Nitric stopped asking one AI agent to do everything
articles.text:
Why Nitric stopped asking one AI agent to do everything
We’re a team of five engineers, and we used to wake the on-call engineer three or four times a week over production incidents. Most were noise rather than serious outages, but at two in the morning, being overly cautious seemed preferable to letting a genuine problem slip through the cracks.
We’ve since reduced both unnecessary overnight interruptions and recurring issues by iterating on triage and following investigations through to fixes. Specialized AI agents help us investigate incidents, organize follow-up work, and prepare changes, with engineers reviewing and correcting the work along the way.
What surprised us was how much more comfortable we became relying on the process. Engineers could inspect an assessment, challenge its assumptions, and use those corrections to improve how we handled later incidents. As follow-up fixes addressed recurring issues, we felt more confident about when to wake the on-call engineer.
That experience has made us question the shape of the work we give our agents. A capable coding agent could potentially investigate an incident, raise a ticket, and prepare a fix, so why divide those responsibilities?
“When an agent’s work needs correction, can you identify the responsibility involved and make a change you can evaluate independently?”
For us, it’s about improving one part of the workflow and judging whether the change helped. When an agent’s work needs correction, can you identify the responsibility involved and make a change you can evaluate independently?
A shared workspace for people and agents
We’re building Sugabots as an open-source, self-hosted workspace where a team can work with several agents on the same task. Engineers can ask questions, contribute evidence, review findings, and bring in another agent, with those exchanges available to other participants.
We organize that work into shared environments called pods, with connections to external systems through MCP. Each agent can have its own model and instructions, while the pod’s connections and tool policies define the access its agents share. The team can configure agents for specific responsibilities and refine their instructions as engineers review the work. Our incident workflow has helped us explore which responsibilities benefit from that separation.
How we run incident triage in Sugabots
Our incident workflow depends on each engineer or agent being able to continue from the evidence, decisions, and corrections recorded during the investigation.
Our Sentry triage agent investigates new, regressed, or escalating issues and decides whether to alert the on-call engineer, request an in-hours review, hand a small fix directly to an implementation agent, or keep the issue in Sentry for monitoring. It records follow-up work in Linear, where a backlog agent helps organize tickets, and the implementation agent can prepare a GitHub pull request for review.
Engineers participate throughout, reviewing findings, challenging urgency assessments, correcting assumptions, and deciding whether to ship a proposed change. The investigation remains available as work moves between people and agents.
Safeguards back that growing confidence. The instructions call for urgent escalation when an issue could plausibly be a production outage, and urgency is uncertain. Issues classified as noise are archived until escalating, and Sentry retains a direct spike-alert route to incident.io as a backup.
The follow-up matters as much as the initial assessment. Previously, the on-call engineer might investigate an alert, determine it could wait until office hours, and return to other work. Recording the underlying problem in the backlog and prioritizing it gave the team a chance to resolve it before the next on-call engineer encountered the same alert.
Having the backlog agent record follow-up work in Linear gives the team a consistent way to prioritize fixes for the recurring issues behind the interruptions.
Specialize around a decision
We configure each agent for a particular responsibility, choosing its model and instructions to suit the work and defining what a useful result looks like.
We chose Opus 5.5 for Sentry triage, and its instructions cover evidence gathering, classification, escalation, handoffs, and recovery from tool failures. This abbreviated excerpt shows the decisions we ask it to make:
Inspect the full Sentry issue, including customer impact, affected users, release, and event trend, then check for existing tickets or incidents.
Choose an outcome:
- Urgent: active customer harm requiring immediate attention; alert the on-call engineer through incident.io.
- In-hours review: a defect requiring engineering judgment that can wait; notify the on-call engineer at low urgency.
- Auto-fix: a small, non-urgent code change outside restricted areas such as authentication, billing, and migrations; brief the implementation agent to prepare a PR.
- No action: expected or transient noise; archive until escalating so a spike brings it back.
State the evidence and uncertainty behind the decision. Implementation briefs must stand alone and include the relevant findings and links.
The backlog manager’s instructions reflect the decisions involved in organizing follow-up work: checking for duplicates, looking up the current Linear cycle, and distinguishing actionable work from issues that need an engineer to clarify scope or make a design decision. Those rules provide defaults while preserving the team’s explicit choices about priority, assignment, and scheduling, and we can refine them independently of the criteria used to assess an incident’s urgency.
Triage and implementation make a useful comparison. Triage asks whether the available evidence justifies interrupting an engineer. Implementation asks what change would resolve the problem and how to verify it. Those decisions have different failure modes: a missed urgent incident, an unnecessary interruption, or a plausible fix that introduces another bug.
“Triage asks whether the available evidence justifies interrupting an engineer. Implementation asks what change would resolve the problem and how to verify it. Those decisions have different failure modes.”
We’ve found it useful to maintain those responsibilities separately because we can refine how incidents are classified while keeping the implementation instructions stable. If an investigation leads to an ineffective fix, we can examine the assessment’s accuracy, the evidence preserved in the ticket, and how the implementation addressed the recorded problem. Each gives us a specific part of the workflow to improve.
Each responsibility also gives us concrete questions to evaluate:
- Triage: Did it escalate genuinely urgent incidents? Did it unnecessarily interrupt an engineer?
- Backlog management: Did it record the follow-up work, recognize existing tickets, and preserve enough evidence to act on it?
- Implementation: Did the proposed change address the problem, and what did an engineer need to correct before accepting it?
We need to evaluate the reduction in wake-up calls alongside how we handle genuinely urgent incidents, including any that triage missed. Fewer interruptions could reflect both better classification and fixes that reduce the volume of incidents arriving. Those outcomes help us judge how the workflow is performing and where to improve it.
The same question applies to the agents already in your workflow: when their output improves, can you explain what improved and what evidence supports that judgment? Separating responsibilities gives you a narrower decision to examine and a clearer basis for evaluating changes.
Match permissions to responsibilities
Separating responsibilities also helps us decide which tool actions each agent needs and when an engineer should approve them.
Our triage instructions include specific write actions: creating Linear issues, sending alerts through incident.io, and archiving Sentry issues until escalating. Tool access needs to reflect those responsibilities, including which actions require an engineer’s approval.
Agent-specific instructions define responsibilities within the access available to the pod; they do not enforce separate permissions for agents sharing that pod.
In Sugabots, the team configures tool-level Off, Ask, and Allow policies on a pod’s connections, and every agent in that pod inherits those policies. Configuring them once gives the team a consistent set of rules for automatic actions, engineer approvals, and disabled tools, including when another agent joins the work.
Triage needs access to evidence and a way to escalate, while implementation needs enough access to prepare a change. Genuinely different access boundaries require separate enforcement, potentially through different pods with different tool policies or appropriately scoped connections. Merge and deployment authority also need explicit policies and, where available, appropriately scoped credentials.
Separate the working context from the investigation
There are three things here with different useful lifetimes:
- Configuration: the maintained model, instructions, tools, and expectations for a responsibility.
- Execution context: the messages and tool results available to the model while it works on a particular task.
- Shared history: the record of evidence, hypotheses, corrections, and decisions that people and agents accumulate.
Consider an investigation where the agent rules out an outage and concludes that an issue can wait until office hours. After enough tool calls, its context may need to be compacted. A summary might preserve the conclusion while omitting the evidence that ruled out the outage.
That detail becomes important if an engineer challenges the assessment. Keeping the original history gives them a way to inspect the reasoning and evidence behind the summary. The agent can work with a compacted context while the fuller record remains available for inspection or retrieval.
To continue the investigation, the next agent needs the relevant evidence and corrections selected from that record and passed along in a brief, or retrieved as it works. Preserving the conversation gives us a source to draw from; selecting the working context remains an explicit part of the handover.
Keep people in the investigation
The same distinction matters when work moves between engineers. An engineer may recognize a pattern the agent missed or explain why an apparently sensible fix would introduce a regression elsewhere in the codebase. That contribution needs to remain available to the engineer or agent continuing the investigation or preparing the fix.
In separate chats, people become responsible for carrying those corrections across. Even when both agents can inspect the same repository and tickets, each conversation contains a different account of what the team has learned.
In Sugabots, engineers can contribute to the shared discussion, leaving their corrections alongside the findings that prompted them. The next engineer can see how the investigation changed direction, and an agent continuing the work can receive that correction with its brief.
MCP gives the agent access to evidence, while a shared workspace gives the team access to the investigation.
When is another specialist worth it?
Each additional specialist brings configuration to maintain and a handover whose context needs care. Splitting agents by language, service, or deployment environment is useful when that boundary helps the team maintain and evaluate the work.
Our current divisions follow responsibilities that already existed: the on-call engineer assessed urgency, the team organized follow-up work in the backlog, and engineers prepared and reviewed fixes. Giving agents distinct configurations for those responsibilities lets us improve each part of the workflow independently.
For a team trying this, I’d start with one recurring responsibility where you can describe a useful result and recognize a bad one. Write down the success criteria, including the errors that matter: for triage, that means examining missed urgent incidents as well as unnecessary escalations. Define the evidence the agent needs, choose a configuration that enforces the required tool access, and specify when an engineer should review its findings or approve an action.
Keep the investigation history, including the evidence behind decisions and the corrections engineers make, so the next engineer or agent can continue from it. Review those corrections to decide whether the instructions, available evidence, permissions, or handover need to change. Earlier investigations can then provide cases to revisit alongside new work, checking whether a change addresses the original mistake without introducing another.
“Increasingly, I’m interested in whether we can define an engineering responsibility clearly enough that every investigation, correction, and reviewed fix helps us improve how we handle the next one.”
That may justify a dedicated agent, or it may be enough to load a reusable configuration when the job appears. The question is whether the separation makes the work easier to maintain and evaluate.
We started by wondering whether we should specialize our agents. Increasingly, I’m interested in whether we can define an engineering responsibility clearly enough that every investigation, correction, and reviewed fix helps us improve how we handle the next one.
Try Sugabots
If you’d like to try this approach with your team, Sugabots is open source and self-hosted. Start with one recurring engineering task and a colleague who can review the agent’s work, then use the shared discussion and corrections to refine how it handles that responsibility.
If the project looks useful, give Sugabots a star on GitHub and share it with a team that might benefit. Stars and recommendations go a long way in helping an open-source project reach the engineers who could use it or contribute to it.

articles.title: Seed funding’s new reality check in the age of AI
articles.text:
Seed funding’s new reality check in the age of AI
At TechSparks 2026, investors from Snowflake for Startups, 247VC, and Endiya discussed how AI is changing seed-stage investing and why founders need to demonstrate more than a working product to secure funding.
AI has made it easier for founders to build products, test ideas, reach customers and, in some cases, generate revenue earlier. But as the barriers to starting a company fall, are investors raising the bar for their first institutional cheque?
This was the central question at ‘First Cheque, Harder Questions: The New Seed Playbook’, a panel discussion at TechSparks 2026.
The session featured Yoonmin Cho, APJ Lead, Snowflake for Startups; Shashank Randev, Founder and General Partner, 247VC; and Anvesh Ramineni, Venture Partner, Endiya. Moderated by Shubhangi Mishra, Senior Creative Lead, YourStory, the discussion examined what investors now expect at the seed stage and whether traditional startup metrics still hold the same weight.
The AI advantage comes with a catch
Cho said AI has changed the venture capital ecosystem, particularly after a period of slower funding. At Snowflake, there is considerable interest in enterprise AI, especially vertical AI, along with emerging opportunities in frontier AI.
While AI has made product development more accessible, Cho said founders still need to focus on business fundamentals. A clear competitive advantage, whether through domain expertise, distribution or other strengths, is increasingly important.
Randev said AI is also changing how investors evaluate enterprise technology companies.
Advances in AI are helping deeptech startups develop prototypes and move towards product-market fit faster, but enterprise technology faces a different challenge. AI is replacing several standalone enterprise products, making it harder to identify which solutions will remain relevant over time.
“I think it’s becoming a little more tricky to understand which product in an enterprise tech ecosystem will survive a five-year journey,” he said.
Randev added that AI has disrupted enterprise technology models that have existed for 10–15 years, complicating how investors assess individual products and their place in the value chain.
Ramineni agreed that AI has reduced the manpower needed to build a minimum viable product (MVP) or demo. However, because similar technology is available to everyone, a working product is no longer enough to stand out.
“What founders really need to work on is beyond the product itself. What do they bring to the table that can set them apart from everyone building in the same industry?” he said.
Ramineni also sees an opportunity for Indian startups in vertical AI.
While India may not have foundational AI capabilities comparable to companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, it has considerable domain expertise.
He cited semiconductor design, noting that 30% of the global semiconductor design workforce is based in India. Access to specialized talent and industry knowledge could help Indian startups build competitive vertical AI applications.
What seed-stage investors look for
With MVPs becoming easier to develop, investors are looking more closely at the founders, the problems they are solving, and their competitive advantages.
For Cho, the starting point is understanding customers and identifying problems they are willing to pay to solve.
She said startups must approach their work as businesses rather than simply product-development exercises. Founders need to understand customer pain points and workflows, build strong teams, and develop expertise that competitors cannot easily replicate.
They must also provide tangible evidence of why their businesses can succeed.
Randev outlined five parameters he considers when evaluating startups: the founders’ backgrounds and complementary skills; their understanding of the total addressable market (TAM) and go-to-market strategy; the business model; intellectual property or other competitive advantages; and the value investors can add after investing.
In deeptech, he said, teams need both technical expertise and the ability to build a business.
However, founder vision remains particularly important.
“At least one founder needs to have a vision. Without that, it’s very difficult for VCs to inculcate that vision. We are backing the founder,” Randev said.
He referred to investments in the battery ecosystem, plastic segregation robotics, and 3D metal printing. Despite operating in specialized sectors, the founders shared a clear vision of what they wanted to build and how they intended to grow their companies.
Ramineni said MVPs and demos have become basic expectations rather than reasons to invest.
Founders must demonstrate an advantage that competitors cannot easily copy. This could come from proprietary distribution networks, deep domain expertise, or an established reputation in their industry.
A product that another company can replicate within days is unlikely to provide a lasting advantage, although deeptech and biotech businesses differ because of their underlying technology.
In enterprise AI, Ramineni said investors are also looking beyond basic workflow automation.
Products that can be easily replicated or replaced may struggle to retain customers. Instead, solutions that become embedded in an enterprise's operations are more likely to create long-term value.
He pointed to systems of record that build a context layer around an organization’s business processes. As these systems become more closely integrated with operations, they become harder to replace.
Data governance: A priority from day one?
As startups adopt AI, data governance, security, and infrastructure are becoming important considerations. But should founders prioritize these before achieving product-market fit?
Cho said the answer depends on the product and its customers.
“If you’re building a product that deals with sensitive data, or you’re working with enterprise customers, you definitely need to think about the governance and safety, security from the beginning,” she said.
Addressing these requirements later can be considerably more expensive, particularly for companies handling sensitive information or serving enterprise customers.
Cho cited a company that invested in a stable data platform after its CTO recognized the time and resources involved in repeatedly hiring, training, and replacing engineers to manage its data infrastructure.
The decision was based on the company’s business priorities rather than the technology itself.
She said founders should make infrastructure and platform decisions based on business needs, particularly when those investments help them operate more efficiently, move faster, and reach customers sooner.
Beyond traditional startup metrics
The discussion also examined the indicators investors now consider when evaluating seed-stage startups.
For Cho, repeat users are an important sign of sustained customer demand.
Randev looks for customer retention and recurring engagement in enterprise and consumer technology businesses. However, he said deeptech and advanced manufacturing startups can still attract investment at the prototype stage.
Ramineni said the broader question is whether the founder is the right person to solve a critical problem.
Investors want to know whether founders understand their users, buyers, and decision-makers well enough to build products customers will pay for.
As AI reduces the time and resources needed to develop products, investors are placing greater emphasis on founder expertise, customer understanding, and competitive advantages that can last beyond the initial product launch.

articles.title: Microsoft corrige plus de 1 200 failles Windows, dont une brèche d'Outlook déjà exploitée par des pirates
articles.text:
Réglé comme une horloge, Microsoft a déployé son traditionnel Patch Tuesday. Cette fois, l’éditeur corrige un total de 1 235 failles de sécurité. C’est un peu moins que le mois dernier. En octobre, Microsoft avait pulvérisé son propre record avec 1 411 failles corrigées en une seule mise à jour. Le rythme des correctifs déployés par Microsoft reste néanmoins hors norme.
Comme le mois dernier, cette avalanche de correctifs s’explique par l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle. Pour débusquer des failles dans son code, Microsoft se sert désormais massivement de grands modèles de langage. Ceux-ci permettent d’analyser des millions de lignes de code en un temps record.
L’éditeur de Redmond n’est évidemment pas un cas isolé. Tous les géants de la tech, de Microsoft à Apple en passant par Google, ont intégré l’IA dans leurs processus de traque. Pour Tyler Reguly, le directeur adjoint de la recherche et développement en sécurité chez Fortra, Microsoft est surtout en train de faire le ménage dans de vieux bugs.
« Nous assistons à la poursuite de ces chiffres élevés, alors que Microsoft continue de corriger des problèmes cachés depuis longtemps, qui sont mis au jour par l’IA. Bientôt, cependant, ces chiffres commenceront à baisser, à mesure que les derniers de ces problèmes seront résolus », estime l’expert dans une réaction adressée à 01net.
Une faille d’Outlook déjà exploitée par des pirates
Parmi cette montagne de correctifs, on trouve une faille de sécurité qui a déjà été exploitée par des pirates. Elle se situe dans Outlook, le logiciel de messagerie de Microsoft. Une fois exploitée par des hackers, elle permet de dérober des identifiants avec un simple fichier piégé.
« Un attaquant non authentifié pourrait envoyer un fichier de message spécialement conçu et convaincre un utilisateur de l’ouvrir dans une version vulnérable de Microsoft Outlook », explique Microsoft.
Une fois ouvert, le fichier pousse Outlook à se connecter à un serveur malveillant, contrôlé par les pirates, sans afficher l’avertissement de sécurité prévu. Dans la foulée, l’ordinateur transmet automatiquement au serveur une empreinte chiffrée du mot de passe de l’utilisateur, le « hash NTLM ». Les pirates peuvent ensuite tenter de déchiffrer cette empreinte pour retrouver le mot de passe, ou s’en servir pour usurper l’identité de la victime.
« Tout le monde devrait s’efforcer de mettre à jour Outlook dès que possible », estime Tyler Reguly.
Au total, le Patch Tuesday de novembre corrige 66 failles jugées « critiques ». Parmi elles, 48 permettent d’exécuter du code à distance sur un ordinateur, c’est-à-dire d’y lancer un programme malveillant. Office est particulièrement touché, avec plusieurs failles critiques dans Word, Excel et Outlook. Dans la plupart des cas, il suffit d’ouvrir un document piégé pour que l’attaque se déclenche.
À lire aussi : 31 ans d’agacement – Windows 11 teste une option pour faire taire les touches rémanentes
Des équipes informatiques épuisées
Ce déluge de correctifs incessant met évidemment les entreprises sous pression. Avant d’installer une mise à jour sur tous leurs ordinateurs, les équipes informatiques ont l’habitude de la tester sur quelques machines. Avec plus de 1 000 failles à traiter chaque mois, la tâche est devenue colossale et finit par épuiser les équipes de sécurité.
« Je ne sais pas pour les autres, mais moi, je suis fatigué. J’imagine que si je le suis, les administrateurs et les équipes opérationnelles du monde entier le sont aussi. […] La question n’est pas de savoir si le nombre de vulnérabilités va diminuer, mais quand », confie Tyler Reguly, qui conseille aux entreprises de ne pas céder à la panique, de se concentrer sur les failles réellement exploitées, et de renforcer la sécurité de leurs systèmes plutôt que de « courir après les vulnérabilités ».
Pour mettre votre PC à l’abri des cyberattaques, installez dès maintenant la mise à jour de sécurité de novembre 2026. Ouvrez les Paramètres de Windows, allez dans Windows Update, puis cliquez sur « Rechercher des mises à jour ». Windows télécharge et installe le correctif tout seul. Il ne reste plus qu’à redémarrer l’ordinateur.

articles.text:
Happy midweek. ☀️️
The creativity in several “how to check if you’re dating a spy” content I’ve seen all week is absolutely hilarious. 😂
Forget asking your partner, “Where is this relationship going?” The new question is, “Who sent you?”
Apparently, falling in love now requires a background check and some counterintelligence training. Dating was already hard enough. Now, tech bros have to worry about national security. Poor Jensen Huang.
Elsewhere in global tech, Anthropic, soon to be known as “ANT” on the stock market, has set its IPO price range at $70–$78 per share ahead of its much-anticipated public listing. Who’s ready for another AI payday after CoreWeave? (Yes, the SpaceX omission was intentional. 💀)
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
M&A
Nigerian cross-border payments fintech Raenest acquires UK remittance company Remitise
Behind the convenience of cross-border payments is a web of licences and partnerships, and sometimes buying that infrastructure is faster than building it from scratch.
What happened? Raenest, a Nigerian fintech that provides multi-currency accounts and international payment services, has acquired Remitise, a UK-based payments company registered with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The acquisition gives Raenest an existing regulatory foothold in the UK as it looks to strengthen its operations and expand its cross-border financial services.
Explain like I’m new here: Raenest already has an International Money Transfer Operator (IMTO) licence from Nigeria’s Central Bank, as well as money services and payment service registrations in Canada. Remitise adds a UK regulatory presence. This could allow Raenest to bring more of the UK side of its payment operations under its own control, rather than relying on external providers.
There is a catch: Remitise is registered as a small payment institution in the UK. Since it doesn’t operate a fully authorised payment service, its average monthly transaction volume is limited to €3 million ($3.3 million).
Raenest said it has processed over $3 billion in total payments since its inception in April 2022; the annualised figure comes to just over $54.5 million, using simple back-of-the-napkin maths.
Now, if that limit ever becomes a problem for Raenest, it could do two things: keep Remitise’s payment activity within the existing limit or pursue additional regulatory approval as its UK business grows. The fintech will still need banking and settlement partners to move funds between the UK and Nigeria.

Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay.
Government
South Africa plans nuclear comeback
South Africa wants more nuclear power, and its energy minister is practically inviting a lawsuit.
“We are going to build nuclear [power plants] in this country. Take us to court,” Kgosientsho Ramokgopa declared on Tuesday. That’s one way to introduce an energy plan.
What’s happening? The government wants to procure 5.2 gigawatts (GW) of nuclear power, with the first new reactor potentially online by 2036. It will publish its case later this month, allow 60 days for public comment, and seek formal approval before June 2027. Eskom, the South African government-owned utility company, has identified two sites in the Western and Eastern Cape.
Explain like I’m new here. South Africa already has a nuclear power station, Koeberg, but hasn’t built another in four decades. It wants reliable electricity alongside expanding wind and solar generation. However, nuclear procurement has a courtroom habit. In 2017, Judges overturned earlier plans, and Ramokgopa withdrew a 2.5GW proposal in 2024 after legal challenges.
Here’s the problem: The price tag, funding arrangements, and impact on electricity tariffs remain unknown. South Africa also lacks recent experience building nuclear reactors. Ramokgopa himself pointed to Eskom’s troubled Medupi and Kusile coal plants as examples of how not to execute a major project.
Zoom out: Better public consultation might help the government avoid another legal defeat. But clearing the courts is only the beginning. It still has to persuade funders, manage construction costs, and show consumers that nuclear power won’t become another expensive promise.
Capital Markets
Dangote Cement abandons London listing
Aliko Dangote, Africa’s wealthiest man, is having two very different conversations with investors. At home, they’re queuing to buy shares in his refinery. In London, his cement company has decided to call off the party.
What’s happening? On Tuesday, Dangote Cement abandoned plans for a secondary listing on the London Stock Exchange (LSE), Bloomberg reported, citing market conditions and strategic priorities. The company had been preparing to sell about $1 billion worth of shares, even hosting investors in London, the United Kingdom, in September. It hasn’t announced a new date.
Meanwhile, back home:Bloomberg reported on Tuesday that Dangote’s refinery attracted $4.1 billion in share applications, nearly three times the $1.6 billion it sought in Africa’s largest IPO. Talk about contrasting fortunes.
Explain like I’m new here. These are two different transactions. Dangote Cement already trades on Nigeria’s stock exchange. Its proposed London listing would have allowed existing shareholders, including Dangote Industries, to sell part of their holdings to international investors. The cement company wouldn’t receive the proceeds.
However, the refinery offered new shares to fund its expansion, including plans to double production capacity.
Zoom out: This isn’t necessarily evidence that foreign investors have lost interest in Dangote Cement. The company withdrew its offering before the listing, and market conditions can affect what investors are willing to pay. One transaction would have helped existing shareholders cash out, while the other invites investors to finance future growth.
And while the refinery has attracted strong demand, applications aren’t the same as money raised. Its final share allocations are still pending.
Telecoms
Vodacom plans satellite-to-phone service in South Africa by 2027
Fibre cuts and the cost of building towers in remote areas can all leave gaps in terrestrial coverage. Satellite Internet offers one way around some of those problems, and now, mobile operators are looking to take that same idea and connect phones directly to satellites without needing a nearby tower.
What happened? Vodacom, a leading South African telecoms company, plans to launch a direct-to-cell satellite service in the country by the end of 2027. Its most likely partner is AST SpaceMobile, a US-based company building a satellite network designed to connect directly to ordinary smartphones.
With satellite-to-phone, a compatible phone could connect to a satellite orbiting Earth, which would act like a mobile base station in space. It could extend coverage to places out of Vodacom’s terrestrial network reach.
Explain like I’m new here: Vodacom has worked with AST since 2020 and has tested the technology. In 2023, Vodafone and AST completed what they described as the first space-based 5G voice call using an unmodified Samsung Galaxy S22. However, Shameel Joosub, Vodacom’s chief executive officer, said the partners still need to conduct more detailed testing before launch.
Vodacom is not the first to get here. In 2023, Lynk Global signed an agreement with Vodafone Ghana to extend satellite-to-phone coverage to its subscribers. In August, Airtel Africa and Starlink activated a commercial satellite-to-mobile service in the Democratic Republic of Congo, initially supporting text messages and light data services such as WhatsApp. MTN South Africa also tested satellite-to-phone technology with Lynk in 2025.
There are limits: Satellite-to-phone is not a replacement for terrestrial networks, and early services may offer only intermittent coverage or basic messaging and data. Joosub has also said the service will not work with 2G and 3G phones. Vodacom and AST (or whichever partner Vodacom selects) will also have to work through the practicalities of launching and operating the service before it goes live.

articles.title: Los buitres mantienen en su interior bacterias propias de cada especie a pesar de que se alimentan de carroña
articles.text:
Los buitres se enfrentan a diario a un festín que para cualquier otro animal podría ser una causa de muerte casi inmediata. Y es que, al alimentarse de cadáveres que están en descomposición, también se están comiendo un cóctel masivo de microorganismos y bacterias que son potencialmente mortales.
Lo que se pensaba. La intuición sugería que esta dieta tan extrema terminaría por igualar la flora bacteriana de las distintas especies carroñeras, dotándolas de un microbioma que estuviera especializado en poder procesar la carne podrida. Sin embargo, un nuevo estudio acaba de desmontar esta idea, puesto que la genética y la especie de cada individuo actúan como un filtro anatómico mucho más estricto que el menú que comparten.
El estudio. Ha sido publicado en PNAS y ha estado liderado por el propio CSIC, y recoge cómo los investigadores analizaron muestras de 155 aves silvestres en el Pirineo, la gran mayoría en territorio de Aragón. Aquí el trabajo incluyó ejemplares de las cuatro especies de buitres europeos, es decir, el quebrantahuesos, el buitre leonado, el alimoche y el buitre negro, además del milano real, una rapaz que ejerce como carroñera, pero no de forma exclusiva.
Aquí, el investigador Michael Wink lo explica perfectamente: “Uno de los hallazgos más interesantes es que no existe un único microbioma característico de los buitres. Aunque distintas especies puedan alimentarse del mismo cadáver y entrar en contacto con bacterias similares, cada una mantiene comunidades microbianas diferentes. Esto demuestra que la mera exposición a un microorganismo no basta para que se establezca y persista en el organismo”.
Se analizó. En lugar de limitarse al tracto digestivo, los investigadores secuenciaron el ADN microbiano de cuatro zonas corporales distintas: la cara, la cavidad bucal, la tráquea y la cloaca. Los resultados apuntaron que la especie del ave es el factor dominante en la composición de su microbioma, explicando un 18% de las diferencias biológicas entre las muestras.
El estudio también confirma que las comunidades bacterianas en los polluelos son mucho menos diversas que en los adultos, lo que indica que el microbioma madura a medida que el ave crece y se expone a la carroña, mientras que el sexo apenas altera este equilibrio biológico.
Hay dudas. Por ahora, este estudio es una fotografía de quiénes viven en el cuerpo de estas aves, pero no de qué hacen exactamente. Identificar las funciones específicas de estas bacterias para confirmar si, como apuntaban estudios previos en el Himalaya, son ellas las que inhiben a los patógenos de la carroña o si cumplen otras funciones fisiológicas, será el próximo gran reto.

articles.title: Seagate lanzó un disco externo de USD 699: exige que el comprador añada su propia memoria para funcionar
articles.text:
Seagate lanzó el 10 de noviembre el FireCuda Forge, un disco externo que combina un disco duro de gran capacidad con una unidad SSD (memoria de estado sólido, más rápida) que el comprador debe aportar. Sin ese SSD, el aparato no funciona. Cuesta USD 699 con 8 terabytes y USD 899 con 20.
El equipo está a la venta en la tienda de Seagate, según Ars Technica. The Verge agrega que también se vende en Newegg y Best Buy. Ninguna de las dos versiones trae el SSD incluido, un gasto extra que el fabricante deja en manos del usuario.
Seagate asegura que el sistema, llamado Alkemi, mantiene en el SSD los datos de uso frecuente y deja en el disco duro los menos usados. Ante el ordenador aparece como una sola unidad. La velocidad que declara la empresa llega a 2.500 MB por segundo y guardar información a hasta 2.000 MB por segundo en escritura. Funciona con una conexión USB4 y con Windows 11 o macOS 26 y versiones posteriores, según Ars Technica.
Una memoria de hasta 1 terabyte, con requisitos
Según Seagate, para usar este dispositivo hace falta un disco de almacenamiento interno específico y de alta velocidad, de hasta 1 TB de capacidad. También debe poder leer y guardar archivos rápidamente. La empresa recomienda, además, que el disco incluya una memoria adicional que ayude a mejorar su rendimiento.
Eso limita cuánta información cabe en el lado rápido: un terabyte como máximo. Tom’s Hardware señala que un SSD más veloz o más grande no mejora el rendimiento y que uno de menos de 1 terabyte puede reducirlo.
El medio estadounidense también informó que la compañía había calificado oficialmente pocos modelos: el Samsung 990 Pro, el WD/SanDisk SN850X y el WD/SanDisk SN710. Para instalarlo hay que quitar cuatro tornillos de la base de la carcasa, con una herramienta incluida.
El disco duro interno puede reemplazarse por uno de mayor capacidad, dice la empresa. Un disco duro de 20 terabytes es una capacidad que, según Tom’s Hardware, ningún SSD de consumo de una sola unidad alcanza.
La escasez de memoria encarece el conjunto
Tom’s Hardware vincula el producto con el aumento de precios de los SSD, que atribuye a la demanda de las grandes empresas de IA. The Verge advierte que, en plena escasez de memoria, esta memoria sumará un costo importante al precio de lanzamiento.
Tom’s Hardware calcula que, sin tener un SSD sobrante, el costo total no estará lejos del de las unidades de estado sólido tradicionales. Como comparación, cita un disco SanDisk de 8 terabytes totalmente SSD, aún a la venta a USD 999, aunque con una interfaz más lenta.
Ars Technica recoge que Apple ofrecía los Fusion Drive, que combinaban ambos tipos de almacenamiento y los gestionaban con el sistema macOS. Tom’s Hardware precisa que Seagate vende discos con memoria flash incorporada desde 2007. La diferencia ahora es que el usuario elige el SSD. Ars Technica también señala que la hoja técnica describe un sistema de dos niveles, pero no aclara si usa caché, reubicación automática de datos o una combinación.

articles.title: Angular's TypeScript 7-Powered Compiler Enters Beta with Rust-Based Preprocessor
articles.text:
The Angular team has shared details of a new version of its compiler, the Angular Preprocessor (ngp), which rewrites the analysis stage of the toolchain in Rust to clear the way for TypeScript 7 adoption. Alex Rickabaugh and Mark Techson announced the work on the Angular team blog in late September, shortly after Microsoft shipped TypeScript 7.0, whose Go-based rewrite removed the ts.Transformer API that Angular's ahead-of-time compiler depends on.
The existing compiler, ngc, wraps tsc and uses the Transformer API to turn decorators such as @Component and @Pipe into runtime instructions. The Go port offers no cross-language equivalent, and crossing the JS/Go boundary at every file would be prohibitive. The Angular team's answer is to decouple compilation from TypeScript's APIs and rebuild it on Oxc, the VoidZero Rust toolchain already powering Vite. The team pointed to the plan on X, framing it as a partial rewrite rather than a fresh start.
ngp runs in three stages. A Rust frontend using Oxc analyses files in parallel to discover Angular declarations and resolve metadata. The existing TypeScript template compiler then emits two artefacts, a runtime file containing the transformed component and a .ngtypecheck.ts file holding the Type Check Block (TCB) for template type-checking. Finally a downstream tool, whether tsgo, tsrs, esbuild or Rolldown, handles type-checking and JavaScript emission independently.
The bulk of ngp landed on 8 October in a single commit of more than 370,000 lines, around 56,000 of them Rust. Cédric Exbrayat of Ninja Squad benchmarked the beta against three projects ranging from 15 to 1,714 components and measured a 2x to 3x speedup on cold builds, with memory use on the largest project falling from 2.8 GB to 1.4 GB. Pairing ngp with tsrs and Rolldown gave the fastest pipeline, with tsgo and esbuild only marginally slower. They concluded there is further gains to be made:
This is already very promising, and there are certainly further gains to be made when the team focuses on performance optimization.
Christopher Holder at push-based.io took a different tack, writing vite-plugin-ngp to compile Angular files on demand. On the Super Productivity codebase (252 components), the dev server reached the first page in 10.5 seconds against 17.4 for ng serve, with template edits applying in 112 milliseconds rather than a 2.6 second full reload. On a generated 5,000-component app the gap widened to 1.6 seconds against 28.4. Holder cautioned that the plugin "is a prototype on a prototype" pinned to 22.3.0-next.2.
On Reddit, a number of developers are excited about the update and write up, with one commenting:
Read the whole article. Impressive. The Angular team surpassed my expectations!
VoidZero's own experimental Oxc Angular compiler, covered by InfoQ in April, reported a roughly 97% improvement on narrower workloads but is now described as "actively seeking maintainers". The Angular team confirmed VoidZero's work influenced the architecture and that the two groups have been collaborating, with ngp becoming the official path.
Teams on earlier Angular versions should first run the standard update guide to reach v20 or later. Adoption of ngp is expected to land in a minor release of Angular 22 once TypeScript 7.1 restores the compiler API; until then production builds should stay on ngc.
Angular is Google's open-source, TypeScript-first web framework, widely adopted across enterprise applications and built around standalone components and signal-based reactivity.

articles.title: Fortinet Patches Nearly 100 Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Fortinet on Tuesday dropped 89 new security advisories that address nearly 100 vulnerabilities across its products.
The massive release comes three weeks after the company announced it has integrated frontier AI models into its product security testing and can discover security defects more efficiently.
“This ongoing effort complements the conventional methods we employ to identify and address vulnerabilities. This approach gives customers time to prioritize upgrades before additional technical details become public, which matters even more as AI shortens the time between disclosure and exploitation,” Fortinet says.
Approximately 17 of the newly resolved flaws are critical-severity issues, several of which could be exploited for arbitrary code execution.
Other critical bugs could lead to authentication bypass, LSA broadcast, account takeover, access to other VDOMs and to secure email accounts, IBE webmail session compromise, server-side request execution, malicious/malformed attribute delivery, webmail password resets, and command execution as super admin.
FortiMail received the largest batch of critical fixes, followed by FortiAuthenticator, FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer. New FortiSASE and FortiClient updates also resolve critical issues.
According to Baldur Security principal security consultant Kevin Joensen, the FortiClient bug is exploitable if FortiPAM is enabled and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code if the victim visits a malicious website.
“The root cause is a CORS misconfiguration that allows attacker-controlled web pages to communicate with a local service and reliably execute arbitrary code,” Joensen says. The researcher named the flaw Fortinet2Shell.
Fortinet also patched nearly 80 high-severity vulnerabilities that could lead to XSS attacks, code execution, code injection, arbitrary file uploads, command execution, denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, MitM attacks, privilege escalation, information disclosure, account takeover, unauthorized access, and other unauthorized actions.
Fortinet makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild. Additional information can be found on the company’s PSIRT page.

articles.title: Fresh Prep to acquire meal kit service Goodfood in court-approved sale | BetaKit
articles.text:
Embattled Montréal-based meal kit company Goodfood has been bought out of creditor protection by its Vancouver-based peer Fresh Prep.
The news: The two companies announced the court-approved sale on Wednesday but did not disclose the purchase price. The deal is scheduled to close on Friday.
After closing, Fresh Prep will begin serving approximately 30,000 active Goodfood customers and bring on Goodfood team members. Fresh Prep said the acquisition strengthens its presence in Québec and extends its services to a fifth province, Saskatchewan.
From the source: “We are extremely pleased that the diligent process we have run has led to this announced transaction with Fresh Prep, a quality Canadian company that expects to welcome a significant number of our team members while delivering, in a seamless fashion, the quality meal solutions that our customers are accustomed to,” Goodfood chair Donald Olds said in a statement.
The context: Once closed, the sale will mark the end of a tough run for Goodfood. In 2025, both of the company’s co-founders left the business within months of one another. Shortly after, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency suspended its safe food licence over undisclosed allergens, before reinstating it this past January. Goodfood later reported a 21-percent decrease in its net sales, eventually admitting in July it may have to curtail operations due to mounting debts coming due next year.
In August, Goodfood announced it would seek creditor protection, just days after its CEO, Selim Bassoul, resigned.
Final thought: Despite Bassoul’s efforts to build a more resilient operating model, Goodfood was never able to re-achieve the record revenues it hit in 2021 when the COVID-19 pandemic drove demand for home delivery of groceries and meals. Meanwhile, its new owner, Fresh Prep, made The Globe and Mail’s top growing companies list last year with a three-year revenue growth rate of 118 percent. With over 700 employees, Fresh Prep claims it is Canada’s largest Canadian-owned meal delivery company.
Feature image courtesy Goodfood.

articles.title: Warum verschwand ein Exoplanet plötzlich? Wissenschaftler lösen das Rätsel um TOI-2535 b
articles.text:
Astronomen lösen Rätsel um plötzlich „verschwundenen“ Exoplaneten
Astronom:innen haben das Rätsel um einen Exoplaneten mit der Bezeichnung TOI-2535 b gelöst. Dieser befindet sich etwa 1.000 Lichtjahre von der Erde entfernt war nach sieben Jahren der Beobachtung plötzlich aus ihrem Blickfeld verschwunden.
Der Exoplanet umkreist seinen Heimatstern in nur acht Tagen
Zwischen April 2019 und März 2026 wurde TOI-2535 b regelmäßig mit dem Weltraumteleskop Tess (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) der Nasa beobachtet, wie er seinen Heimatstern in 8,25 Erdtagen umkreiste. Weil er seinen Stern so schnell umkreist, ist er sehr nah an ihm und erreicht dadurch extrem hohe Temperaturen. Deshalb wird er als sogenannter „heißer Jupiter“ klassifiziert.
Doch während der Beobachtungen geschah etwas Seltsames: Die Umlaufbahnen des Exoplaneten verliefen nicht so regelmäßig wie bei anderen Himmelskörpern. TOI-2535 b erreichte seinen erwarteten Punkt auf der Umlaufbahn oft sechs Stunden zu früh oder sechs Stunden zu spät. Im März 2026 Jahres registrierte Tess schließlich nicht mehr die charakteristischen Helligkeitsabfälle des Sterns, die immer dann auftraten, wenn TOI-2535 b vor seinem Heimatstern vorbeizog – ein Vorgang, den man als „Transit“ bezeichnet. Der Planet schien verschwunden zu sein.
Forscher: Das Universum funktioniert nicht wie ein Uhrwerk
Doch dem ist nicht so. Das Forschungsteam nutzte laut Space.com die Daten von Tess, um festzustellen, dass TOI-2535 b von einem bisher nicht beobachteten Nachbarplaneten beeinflusst wird – wobei TOI-2535 b seinerseits ebenfalls eine Anziehungskraft auf diesen Nachbarn ausübt. Dies führt dazu, dass die Umlaufbahnen beider Himmelskörper im TOI-2535-System „ins Wanken“ geraten. TOI-2535 b verschwand aus dem Blickfeld des Weltraumteleskops, weil dieses Wanken dazu führte, dass er nicht mehr exakt vor seinem Stern vorbeizog.
„Wir stellen uns das Universum oft wie ein Uhrwerk vor, in dem alles nach festen Regeln abläuft – doch das stimmt so nicht. Wenn es in einem System mehrere Planeten gibt, können diese die Umlaufbahnen der jeweils anderen beeinflussen“, erklärte Samuel Yee, Mitglied des Forschungsteams an der University of California (USA), in einer Pressemitteilung.
20 starke False-Color-Bilder der Nasa von der Erde und dem Weltall
Forscher:innen sprechen von „äußerst interessanter“ Entdeckung
„Dies ist das extremste Beispiel, das wir bisher gesehen haben, da die beiden Planeten so stark aufeinander einwirken. Die Umlaufbahn des Planeten neigt sich so schnell, dass sein Transit – also sein Vorbeiziehen vor dem Stern – während unserer Beobachtungen verschwand“, sagte er.
Die Wissenschaftler:innen gehen davon aus, dass TOI-2535 b aufgrund seines nahen Nachbarn durch eine „langsame Spiralbewegung“ auf seiner Umlaufbahn nach innen gewandert ist. „Möglicherweise beobachten wir hier einen Prozess, der selten vorkommt und deshalb äußerst interessant ist“, sagte Yee.
Die Forschungsergebnisse des Teams wurden im Astrophysical Journal Letters veröffentlicht.

articles.title: Starlink Mini 2: Neuer Satellitenempfänger soll über 4 Stunden ohne Steckdose auskommen
articles.text:
Starlink Mini 2 mit Akku: SpaceX-Antenne kommt über 4 Stunden ohne Steckdose aus
Gut zwei Jahre nach dem Start des Starlink Mini als Satelliteninternet-Empfänger für unterwegs hat SpaceX jetzt einen Nachfolger vorgestellt. Der Mini 2 hat einen abnehmbaren Akku an Bord und soll die Nutzung auf Reisen noch bequemer machen. Statt eines herkömmlichen Stromkabels gibt es zudem einen USB-C-Anschluss.
Starlink Mini 2: 4,5 Stunden Akkubetrieb
Mit einer Akkuladung soll der Starlink Mini 2 bis zu 4,5 Stunden durchhalten, wie der Anbieter in einem entsprechenden X-Beitrag verspricht. Ins Internet soll es dank integrierten WLAN-Moduls innerhalb von 60 Sekunden gehen – freie Sicht auf den Himmel vorausgesetzt.
Trotz des abnehmbaren Akkus ist die Mini-2-Antenne mit 23,1 Millimetern Dicke deutlich schlanker als die Vorgängerin (38,5 Millimeter). Das zusätzliche Gewicht des Akkus sorgt allerdings dafür, dass Starlink Mini 2 schwerer ist als die originale Mini-Antenne. Hier stehen 1,6 versus 1,16 Kilogramm zu Buche.
Dafür soll die neue Mini-Version robuster sein als die alte und Wind, Sand und Wasser besser trotzen können, wie PC Mag schreibt. Die Zertifizierung IP67 hatte allerdings auch schon die ursprüngliche Mini-Antenne. Dafür kommt Mini 2 mit Wifi 6 statt Wifi 5. Damit steigt die Abdeckung von 111 auf 167 Quadratmeter.
Startpreis inklusive Ein-Jahres-Tarif
Zum Preis hat sich SpaceX noch nicht offiziell geäußert. Laut an Starlink-Kund:innen versendeten E-Mails sollen die ersten Nutzer:innen 999 US-Dollar für das Gerät zahlen. Das beinhaltet allerdings eine einjährige Internetnutzung (Tarif: Starlink Roam Unlimited), der normalerweise 2.100 Dollar kostet.
Mit einem ähnlichen Angebot hatte SpaceX auch beim Start der Starlink-Mini-Antenne im Jahr 2024 operiert. Diese kostete damals 599 Dollar mit Ein-Jahres-Tarif. Mittlerweile ist der Empfänger schon ab 149 Dollar zu haben.
Mini-2-Antenne soll bald 249 Dollar kosten
Wie der Youtube-Kanal Dishytech in versteckten Daten auf der Starlink-Homepage entdeckt hat, könnte Starlink Mini 2 zu einem Preis von 249 Dollar in den Handel kommen. Ein Wechselakku würde demnach 50 Dollar kosten. Allerdings ist es dank USB-C-Anschluss einfacher möglich, eine beliebige Powerbank zu nutzen.
Aktuell können nur eingeladene Nutzer:innen in den USA die neue Mini-Version vorbestellen, gegen eine Einzahlung von 100 Dollar. Die Ausweitung des Programms auf weitere Nutzer:innen und Länder soll „bald“ erfolgen. Die ersten Geräte sollen ab Mitte Dezember 2026 verschickt werden. In Deutschland dürfte es entsprechend frühestens 2027 losgehen.

articles.title: Kunal Shah outlines WhatsApp’s next phase with AI, payments, richer conversations
articles.text:
Kunal Shah outlines WhatsApp’s next phase with AI, payments, richer conversations
WhatsApp’s next chapter could transform it from a messaging platform into an everyday digital services hub, combining richer conversations, seamless payments and AI-powered assistance.
WhatsApp is preparing to move beyond messaging, making conversations more expressive, bringing everyday transactions into the app and using artificial intelligence (AI) to handle practical tasks. CEO Kunal Shah set out these priorities in a post on X, more than four months after succeeding Will Cathcart as WhatsApp’s global head.
Shah said the app would evolve voice notes, groups, stickers and video as communication habits change. WhatsApp has more than three billion users worldwide and over 500 million in India, its largest market. According to Shah, users send more than 10 billion voice messages and four billion stickers daily, while the platform handles over 100 billion messages and two billion calls every day.
“We want anything you do on WhatsApp to be as simple as sending a message,” Shah wrote.
The second priority is making everyday tasks easier to complete within a chat. Shah said WhatsApp was working with financial services and telecom partners to reduce the steps involved in bill payments, borrowing and staying connected while travelling.
The expansion is already taking shape in India. WhatsApp introduced prepaid mobile recharges for Jio, Airtel and Vi in April and announced a gradual roll-out of bill payments in September through Bharat Connect, the network connecting billers with payment providers. Meta said the service would provide access to 22,722 billers across 30 categories, including electricity, water, insurance and loan repayments.
UPI processed approximately 2,547 crore transactions in October, showing the scale of the digital payments market.
AI is the third strand. Shah said it should find information, manage routine tasks and help users avoid missing bookings or appointments, although he did not provide details or a launch timetable for new consumer-facing features. Meta launched Business AI for eligible Indian small businesses in May, enabling automated replies, product recommendations and appointment handling in native Indian languages.
The company also said UPI payments within AI-assisted chats would be introduced, describing the capability as forthcoming.
The wider industry is moving in similar directions. Google and Apple began a beta roll-out of end-to-end encrypted RCS messaging between supported Android and iPhone devices in May. Meanwhile, Reuters reported in September that NPCI was developing a registry to verify AI agents making UPI payments, highlighting questions around user authorisation and liability when software acts on a customer's behalf.
Trust remains a significant consideration. Shah reiterated that personal messages and calls would remain end-to-end encrypted. “Trust takes years to earn and a moment to lose, and I don’t take that lightly,” he wrote.
As WhatsApp adds financial and AI services, it will need to explain how payment information and automated functions are handled alongside private conversations.
“The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” Shah said.

articles.title: Bay Raises $50 Million to Control What Enterprise AI Agents Can Do
articles.text:
Tel Aviv-based Bay has emerged from stealth with $50 million funding (comprising a $37 million Series A round led by Battery Ventures and a previously undisclosed $13 million seed funding led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners). Bay was founded in February 2026 by Yuval Zacharia (CEO), Boris Danilovich (VP of R&D), and Aner Morag (CPO). All three are alumni of the Israeli Military Intelligence (IDF Unit 8200).
In business, companies cannot ignore the economic advantage offered by AI agents, but nor do they always know what any individual agent might do. Agentic AI behavior is decided at runtime by each agent acting on its user’s behalf and with its user’s permissions.
Bay is designed to allow companies to install and employ AI agents confident that they will not run amok with unintended actions. It provides a single control plane that discovers, understands and controls agents wherever they run.
When installed, Bay automatically builds a full inventory of the AI agents, coding assistants, MCP servers, skills, extensions and local models in use, and maps how they connect, including risky combinations of tools. It follows each agent session from the first prompt to the final action. Its Enforcer component evaluates every proposed action in the context of the full session and decides in milliseconds whether to allow the action, refer it to the user, redirect it based on policy, or simply deny it.
The policy guiding Enforcer’s actions is automatically built and maintained by Bay’s embedded AI system (Lighthouse) based on the organization’s own activity history.
By focusing on the agents’ actions, Bay protects against dangerous agent activity regardless of whether the cause is malicious human-directed prompt injection or organic agent purpose drift.
“Before we even decided what to build, we agreed on three non-negotiables,” Bay’s CEO and co-founder Yuval Zacharia told SecurityWeek: “effortless deployment, immediate time to value, and a clear path to operationalization.”
These principles became the design foundation for Bay. “The first drove us to build a flexible, agentless architecture that can be deployed across an entire fleet in under five minutes,” she continued. “The second led to patented technology that retrospectively analyzes 30 days of historical logs, allowing customers to see what Bay would have delivered had it been running in their environment. This makes it possible to demonstrate business value almost immediately and complete a proof of value in less than 14 days.”
The third, she concluded, “shaped how we approach day-to-day operations, with clear ownership, AI-driven policy creation, and a product designed to become part of how teams actually work.”
The funding will be used to further develop the product and expand the firm’s engineering team, and to invest in go-to-market plans across the US and Europe, “Longer term,” explains the firm, “we want Bay to be the core control layer for enterprises putting AI agents to work at scale. As agents take on longer-running, more autonomous work, Bay’s job is to make sure organizations can trust them with it, and to keep expanding what agents can safely do on their own.”

Vai acabar: Motorola Edge 70 Pro registra inédito 45% OFF na Black November
Celular premium da Motorola com 12 GB de RAM, bateria de 6.500 mAh e câmeras de 50 MP está em oferta relâmpago na Black November 2026 do Mercado Livre
O Motorola Edge 70 Pro (256 GB) está em oferta relâmpago no Mercado Livre por R$ 2.494,40 no Pix com o cupom TVCEL1011. O valor representa um desconto especial de 45% dado na Black November em relação ao preço original de R$ 4.499. O celular premium lançado em 2026 conta com um hardware poderoso, com destaques para a autonomia e as câmeras.
O dispositivo utiliza câmeras de alta resolução de 50 MP. As traseiras são: principal com sensor Sony Lytia 710, ultrawide com ângulo de 122° e teleobjetiva com zoom óptico de 3,5x para aproximar objetos distantes. Já a lente frontal suporta selfies com HDR e vídeos em 4K. Além de bons resultados para fotos, o sistema conta com recursos de IA pela Moto AI.
O Motorola Edge 70 Pro também chama a atenção pela bateria gigante de silício-carbono de 6.500 mAh, inclusive superior a do Signature, topo de linha da marca. A fabricante promete autonomia de até 49 horas, o que deve assegurar dois dias de uso moderado longe da tomada. Além disso, o carregamento de 90 W promete recuperar rapidamente a energia.
Em relação a performance, o processador MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Extreme somado a 12 GB de RAM, assegura desempenho robusto para multitarefas; assim como para rodar jogos pesados e executar edições de vídeos.
A tela AMOLED com taxa de atualização de 144 Hz e brilho de 5.200 nits proporciona uma navegação extremamente fluida além de visibilidade clara mesmo sob a luz direta em dias ensolarados. O revestimento do vidro Gorilla Glass 7i ainda promete oferecer alta durabilidade contra possíveis quedas e arranhões acidentais.
Além disso, o dispositivo inclui a combinação das resistências militar MIL-STD-810H, IP68 e IP69. O que em tese, significa resistir a ambientes empoeirados, imersão em água e até condições extremas de altitude e temperatura.
Corra para garantir o Motorola Edge 70 Pro (256 GB) disponível com 45% de desconto na Black November 2026, por R$ 2.494,40 no Pix com o cupom TVCEL1011.
A Black November é o período que antecede a Black Friday 2026, marcada anualmente para a última sexta-feira do mês. Desde o início do mês, você já pode encontrar preços mais baixos e condições especiais no varejo. Portanto, acompanhe o Achados que diariamente separamos as melhores ofertas de eletrônicos.
