articles.title: Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
articles.text:
Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.
Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
Here are some of the experimental ‘sneaks’ being showcased at Adobe Max.
The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.
You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in.
This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides far less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention.
There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle.
Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward.
Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects.
Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools.
These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that might eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology.
A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects.
“Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told The Verge. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”

articles.title: Apple corrigió un error de iMessage que permitía a un extraño entrar a un chat grupal y leerlo
articles.text:
Apple lanzó iOS 27.2.1, una actualización que corrige nueve fallas de seguridad, entre ellas dos de iMessage: una permitía que un atacante remoto se uniera a un chat grupal y recibiera sus mensajes, según las notas de seguridad que publicó la empresa.
La compañía no informó que las fallas se hayan explotado en ataques reales. El sitio MacRumors advirtió que, con los detalles ya públicos, los equipos sin actualizar quedan más expuestos. La versión llega dos semanas después de iOS 27.2 y no trae funciones nuevas.
Está disponible para el iPhone 11 y modelos posteriores. También hay versiones para iPad, Mac, Apple Watch y Apple Vision Pro. En el iPhone, se instala desde Ajustes, en General y luego en Actualización de software.
Dos fallas en los chats grupales de iMessage
La primera falla, según Apple, era un problema de autorización: un atacante remoto podía sumarse a un grupo de iMessage sin ser invitado y recibir los mensajes del chat. La empresa la corrigió con una validación más estricta. Un investigador anónimo la reportó.
La segunda afectaba a alguien que ya había sido añadido al grupo: podía ver los mensajes enviados antes de su ingreso. Apple la resolvió eliminando el código vulnerable. También la descubrió un investigador anónimo.
Las notas de Apple no indican que alguna conversación haya sido leída ni cuántos usuarios resultaron afectados. Describen lo que un atacante podría haber hecho, no lo que ocurrió.
Bluetooth y AirPlay: emparejamientos sin permiso
La mayoría de las correcciones se concentra en conexiones inalámbricas. En CoreUtils, un componente del sistema, Apple corrigió un error que permitía que un dispositivo Bluetooth malicioso se emparejara con el iPhone sin intervención del usuario. Otro permitía a un atacante cercano eludir el límite de intentos de códigos de emparejamiento.
Hay además tres correcciones del límite de intentos del código de AirPlay, la función que envía audio y video a otros equipos. Dos requerían estar al alcance del Bluetooth. La tercera, en el proceso rapportd, bastaba con estar en la misma red.
Otra falla de Bluetooth permitía a un atacante cercano dañar la memoria de un proceso del sistema. Apple corrigió un error de manejo de memoria que lo hacía posible. Cuatro de las vulnerabilidades las halló la propia Apple, que se acredita su descubrimiento en las notas.
También se corrigió el acceso a datos sensibles
Apple parchó App Intents, el sistema que expone acciones de las aplicaciones a funciones como Atajos y Siri. Según la empresa, un problema de autorización permitía que una app accediera a datos sensibles del usuario. La compañía no precisa de qué datos se trata.
La actualización incluye además una corrección en brotli, una herramienta de compresión de datos, donde un archivo manipulado podía dañar la memoria del equipo. Apple la atribuyó a una validación insuficiente de la entrada.
Quienes no tengan iOS 27 también recibieron correcciones. Apple publicó iOS 26.7.3, que según MacRumors resuelve los dos errores de iMessage, y iOS 18.7.12, que, según el sitio heise online, corrige seis de las fallas pero no incluye los parches de iMessage.
Cómo funciona iMessage en el iPhone
iMessage funciona integrándose dentro de la aplicación Mensajes del iPhone mediante el envío de datos a través de Wi-Fi o red móvil hacia los servidores de Apple, en lugar de utilizar las redes tradicionales de telefonía.
Cuando redactas un mensaje, el dispositivo detecta automáticamente si el receptor tiene un equipo de Apple activo en la plataforma; de ser así, la conversación se muestra con globos de color azul y se transmite protegida con cifrado de extremo a extremo, lo que garantiza que solo emisor y receptor puedan leer el contenido y permite compartir fotos en alta resolución, notas de voz, reacciones, indicadores de escritura y confirmaciones de lectura.
Si el contacto no utiliza un dispositivo Apple o no cuenta con conexión a internet, la aplicación conmuta automáticamente al envío por SMS/MMS tradicional (o RCS, según la compatibilidad y configuración), identificándolo mediante globos de color verde.

articles.title: How Millions of Electric Motors Still Rely on an 1866 Idea
articles.text:
This article is brought to you by Innomotics.
In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.
1866: The breakthrough that powered the future
The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.
This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics
The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.
One principle. Millions of motors.
More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.
Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics
Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.
Award-winning innovations
Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.
Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics
AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.
Perfect Harmony GH180: Proven drive technology for modern industry
For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.
Winding lifetime analysis: The service to know more and risk less
Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.
The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics
160 Years Later. Still Running.
What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.
As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.
Video: Innomotics
For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.
Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.
Discover how Innomotics is driving the future of industry: https://www.innomotics.com/hub/en/company/about-innomotics/dynamo-electric-principle
Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

articles.title: SpaceX intentará atrapar con su torre el propulsor y la nave de Starship el 13 de noviembre
articles.text:
SpaceX intentará el viernes 13 de noviembre algo que nunca hizo: recuperar con su torre de lanzamiento tanto el propulsor Super Heavy como la nave Starship en el mismo vuelo. La empresa fijó una ventana de 75 minutos desde las 4:45 p.m. de Texas (22:45 GMT), sujeta a aprobación regulatoria.
La compañía describe el Vuelo 15 como el primero que devolverá ambas piezas a la base de lanzamiento. Si sale bien, dijo SpaceX, será la primera recuperación completa de un sistema de lanzamiento orbital. Starship es el cohete más grande jamás construido y se diseñó para reutilizarse por completo.
La captura consiste en que dos brazos mecánicos de la torre, apodados “palillos chinos” (chopsticks), sujeten la pieza en el aire cuando regresa al punto de partida en Starbase, en el sur de Texas. SpaceX atrapó el propulsor en tres vuelos anteriores, según Space.com, pero nunca intentó hacerlo con la nave.
Dos capturas, con 22 horas de diferencia
El propulsor, el Booster 22, volverá primero. Según el cronograma de SpaceX, tras separarse de la nave encenderá motores para regresar y será atrapado unos 6 minutos y 35 segundos después del despegue. Será el primer intento de captura de un propulsor de la versión 3, la más reciente.
La nave seguirá viaje. SpaceX prevé que se ubique en una órbita de unos 275 km de altura, despliegue 26 satélites Starlink V3 y dé unas 14 vueltas a la Tierra durante un vuelo de más de 22 horas. La captura de la nave figura en el cronograma a las 22 horas y 32 minutos del despegue.
Ese regreso es más difícil que el del propulsor. La nave vuelve de más lejos y a mayor velocidad, de modo que soporta más calor al reingresar. Space.com lo describe como una maniobra más compleja y exigente que la del propulsor.
Una ruta sobre zonas habitadas
En vuelos anteriores, la nave terminaba cayendo al océano sobre zonas despobladas. Para volver a Starbase, SpaceX explicó que debe atravesar el norte de México y el sur de Texas. La empresa dijo que la trayectoria esquiva las grandes ciudades del valle del Río Grande y pasa al norte de la isla South Padre antes de virar sobre el golfo.
La compañía condicionó el regreso a la salud de la nave. Los controladores revisarán durante las horas en órbita los motores, la energía, las comunicaciones, las computadoras y los tanques. Solo permitirán volver si el estado cumple condiciones que SpaceX definió y que, según indicó, la FAA aprobó. Si no, la nave puede terminar la misión sobre el océano.
Antes de regresar, la nave intentará una secuencia de maniobras: un giro en el aire para quedar vertical, el encendido de tres motores, luego dos y finalmente uno, hasta quedar casi inmóvil entre los brazos de la torre. Al sentir el contacto, apagará el último motor.
El primer vuelo orbital completo de la serie
El Vuelo 14, el 28 de septiembre, fue la primera vez que Starship alcanzó la órbita, según Space.com. También desplegó 26 satélites Starlink V3. La publicación agrega que son la primera tanda de una constelación que, según Elon Musk, llegará a unos 100.000 satélites.
Para este vuelo, SpaceX acondicionó el Booster 22, que el 10 de noviembre llegó a la plataforma de lanzamiento. Allí se hicieron pruebas finales de captura, incluida una de sujeción a la altura prevista, informó la empresa en la red social X.
SpaceX advierte que el cronograma es dinámico y puede cambiar. La transmisión en vivo empezará unos 30 minutos antes del despegue y seguirá hasta la captura de la nave, según la página oficial del vuelo. La ventana de lanzamiento abre el viernes 13 de noviembre a las 4:45 p.m. hora de Texas.

articles.title: „Wir haben es schon einmal geschafft”: Was Österreichs Protestkultur über Tech-Widerstand lehrt
articles.text:
Bürgerprotest: Was ein nie gestartetes AKW über Googles Rechenzentrum lehrt
„Another Zwentendorf is possible“ steht in großen schwarzen Lettern auf dem Transparent vor mir. Ich bin in Linz, der drittgrößten Stadt Österreichs, und besuche das Ars-Electronica-Festival. Rund 30 Kilometer außerhalb, in Kronstorf, entsteht das größte Rechenzentrum des Landes. Ein Hyperscaler, der einmal so viel Strom verbrauchen soll wie die Hauptstadt Wien.
Der Standort ist das Gegenteil einer Millionenmetropole. Das beschauliche Kronstorf zählt gerade einmal 3500 Seelen. Vor 18 Jahren hat der Tech-Konzern Google dort ein Stück Land erworben und mit den Jahren wurde das Vorhaben immer größer. Was einst als Cloud-Infrastruktur und wirtschaftliche Chance angepriesen wurde, steht heute vor allem für zwei Buchstaben: KI. Das Rechenzentrum soll die enormen Rechenkapazitäten dafür bereitstellen.
Die ökologischen Kosten trägt die Region. Nicht einmal eine Umweltverträglichkeitsprüfung ist vorgesehen. Und das, obwohl das Rechenzentrum erwärmtes, mit Chemikalien versetztes Wasser in die Enns leiten wird. Die Genehmigungen sind erteilt, die Bagger rollen. Die Geschichte aus Kronstorf scheint auserzählt und wird – so scheint es – mit der Inbetriebnahme des Rechenzentrums enden. Doch seit dem Sommer regt sich Widerstand. Bürger:innen haben Initiativen gegründet und fordern neben Transparenz und einer umfassenden Prüfung der Umweltfolgen einen sofortigen Baustopp und ein Moratorium für den Bau weiterer Rechenzentren.
Was ein Atomkraftwerk über den Kampf gegen Tech-Giganten lehrt
Ich bewundere den Protest in Zeiten, in denen Big Tech übermächtiger wirkt denn je. Was motiviert die Menschen, die protestieren? „Dass wir das schon einmal geschafft haben. Hier in Österreich. In Zwentendorf“, schießt es mir von einer der Initiatorinnen entgegen. Zwentendorf. Ich verstehe sofort. Denn der Ort steht in Österreich für einen historischen Erfolg der Anti-Atomkraft-Bewegung. In Zwentendorf steht Österreichs einziges Atomkraftwerk – das zwar fertiggestellt wurde, aber nie ans Netz ging. Milliarden Schilling flossen in den 1970er Jahren in seinen Bau. Gestoppt wurde es letztlich durch einen breiten Protest und eine Volksabstimmung. Zu groß waren die Sicherheits- und Umweltbedenken der Bevölkerung.
Bis heute produziert Österreich keinen Atomstrom und erneuerbare Energien decken 90 Prozent des gesamten Strombedarfs. Natürlich ist das nicht allein auf Zwentendorf zurückzuführen. Aber damals geschah etwas Fundamentales. Die Bewegung stellte infrage, was die Politik lange als unausweichlich betrachtete: dass Atomkraft zu einer modernen Energieversorgung gehöre und um jeden Preis umgesetzt werden müsse. Der Protest zeigte, dass selbst fertiggestellte Milliardenprojekte scheitern können.
Bürgerprotest: Wenn alle Beteiligten dieselbe Zukunft vor Augen haben
Zwentendorf zeigt: Protest kann mehr als ein einzelnes Projekt stoppen. Er kann den Horizont des politisch Vorstellbaren verschieben. Eine schon beschlossene und fast unumkehrbar wirkende Zukunft wurde durch Bürgerprotest politisch wieder verhandelbar. Was gestern alternativlos erschien, ist morgen voller Möglichkeiten. Die Bewegung gegen das AKW Zwentendorf war nicht deshalb erfolgreich, weil alle Beteiligten dieselbe Zukunft vor Augen hatten, sondern weil sie gemeinsam die Vorstellung infrage stellten, dass es nur eine mögliche Zukunft gebe.
Widerstand ist nur auf den ersten Blick ein Nein. Oft ist er Wegbereiter für Zukünfte, die zuvor kaum jemand für möglich gehalten hätte. Ob wir in 50 Jahren auf Kronstorf genauso dankbar zurückblicken wie heute auf Zwentendorf, entscheidet sich jetzt. Es entscheidet sich daran, ob wir es wagen, das scheinbar Unausweichliche infrage zu stellen und uns auf eine Zukunft einzulassen, die wir uns heute noch nicht einmal vorstellen können.

articles.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
articles.text:
Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023).
QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.
Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.
Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.
What we’re building and why it’s unique
Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.
Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.
Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.
Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.
The challenges of consensus at a global scale
While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.
Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.
Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.
Destructive interference and leaders
Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.
Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.
Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.
When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.
To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.
The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.
When leader recovery is unstable
When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.
Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.
Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.
Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.
Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.
When fault detection goes awry
The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.
In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.
In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.
The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.
In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.
Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.
When fault detection is slow
Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.
Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.
Why QuePaxa is the right fit
We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.
The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.
In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.
Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.
The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.
One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.
However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.
This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.
However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.
If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.
How QuePaxa works under the hood
To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.
QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:
- Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.
- Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.
- Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.
- Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.
Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.
The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.
In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.
Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.
Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.
Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.
Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.
Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.
This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.
Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.
Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.
No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.
How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible
In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.
The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.
QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.
What we’ll be showing next
Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.
Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.
That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.
Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

articles.title: Estados Unidos batirá en 2026 su tercer récord seguido de consumo de electricidad, con la IA como motor
articles.text:
El consumo de electricidad en Estados Unidos llegará a un récord de 4.306 mil millones de kilovatios hora en 2026 y a unos 4.370 mil millones en 2027, según la Administración de Información de Energía (EIA), el organismo estadístico del Departamento de Energía.
En 2025 el consumo fue de 4.216 mil millones, también un máximo histórico. Si la proyección se cumple, 2026 será el tercer año consecutivo de récord, según Reuters sobre el informe que la EIA publicó el 10 de noviembre.
La agencia atribuye el aumento sobre todo a los centros de datos dedicados a la inteligencia artificial y a que hogares y empresas usan más electricidad y menos combustibles fósiles para calefacción y transporte.
El texto de la EIA explica el alza de otro modo: señala como causas la demanda del sector comercial, que agrupa comercios, oficinas y otros servicios, y las altas temperaturas del último verano.
El sector comercial pasará a los hogares
Las ventas de electricidad al sector comercial llegarán en 2026 a 1.557 mil millones de kilovatios hora, según las tablas de la EIA. Los hogares consumirán 1.546 mil millones, de modo que el sector comercial quedará por encima del residencial.
Ambos superan sus marcas de 2025: 1.503 mil millones para el comercio y 1.519 mil millones para las viviendas. La industria, con 1.061 mil millones, quedará apenas debajo de su máximo de 2000, de 1.064 mil millones.
En 2027 la brecha se ampliará. La EIA proyecta 1.600 mil millones para el sector comercial y 1.539 mil millones para el residencial, que bajará por un verano que prevé más templado. La industria subiría a 1.086 mil millones, un nuevo récord.
La generación de las compañías eléctricas llegará a casi 4.390 mil millones de kilovatios hora en 2026, un 2,7% más que el máximo anterior. En 2027 crecerá más despacio, un 1,2%, según la agencia.
Las renovables cubren buena parte del aumento
La EIA prevé que la energía solar a gran escala pase de aportar el 7% de la electricidad en 2025 al 8% en 2026 y a casi el 10% en 2027. El viento subirá del 11% al 12%. Entrarán en servicio 72 gigavatios de nueva capacidad solar y 20 de eólica entre este año y el próximo.
El gas natural seguirá cerca del 40% de la generación y la energía nuclear en el 18%. El carbón caerá del 17% al 15% hacia 2027, con el retiro previsto de 13 gigavatios de plantas hasta fines de ese año.
La tarifa residencial promedio subirá de 17,2 centavos de dólar por kilovatio hora en 2025 a 18,2 centavos en 2026 y a 18,7 centavos en 2027, de acuerdo con las proyecciones de la agencia, un aumento de más de 5% en el primer salto.
La pausa a nuevos centros de datos ya movió las previsiones. En agosto de 2026, la EIA redujo su estimación de crecimiento de la carga eléctrica de Texas en 2027 del 14% al 6%, tras el anuncio del gobernador del estado, el 3 de agosto, de frenar el desarrollo de nuevos centros de datos, según Reuters.
Empresas que construyen centros de datos para IA pagarían USD 380 millones más en intereses
Los desarrolladores de centros de datos para inteligencia artificial afrontarían al menos USD 380 millones adicionales en intereses al refinanciar en 2027 USD 13.400 millones de deuda a tasa fija, según BloombergNEF.
El cálculo supone que los rendimientos del Tesoro estadounidense permanezcan en los niveles de octubre de 2026, lo que elevaría las tasas 2,85 puntos porcentuales.
El mayor costo llega mientras los prestamistas revisan los proyectos de IA y sus flujos de caja. Goldman Sachs prevé que los grandes proveedores de nube emitan USD 420.000 millones de deuda en 2027. Moody’s alerta sobre vencimientos que presionarán a deudores débiles.

articles.title: Streaming is still trying to be TikTok
articles.text:
At Skydance’s first employee town hall after it acquired Warner Bros. Discovery in October, CEO David Ellison told staff that the company behind Paramount Plus and HBO Max was competing for people’s attention with some of the world’s biggest tech companies. Months earlier, he’d singled out a way to get viewers to spend more time with Paramount’s programming. A feed of short vertical videos, he said, was “critical to our future.”
Streaming is still trying to be TikTok
It hasn’t proven that short-form video will help.
It hasn’t proven that short-form video will help.
On Skydance’s earnings call Monday, Ellison put a name to the competition. Add up all of Paramount’s and Warner Bros. Discovery’s broadcast, cable, and streaming properties, he said, and they still trail YouTube in US television watch time, according to Nielsen. Ellison said Paramount Plus engagement had risen more than 20 percent since Skydance acquired Paramount last year. He didn’t mention how the clips feed panned out.
Over the past year, Disney Plus, Paramount Plus, Netflix, and HBO Max have introduced swipeable feeds of short videos in their mobile apps. A great scene can help a subscriber pick a show. A steady stream of clips could also get them to open the app when they only have a minute to spare. The bet is that both will make the subscription feel more worth paying for. But so far, the streamers have shared little about whether these feeds have succeeded in giving people another reason to stay subscribed.
On YouTube, a few clips can be the whole visit. YouTube accounted for a record 15.8 percent of viewing through US TV sets in August, according to Nielsen. YouTube also leads in time spent watching video on phones, where it competes with TikTok and Instagram, says Ross Benes, a senior analyst at eMarketer. The firm estimates that US adults spend a little over an hour and a half a day watching video on mobile devices and about two and a half hours on connected TVs. It counts simultaneous phone and TV viewing in both totals.
The streamers have plenty of shows to clip, but they’re up against social apps with millions of people making something new reacting to that existing content every day. A scene in a streaming app is a pitch for the full episode. On TikTok or YouTube, a creator’s reaction to that same episode can be the reason you open the app in the first place. There’s something to come back for, even when the show is between seasons.
About 43 percent of Disney Plus mobile users had interacted with Verts by October, Disney said. The feed launched in March and lets viewers swipe through scenes, save titles, or jump straight into a movie or show. Disney didn’t say whether Verts gets people to watch more movies and shows or stay subscribed longer. Verts accounted for 65 percent of user-initiated short-form video starts in the ESPN app. A highlight from last night’s game gives fans something to watch even if they have no plans to sit through a full game.
On Disney Plus, the company is turning to fan-made videos in a more direct bid to compete with social video. In August, Disney announced a US pilot with TikTok to bring clips about its movies and shows into Verts. The feed will feature a curated selection from creators who opt in, and the clips will appear on both apps. On Disney’s August earnings call, CEO Josh D’Amaro said the deal could make Disney Plus a “stickier app” where people stay longer and discover more, which “benefits our whole ecosystem.” An internal roadmap reviewed by Business Insider targets early 2027 for adding creator content and calls for sports and news clips and short-form series such as microdramas.
Disney has shown that people will use a clips feed inside a streaming app. The next question is whether the feed becomes a reason to open the app in the first place, and another reason to keep paying for it.
Paramount is looking beyond its own catalog, too. After adding a clips feed to Paramount Plus in April, it was exploring user-generated video for a possible free tier by September. On Paramount’s May earnings call, Ellison said viewers were going from clips to news, sports, and entertainment, without saying how often.
HBO Max began testing Shorts with select US iPhone users in July, letting viewers jump straight from a clip into a movie or show. Skydance’s third-quarter results excluded HBO Max because the quarter ended six days before the Warner Bros. Discovery deal closed. The company gave no usage figures for either feed on its November call.
At Netflix, Jefferies estimates that average monthly viewing fell from 66 hours per member in the first half of 2023 to 49 in the first half of 2026. On Netflix’s October earnings call, co-CEO Greg Peters pointed to lower cancellation rates in the US and globally as evidence that engagement remained healthy.
On the same call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos downplayed the role of short-form video six months after Netflix made Clips a centerpiece of its mobile redesign. He grouped short-form video with other early experiments and said Netflix’s core entertainment business still accounted for roughly 95 percent of spending and nearly all revenue. Netflix plans to roll out themed Clips feeds in 2027, but it hasn’t said whether Clips gets people to watch more.
Making money from the feed itself is harder. Benes says ads on phones generally fetch less than ads on TVs, and a short clip has less room for ad breaks than a movie or an episode. “I just don’t see it being like a big success for them,” he says. He sees a more plausible role for these feeds as something to scroll through on your phone while the TV is on.
Streamers may end up borrowing something useful from TikTok: a better way to browse. Their business still depends on what people settle in to watch.

articles.title: Starlink Mini 2 : l'antenne satellite nomade a enfin sa batterie
articles.text:
Les fuites duraient depuis l’été. Starlink a officialisé la Mini 2 dans une courte vidéo publiée sur X, le 10 novembre. Le message tient en une phrase : jusqu’à 4,5 heures de connexion sur une seule charge grâce à une batterie « à changement rapide », ou une alimentation par USB-C si une prise traîne dans le coin.
Ce qui change par rapport à la première Mini
La première Starlink Mini, lancée en 2024, avait déjà rendu l’internet par satellite transportable et accessible (on vous racontait en 2025 que l’antenne nomade passait sous les 200 euros). Mais elle avait un défaut agaçant pour un appareil censé partir à l’aventure : il fallait la brancher sur un câble d’alimentation, donc trimballer une grosse batterie externe ou rester près de la voiture.
La Mini 2 règle le problème. Selon la fiche technique publiée par Starlink, la batterie fait 71 Wh pour 490 grammes et se clipse à l’arrière de l’antenne. On peut en glisser une seconde dans le sac, vendue séparément. Elle sert aussi de batterie externe : son port USB-C délivre jusqu’à 60 W, de quoi recharger un ordinateur portable.
Le reste de la fiche technique est plutôt chouette : Wi-Fi 6 intégré couvrant jusqu’à 167 m², certification IP67 contre la poussière et l’immersion, un pas de vis standard d’appareil photo pour la fixer sur un trépied, une béquille, et une connexion annoncée en 60 secondes environ, à condition d’avoir une vue dégagée sur le ciel. L’antenne mesure 263 × 314 mm pour 23,1 mm d’épaisseur et pèse 1,6 kg avec batterie et béquille.
Plus lourde, et toujours pas en France
Ce gain d’autonomie se paie sur la balance : la première Mini pesait autour de 1,1 kg. La Mini 2 prend donc environ un demi-kilo de plus, mais gagne en finesse. En van ou en bateau, peu importe, mais pour une randonnée de plusieurs jours, ça se discute.
Les fuites de l’été, signées par le chercheur Oleg Kutkov, évoquaient aussi un nombre d’éléments d’antenne en légère baisse et un débit montant plus modeste, selon Notebookcheck. Starlink n’affiche aucun chiffre de débit sur sa page : il faudra attendre les premiers tests pour savoir si l’autonomie s’est payée en vitesse.
Côté prix, Starlink n’a rien annoncé. Le site spécialisé DishyTech a repéré dans l’API de Starlink un « Mini 2 Beta Kit » à 249 dollars et une batterie à 50 dollars, des tarifs de phase de test qui peuvent encore bouger.
Pour la France, il faudra patienter : les précommandes sont réservées à certains clients américains invités par Starlink, qui promet une ouverture à « plus de clients et de pays » sans calendrier.

articles.title: Imagem histórica de buraco negro resiste a novo teste científico
articles.text:
Uma análise independente dos dados usados para produzir a primeira imagem de um buraco negro, divulgada em 2019, confirmou a estrutura brilhante em forma de anel ao redor de uma região escura. Os resultados foram publicados em 11 de novembro na revista científica Nature.
O estudo corrobora amplamente as descobertas originais do Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), mas mantém em aberto questões sobre a distribuição do brilho e os métodos utilizados para reconstruir a imagem.
Reanálise reforça resultado de 2019
A colaboração internacional EHT apresentou, em 2019, a primeira imagem da sombra de um buraco negro. O registro mostrava um anel brilhante ao redor de uma região central escura, estrutura compatível com as previsões da teoria da relatividade geral de Albert Einstein.
Para produzir a imagem, o projeto combina observações simultâneas de radiotelescópios instalados em diferentes continentes. Juntos, os equipamentos funcionam como um único telescópio virtual, com resolução equivalente à de uma antena com dimensões próximas às da Terra.
A reconstrução, porém, enfrenta limitações. Como os radiotelescópios não cobrem toda a superfície terrestre, existem lacunas nas observações, que precisam ser compensadas por métodos matemáticos e modelos computacionais. As escolhas feitas nesse processo podem influenciar o resultado final.
Foi justamente esse aspecto que motivou questionamentos sobre a imagem original. A partir de 2022, o astrofísico Junichiro Makino, da Universidade de Kobe, no Japão, e seus colaboradores passaram a contestar as conclusões do EHT. Ao aplicar uma das técnicas utilizadas pela colaboração, mas com premissas diferentes, a equipe obteve uma imagem em que as emissões de rádio apareciam concentradas em uma estrutura irregular, sem formar claramente um anel.
Nova análise mantém a estrutura anular
Diante dessas divergências, Samuel Lai, astrofísico da Organização de Pesquisa Científica e Industrial da Commonwealth (CSIRO), da Austrália, e seus colaboradores desenvolveram métodos próprios para examinar novamente os dados. Os resultados coincidiram amplamente com os apresentados pelo EHT em 2019.
Segundo Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, astrofísico da CSIRO e coautor do estudo, diferentes modelos utilizados para orientar uma rede neural podem levar a reconstruções ligeiramente distintas.
“Dependendo do seu modelo prévio, você pode seguir direções um pouco diferentes”, explicou. Apesar dessas variações, o pesquisador destacou que a nova equipe também encontrou uma estrutura semelhante a um anel.
Divergências ainda não foram resolvidas
Makino, porém, continua questionando os resultados. Uma das diferenças apontadas pelo pesquisador está na localização dos pontos mais brilhantes ao redor da estrutura central, que muda conforme o método de reconstrução utilizado.
“Se ambos os métodos são matematicamente sólidos, é um pouco difícil entender por quê”, afirmou.
Assim, a nova análise reforça a existência de uma estrutura geral em forma de anel, mas não estabelece que todos os detalhes da imagem estejam definitivamente confirmados. A distribuição do brilho continua sendo um dos pontos de divergência entre as diferentes reconstruções.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Más de 35.000 aplicaciones creadas con Grok quedaron abiertas a cualquiera, con datos médicos y de empleados
articles.text:
Una firma de seguridad informática encontró que más de 35.000 aplicaciones creadas con Grok, el asistente de inteligencia artificial de Elon Musk, podían abrirse sin iniciar sesión. Entre ellas había documentos confidenciales de la propia empresa, resultados médicos de pacientes y listas de empleados de compañías grandes.
La firma, Claroc, publicó el hallazgo el 10 de noviembre. Probó 43.551 direcciones de aplicaciones publicadas con Grok: 37.571 seguían en línea y 35.578 (94,7%) se abrían para cualquiera, sin pedir identificación. Solo 1.993 respondían con un error de acceso denegado.
Claroc calculó que una de cada 10 aplicaciones abiertas contenía material sensible, datos internos de empresas o información personal, y que cerca del 2% guardaba material de gravedad alta o crítica. La mayoría eran juegos, páginas de presentación y calculadoras.
Grok permite describir una aplicación en el chat para que el asistente la programe y luego publicarla en una dirección propia, que termina en grok.me. Según Claroc, al publicar una aplicación en su cuenta de prueba, la opción preseleccionada era “cualquiera con el enlace”.
Los documentos de SpaceXSI y de empresas grandes
SpaceXSI es el nombre de la compañía que surgió de la fusión de SpaceX y xAI, según Ars Technica. Claroc encontró 24 aplicaciones abiertas creadas por empleados de SpaceXSI y de X: un plan de incorporación confidencial para un nuevo vendedor, un mapa de 594 cuentas de clientes y varias propuestas publicitarias, una de ellas dirigida a una agencia del gobierno de Estados Unidos.
Entre los datos de otros usuarios, la firma confirmó a mano una lista de más de 3.500 empleados de un grupo hospitalario, el resumen de cuidados intensivos de un paciente con análisis e imágenes, y el listado de los bomberos de un cuartel con nombre y número de placa. También halló una planilla de horas cuyo código mostraba contraseñas de 18 cuentas en texto plano.
Además de SpaceXSI y X, 30 organizaciones identificables tenían datos internos expuestos. 26 tienen más de mil empleados y seis figuran entre las 500 mayores empresas de Estados Unidos. Claroc no las nombra. Ars Technica cita casos como un trabajo de 3.784 exámenes médicos de obreros de una constructora peruana.
Cómo se encontraron sin conocer los enlaces
Los investigadores no recibieron los enlaces: los hallaron en bases de datos públicas de consultas DNS, el sistema que traduce una dirección web en el servidor donde está alojada.
Como cada aplicación tiene su propio nombre bajo grok.me, ese nombre queda registrado la primera vez que alguien lo abre, y cualquier suscriptor de esos servicios puede buscarlo por patrón.
El investigador Asaf Aprozper, de Claroc, explicó a Ars Technica que otras plataformas para crear aplicaciones, como Lovable, Bolt y Replit, también dan a cada aplicación su propia dirección y dejan el mismo rastro. Claroc comparó con ChatGPT, que en su prueba dejó la opción “solo yo” por defecto al compartir una aplicación.
Meta ya suspendió una función parecida en Muse, su agente de IA, tras detectarse una filtración similar, según Ars Technica. En julio, un investigador había mostrado que Grok Build subía repositorios completos de código a un servidor de la empresa, y Musk dijo entonces que se borrarían esos datos.
La respuesta de SpaceXSI
Claroc avisó a SpaceXSI el domingo 8 de noviembre. Al no recibir respuesta, un integrante de la firma etiquetó en X a Musk y al responsable de Grok, Matt Palmer, según Ars Technica. La empresa empezó a retirar los enlaces de sus propias aplicaciones pocas horas después de que Ars le enviara preguntas, y las 24 devolvían un error de aplicación no encontrada.
SpaceXSI dijo a un periodista que cubre el caso que las aplicaciones de Grok son privadas hasta que su creador decide compartirlas y que publicar exige varios pasos.
Añadió que las cuentas de sus empleados quedan en “solo tú” por defecto. Claroc respondió que sus 24 aplicaciones estaban abiertas igualmente y que la opción por defecto para usuarios comunes sigue siendo “cualquiera con el enlace”.

articles.title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
articles.text:
As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s emphasis on zero waste puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, less than 7% of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over 2 billion tons of trash per year — a figure that could nearly double by 2050.
AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills.
“A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.”
See how four members of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation.
Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products.
The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product.
“The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.”
The company uses NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%.
In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%.
At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items.
EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia.
“Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.”
EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on NVIDIA data center GPUs, optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.
Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries.
Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it.
U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second.
“Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.”
Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six.
Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of food-grade plastics by 12%. Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants.
Europe generates nearly 7 million tons of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried.
reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category.
“Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.”
As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with NVIDIA TensorRT software and running on NVIDIA Jetson modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud.
The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe.
